questions.stem: A rhombus has sides of length 10, and its shorter diagonal is also 10. What is the area of the rhombus?
questions.explain: The shorter diagonal splits the rhombus into two equilateral triangles of side 10. Each has height 5√3, so the longer diagonal is 2 × 5√3 = 10√3. Area = ½ × d₁ × d₂ = ½ × 10 × 10√3 = 50√3 (or two triangles of 25√3 each). 100 is side², which is only right for a square; 25√3 is just one of the two triangles; 100√3 is the product of the diagonals without the ½.

questions.stem: A ship's ballast tank can be filled by its intake pump in 6 hours and emptied by its drain in 9 hours. The tank starts empty and the intake pump runs alone for 2 hours. Then the drain is accidentally opened as well, and both run together. How many more hours does it take to fill the tank?
options: 18 hours
12 hours
16 hours
2.4 hours
questions.explain: In the first 2 hours the pump fills 2/6 = 1/3 of the tank, leaving 2/3. With both open the net rate is 1/6 − 1/9 = 3/18 − 2/18 = 1/18 tank per hour, so 2/3 takes (2/3) × 18 = 12 hours. 18 hours fills a whole empty tank at the net rate; 16 hours subtracts the first 2 hours from 18; 2.4 hours adds the drain's rate instead of subtracting it (2/3 ÷ 5/18).

questions.stem: Crew A can repaint a hangar floor in 10 days and Crew B can do it in 15 days. Both crews work together for 3 days, then Crew A is reassigned and Crew B finishes the job alone. How many days does the whole job take?
options: 7.5 days
6 days
13.5 days
10.5 days
questions.explain: Together: 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 of the job per day, so 3 days complete 3/6 = 1/2. Crew B does the other 1/2 at 1/15 per day: 7.5 days. Total = 3 + 7.5 = 10.5 days. 7.5 days is only Crew B's solo stretch; 6 days is the time if both worked the whole job together; 13.5 days credits only Crew A's work (3/10) for the first 3 days, leaving 7/10 for B (10.5 days) plus 3.

questions.stem: A patrol boat must check a buoy 60 nautical miles from its base and be back within 5 hours. It travels out at 20 knots, spends 30 minutes at the buoy, then returns. What speed must it average on the way back to arrive exactly at the 5-hour mark?
options: 30 knots
24 knots
40 knots
28 knots
questions.explain: Outbound time = 60 ÷ 20 = 3 hours. With the 0.5-hour stop, 5 − 3 − 0.5 = 1.5 hours are left for the 60-mile return, so speed = 60 ÷ 1.5 = 40 knots. 30 knots forgets the stop (60 ÷ 2); 24 knots is the overall average, 120 ÷ 5; 28 knots averages speeds, solving (20 + v)/2 = 24, which is never valid when the times differ.

questions.stem: Ship A leaves port at 0800 heading due north at 12 knots. Ship B leaves the same port at 0900 heading due east at 20 knots. How many hours after Ship B departs are the two ships 100 nautical miles apart?
options: 4 hours
5 hours
2.75 hours
3.125 hours
questions.explain: Let t be the hours after 0900. Ship A has sailed 12(t + 1) north and Ship B 20t east, at right angles, so the gap is a hypotenuse. Try t = 4: A = 60, B = 80, and √(60² + 80²) = 100 ✓ (a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 20). 5 hours is measured from Ship A's departure instead of Ship B's; 2.75 hours adds the distances, 12(t + 1) + 20t = 100, as if they sailed in a straight line; 3.125 hours is 100 ÷ (12 + 20), which ignores both the right angle and the head start.

questions.stem: A patrol aircraft with an airspeed of 250 mph flies straight out from an island air station into a steady 50-mph headwind, then turns and flies straight back with the same wind behind it. It has fuel for exactly 5 hours of flying. How far out can it fly and still make it back?
options: 625 miles
600 miles
500 miles
750 miles
questions.explain: Groundspeed out = 250 − 50 = 200 mph; back = 250 + 50 = 300 mph. Time: d/200 + d/300 = 5, so 3d/600 + 2d/600 = 5, 5d = 3,000 and d = 600 miles. Check: 3 hours out + 2 hours back = 5 ✓. 625 ignores the wind (250 × 2.5); 500 splits the time equally and uses the headwind speed (200 × 2.5); 750 splits the time equally and uses the tailwind speed (300 × 2.5).

questions.stem: A 50-gallon cooling tank holds a mixture that is 20% antifreeze. Some of the mixture is drained and replaced with pure antifreeze so that the tank, still holding 50 gallons, becomes 40% antifreeze. How many gallons must be drained and replaced?
options: 12.5 gallons
10 gallons
16⅔ gallons
25 gallons
questions.explain: Let x be the gallons drained. The tank starts with 0.20 × 50 = 10 gal of antifreeze; draining removes 0.2x and refilling adds x. So 10 − 0.2x + x = 0.40 × 50 = 20, giving 0.8x = 10 and x = 12.5 gallons. 10 gallons forgets that the drained liquid already contained antifreeze; 16⅔ gallons adds antifreeze without draining, (10 + x)/(50 + x) = 0.4; 25 gallons assumes replacing half the tank doubles the strength (it would actually give 60%).

questions.stem: A squadron's annual fuel budget starts at $5,000,000. In year 1 it is cut by 20%. In year 2 it is increased by 15% of the year-1 figure. In year 3 it is cut by 10% of the year-2 figure. What is the year-3 budget?
questions.explain: Apply each change to the previous year's figure: 5,000,000 × 0.80 = 4,000,000; × 1.15 = 4,600,000; × 0.90 = 4,140,000. $4,250,000 adds the percents (−20 + 15 − 10 = −15%) and applies them once; $4,600,000 stops after year 2; $4,275,000 takes the year-2 increase as 15% of the ORIGINAL budget (4,000,000 + 750,000 = 4,750,000, then × 0.9).

questions.stem: An amount deposited at 8% interest compounded annually grows to $11,664 after 2 years. How much was deposited?
questions.explain: Balance = P × 1.08², and 1.08² = 1.1664, so P = 11,664 ÷ 1.1664 = $10,000. Check: 10,000 → 10,800 → 11,664 ✓. $10,800 divides by 1.08 only once (that is the balance after year 1); $9,797.76 takes 16% off the final amount instead of dividing; $10,055.17 divides by 1.16, treating it as simple interest.

questions.stem: Two flight-school classes take the same exam. Class A has 18 students and averages 74. Class B averages 84. The two classes together average 78. How many students are in Class B?
questions.explain: Total points: 18(74) + 84n = 78(18 + n). So 1,332 + 84n = 1,404 + 78n, giving 6n = 72 and n = 12. (Balance view: A sits 4 below 78 and B sits 6 above, so the class sizes are in the ratio 6 : 4, and B = 18 × 4/6 = 12.) 27 flips that ratio; 18 assumes equal classes, which would give an average of 79; 30 is the combined total of both classes.

questions.stem: A Navy commander is 3 times as old as her son. In 12 years she will be twice as old as he will be then. How old will the son be when his mother is exactly 1.5 times his age?
questions.explain: Let the son be s and the mother 3s. Then 3s + 12 = 2(s + 12), so s = 12 and the mother is 36. Their age gap is always 24. When she is 1.5 times his age, 1.5a − a = 24, so a = 48 (mother 72). Check: 72 ÷ 48 = 1.5 ✓. 36 is the number of years from now, not his age; 24 is his age at the 'twice' point in 12 years; 72 is the mother's age at that time.

questions.stem: A jar holds 32 coins, all nickels, dimes and quarters, worth $5.00 in total. There are twice as many dimes as nickels. How many quarters are in the jar?
questions.explain: Let n be the nickels; then dimes = 2n and quarters = 32 − 3n. In cents: 5n + 10(2n) + 25(32 − 3n) = 500, so 25n + 800 − 75n = 500, 50n = 300 and n = 6. Quarters = 32 − 18 = 14. Check: 30¢ + $1.20 + $3.50 = $5.00 ✓. 12 is the number of dimes; 18 is nickels plus dimes; 20 is $5.00 ÷ 25¢, as if every coin were a quarter.

questions.stem: A jet cruises at 480 knots on a 360-nautical-mile leg and burns fuel at 2,400 pounds per hour. For this problem, the fuel weighs 6 pounds per gallon. How many gallons of fuel does the leg use?
options: 400 gallons
180 gallons
10,800 gallons
300 gallons
questions.explain: Time = 360 ÷ 480 = 0.75 hour (45 minutes). Fuel = 2,400 × 0.75 = 1,800 pounds, and 1,800 ÷ 6 = 300 gallons. 400 gallons uses a full hour of burn (2,400 ÷ 6); 180 gallons writes 45 minutes as 0.45 hour; 10,800 gallons multiplies pounds by 6 instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A jet's velocity–time graph rises in a straight line from 0 m/s at t = 0 to 60 m/s at t = 10 s, stays level at 60 m/s until t = 30 s, then falls in a straight line to 0 m/s at t = 40 s. What is the jet's average speed over the 40 seconds?
options: 30 m/s
60 m/s
40 m/s
45 m/s
questions.explain: Distance is the area under the graph: ½(10)(60) + (20)(60) + ½(10)(60) = 300 + 1,200 + 300 = 1,800 m. Average speed = 1,800 ÷ 40 = 45 m/s. 30 m/s averages the lowest and highest speeds; 60 m/s is the top speed; 40 m/s averages the three sections' speeds (30, 60, 30) without weighting by how long each lasted.

questions.stem: A ship's graph of distance from port (nautical miles) against time (hours) is a straight line from (0, 0) to (2, 30), is horizontal from t = 2 to t = 3, then is a straight line from (3, 30) down to (5, 0). What is the ship's average speed over the 5 hours?
options: 12 knots
0 knots
15 knots
6 knots
questions.explain: The graph shows the ship going 30 miles out, stopping for an hour, then coming 30 miles back to port. Total distance traveled = 30 + 30 = 60 nautical miles, so average speed = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 knots. 0 knots is the average VELOCITY (it ends where it started), not speed; 15 knots is the speed on either moving leg; 6 knots counts only the one-way 30 miles.

questions.stem: A car's velocity–time graph rises in a straight line from 0 m/s at t = 0 to 24 m/s at t = 8 s, then stays level at 24 m/s. At what time has the car traveled a total of 240 m?
options: t = 10 s
t = 20 s
t = 14 s
t = 6 s
questions.explain: Area of the first triangle: ½ × 8 × 24 = 96 m by t = 8 s. The remaining 240 − 96 = 144 m at a steady 24 m/s takes 6 s, so t = 8 + 6 = 14 s. 10 s assumes 24 m/s from the start (240 ÷ 24); 20 s uses the first section's average speed, 12 m/s, the whole way; 6 s is only the time on the level section, forgetting to add the first 8 s.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Contractor personnel must follow every command safety instruction while working at the command.
Personnel on temporary additional duty are exempt from command safety instructions.
A visitor who has been briefed on a work area's hazards may enter it without an escort.
Whether a contractor is bound by a particular safety instruction depends on the terms of the contract.
questions.passage: Command safety instructions apply to all military and civilian personnel assigned to the command, including personnel on temporary additional duty. Contractor personnel are bound by these instructions only to the extent specified in their contracts. Visitors shall be briefed on the hazards of any work area they enter and shall be escorted while in that area.
questions.explain: 'Contractor personnel are bound by these instructions only to the extent specified in their contracts' — the contract decides. 'Every instruction' over-claims beyond what a contract may specify; personnel on temporary additional duty are expressly INCLUDED, not exempt; and visitors must be briefed AND escorted, so the briefing does not replace the escort.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: A brake rider is required for every aircraft tow ashore.
An aircraft towed across level ground ashore in a 20-knot wind does not require a brake rider.
A tow director is not needed when a qualified brake rider is in the cockpit.
Aboard ship, a brake rider is required only while the ship is underway.
questions.passage: Before any aircraft is towed, a qualified tow director shall be present and in charge of the move. Aboard ship, a brake rider is required in the cockpit for every tow, whether the ship is underway or in port. Ashore, a brake rider is required only when the aircraft is towed on a sloping surface or when the wind exceeds 30 knots.
questions.explain: Ashore, a brake rider is required 'only when' the surface slopes or the wind 'exceeds 30 knots'; level ground in 20 knots meets neither condition. 'Every tow ashore' drops the 'only when' condition; a tow director 'shall be present' before ANY tow; and aboard ship the rule applies 'whether the ship is underway or in port'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Some risk may remain after operational risk management has been properly applied.
Any risk remaining after controls are applied must be elevated to the commanding officer.
The aim of operational risk management is to remove all risk from a mission.
Staff officers may accept risks that fall within their own area of expertise.
questions.passage: Operational risk management is not intended to eliminate risk; it is intended to reduce risk to a level that is acceptable in light of the benefits of the mission. A risk that cannot be reduced to an acceptable level at one level of command shall be elevated to the level that has the authority to accept it. Accepting risk is therefore a command decision, not a staff function.
questions.explain: ORM 'is not intended to eliminate risk' but to reduce it to 'a level that is acceptable', so acceptable risk can remain. Only risk that CANNOT be reduced to an acceptable level is elevated, and to whichever level has the authority — not necessarily the CO; 'remove all risk' reverses the first sentence; and accepting risk is 'a command decision, not a staff function'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Sea fog forms most often during the winter months.
Sea fog forms when cool air moves over warmer water.
A strong wind will not necessarily clear sea fog.
Fog that forms over land on calm nights is denser than sea fog.
questions.passage: Sea fog commonly forms when warm, moist air moves over cooler water. The air is chilled from below until it reaches its dew point, and water vapor condenses into droplets near the surface. Because the process depends on the air being in motion, sea fog can persist even in winds strong enough to scatter fog that forms over land on calm nights.
questions.explain: Sea fog 'can persist even in winds strong enough to scatter' land fog, so wind does not necessarily clear it. The passage never names a season or compares density, and it says WARM air moves over COOLER water — the second choice reverses the direction.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The senior person present may remove classified material whenever the security manager is unavailable.
Classified material can, in some cases, be removed before the security manager knows of the removal.
Written approval from the security manager is required for every removal of classified material.
The security manager must approve an emergency removal in writing after it has taken place.
questions.passage: Classified material shall not be removed from the command without the written approval of the security manager. In an emergency that threatens the material with destruction, the senior person present may direct its removal to a safer location without prior approval. The security manager shall be notified of any such removal as soon as practicable afterward.
questions.explain: In an emergency threatening destruction, removal may happen 'without prior approval', and the security manager is notified 'afterward' — so the removal can come first. The exception is triggered by an emergency, not by the manager being unavailable; 'every removal' ignores the exception; and after the fact the manager is only NOTIFIED, not asked for written approval.

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: A department instruction may amend the manual if the executive officer agrees.
The executive officer approves all changes to the manual.
A division instruction takes precedence over the manual once the instruction has been reviewed.
While a conflict remains unresolved, the manual's provision rather than the division instruction's is the one in effect.
questions.passage: The command's standard organization and regulations manual is the basic directive for the internal organization of the command. Department and division instructions shall be consistent with it, and where a conflict exists, the manual governs until the executive officer resolves the conflict. The manual is reviewed annually and may be changed only with the approval of the commanding officer.
questions.explain: 'Where a conflict exists, the manual governs until the executive officer resolves the conflict.' The manual 'may be changed only with the approval of the commanding officer', which defeats both the department-instruction choice and the executive-officer choice; and 'takes precedence over the manual' reverses which document governs.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Langley was the first aircraft carrier in any navy.
Langley was built from the keel up as an aircraft carrier.
Some techniques used on later carriers were first worked out aboard Langley.
Langley's coal holds were converted to carry fuel for her aircraft.
questions.passage: In 1922 the collier Jupiter was recommissioned as USS Langley, the US Navy's first aircraft carrier. A flight deck was built over her original hull, and her coal holds were converted to store aircraft and spare parts. Langley served largely as an experimental ship, where pilots and deck crews developed launch, recovery and handling techniques later used aboard larger carriers.
questions.explain: Crews aboard Langley 'developed launch, recovery and handling techniques later used aboard larger carriers.' The passage calls her the US Navy's first carrier, not the world's; she was a converted collier, not built as a carrier; and the coal holds stored 'aircraft and spare parts', not fuel.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Passengers may remain aboard during hot refueling in some circumstances.
Hot refueling may be done at any site as long as the aircraft's weapons are safe.
The aircraft commander must off-load passengers before every hot refueling.
Hot refueling is the preferred way to fuel an aircraft that is carrying weapons.
questions.passage: Hot refueling, the fueling of an aircraft with its engines running, is permitted only at sites designated for that purpose and only when the aircraft's weapons are safe. Personnel not directly involved in the evolution shall remain clear of the area. Passengers shall be off-loaded before hot refueling begins unless the aircraft commander determines that operational necessity requires them to remain aboard.
questions.explain: Passengers are off-loaded 'unless the aircraft commander determines that operational necessity requires them to remain aboard' — so sometimes they stay. Hot refueling requires a designated site AND safe weapons, not either one; 'every hot refueling' ignores the 'unless' clause; and nothing calls it 'preferred'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Subordinate commanders plan and direct the overall effort.
Plans made under this principle rarely fail to anticipate events.
The overall commander decides how each subordinate task will be carried out.
The approach is weakened if subordinates do not understand what the commander intends.
questions.passage: Under the principle of centralized control and decentralized execution, a single commander plans and directs the overall effort, while subordinate commanders decide how to carry out their assigned tasks. The approach depends on subordinates understanding the commander's intent, since they will often face situations that the plan did not foresee.
questions.explain: The approach 'depends on subordinates understanding the commander's intent', so without that understanding it is weakened. Planning and directing the overall effort is the single commander's job (reversed); subordinates 'will often face situations that the plan did not foresee' (contradicted); and subordinates, not the overall commander, decide how tasks are carried out.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Thunder can be heard before the flash is seen if the strike is very close.
A longer gap between flash and thunder indicates a more distant strike.
Thunder is produced when the flash of light strikes the clouds.
Lightning is hotter than any other natural phenomenon on Earth.
questions.passage: Lightning heats the air in its path to temperatures several times hotter than the surface of the sun. The sudden heating makes the air expand faster than the speed of sound, producing thunder. Because light travels far faster than sound, an observer sees the flash before hearing the thunder, and the delay between them grows with the observer's distance from the strike.
questions.explain: 'The delay between them grows with the observer's distance from the strike.' The flash is always seen first because light is faster; thunder comes from the rapidly expanding heated air, not light hitting clouds; and the passage compares lightning only with the sun's surface, not with every natural phenomenon.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A watchstander whose relief has already arrived on station may still be responsible for the watch.
An incapacitated watchstander may leave the station as soon as the condition has been reported.
The officer of the deck must personally brief every relieving watchstander.
A relief is complete as soon as the relieving watchstander arrives at the station.
questions.passage: Watchstanders shall not leave their stations until properly relieved. A relief is not complete until the relieving watchstander has been briefed on the status of the watch and has stated that he or she assumes the watch. A watchstander who becomes incapacitated shall report the condition to the officer of the deck, who will arrange a relief.
questions.explain: A relief 'is not complete until the relieving watchstander has been briefed… and has stated that he or she assumes the watch' — arrival alone does not transfer the watch. The incapacitated watchstander reports and the OOD 'will arrange a relief'; nothing permits leaving first. The passage never says who gives the brief, and 'complete on arrival' contradicts the second sentence.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: Earplugs alone satisfy the requirement on the flight deck during flight operations.
All personnel in the hangar bay must wear hearing protection at all times.
A maintainer passing 30 feet from a running engine for only a few seconds must wear hearing protection.
Hearing protection is required only during flight operations.
questions.passage: Personnel shall wear hearing protection whenever they are within 50 feet of an operating aircraft engine, regardless of the duration of exposure. Double hearing protection, consisting of earplugs worn under earmuffs, is required on the flight deck during flight operations. Personnel in the hangar bay are not required to wear hearing protection unless they are within 50 feet of an operating engine or in a posted hazardous noise area.
questions.explain: Protection is required within 50 feet of an operating engine 'regardless of the duration of exposure', so a few seconds at 30 feet still counts. The flight deck requires earplugs UNDER earmuffs; hangar-bay personnel are 'not required… unless' a condition applies; and the 50-foot rule applies at any time, not only during flight operations.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: An aircraft flying at high speed cannot stall.
Stalls occur only when the nose is pitched well above the horizon.
Every type of wing has the same critical angle of attack.
Maintaining a high airspeed does not by itself prevent a stall.
questions.passage: An aircraft stalls when its wing exceeds the critical angle of attack, the angle between the wing's chord line and the relative wind beyond which smooth airflow over the upper surface breaks down. Because the stall is caused by angle of attack rather than by airspeed, a wing can stall at any airspeed and in any flight attitude.
questions.explain: A wing 'can stall at any airspeed and in any flight attitude', because the cause is angle of attack, so speed alone is no guarantee. 'Cannot stall at high speed' and 'only nose-high' both contradict that sentence, and the passage never compares critical angles between wings.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Once authority for a task has been delegated, the subordinate alone is responsible for its outcome.
A commanding officer can remain accountable for a task that a subordinate was authorized to perform.
A commanding officer may not delegate authority over matters affecting the safety of the command.
Subordinates bear no responsibility for duties that have been delegated to them.
questions.passage: The commanding officer's responsibility for the command is absolute. Although the commanding officer may delegate authority to subordinates for the performance of duties, such delegation does not relieve the commanding officer of responsibility for the safety, well-being and efficiency of the command.
questions.explain: Delegation 'does not relieve the commanding officer of responsibility', so the CO stays accountable for delegated tasks. 'The subordinate alone' contradicts that; the passage does not forbid delegating safety-related authority — it says delegation leaves responsibility in place; and it says nothing about whether subordinates also bear responsibility.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Land-based forces cannot be stationed abroad.
Forward-deployed naval forces are positioned near a crisis in order to escalate it.
A naval force in international waters does not need a host nation's agreement to be positioned near a crisis.
Host nations usually refuse requests to station land-based forces on their territory.
questions.passage: Naval forces derive much of their value from their ability to operate in international waters without the permission of other nations. A forward-deployed force can be positioned near a developing crisis, signaling resolve while leaving national leaders free to escalate, hold or withdraw. Land-based forces, by contrast, usually require the agreement of a host nation before they can be stationed abroad.
questions.explain: Naval forces 'operate in international waters without the permission of other nations' and can be 'positioned near a developing crisis'. Land forces 'usually require' agreement — not that they cannot be stationed abroad, and not that nations usually refuse; and leaders remain free to 'escalate, hold or withdraw', so escalation is only one option.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Equipment bearing a caution tag can be operated under certain conditions.
A caution tag prohibits all operation of the tagged equipment.
Equipment with a danger tag may be operated once the instructions on the tag have been read.
Danger tags are used only on electrical equipment.
questions.passage: Tag-out procedures protect personnel by ensuring that equipment cannot be operated in a way that endangers them while work is in progress. A danger tag prohibits operation of the tagged equipment. A caution tag permits operation, but only after the operator has read and complied with the special instructions written on the tag.
questions.explain: A caution tag 'permits operation, but only after the operator has read and complied with' its instructions — operation under conditions. Prohibiting operation is what the DANGER tag does (swapped); reading instructions is the caution-tag condition, not a way around a danger tag; and the passage never limits danger tags to electrical equipment.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A pilot who loses communication should always return to the route filed in the flight plan.
The filed route is flown only when neither an assigned route nor an expected route has been given.
The pilot should fly an expected route even if an assigned route had been received.
A loss of radio communication requires the pilot to land at the nearest suitable airfield.
questions.passage: A pilot who loses radio communication while flying under instrument flight rules shall continue on the route assigned in the last clearance received. If no route was assigned, the pilot shall fly the route that the controller advised may be expected in a further clearance. If no such route was given either, the pilot shall fly the route filed in the flight plan.
questions.explain: The passage sets a priority order — assigned route, then expected route, then the filed route 'if no such route was given either'. 'Always the filed route' and 'expected over assigned' both break that order, and landing at the nearest airfield may be familiar from other procedures but is never stated here.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Members who are on leave during a sweep are excused from testing for that sweep.
Hospitalized members are permanently excused from urinalysis testing.
Members returning from leave must be tested within exactly 24 hours.
A member hospitalized during one sweep may still be tested in a later inspection.
questions.passage: Command urinalysis testing applies to all active-duty members of the command. Members who are on leave on the day of a unit sweep shall be tested upon their return, normally within 24 hours. Members who are hospitalized are excused from that sweep but are not excused from subsequent inspections.
questions.explain: Hospitalized members 'are not excused from subsequent inspections'. Members on leave 'shall be tested upon their return', so they are not excused; the hospital excusal covers only 'that sweep', not permanently; and 'normally within 24 hours' does not mean 'exactly'.

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: If fresh water and seawater are cooled side by side, the fresh water will begin to freeze first.
Newly formed sea ice is saltier than the water around it.
Dissolved salt helps ice crystals form more quickly.
Seawater cannot freeze under natural conditions.
questions.passage: Salt water freezes at a lower temperature than fresh water because dissolved salt interferes with the formation of ice crystals. When sea ice forms, most of the salt is pushed out of the growing crystals, so newly formed sea ice is far less salty than the water around it.
questions.explain: Salt water 'freezes at a lower temperature than fresh water', so as both cool, fresh water reaches its freezing point first. New sea ice is 'far less salty' than the surrounding water; salt 'interferes with' crystal formation rather than helping it; and the passage describes sea ice forming, so seawater can freeze.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A command may designate a smoking area inside a hangar if it is at least 50 feet from the entrance.
Smoking is permitted anywhere on the installation that is at least 50 feet from a building entrance.
A spot 60 feet from a building entrance could still be unsuitable for a designated smoking area.
Every command is required to designate at least one smoking area.
questions.passage: Smoking is prohibited in all aircraft hangars, fuel farms and ordnance handling areas. Commands may designate smoking areas elsewhere on the installation, provided they are at least 50 feet from building entrances and air intakes. No smoking area may be designated within any space where fuel or ordnance is stored.
questions.explain: A designated area must be 50 feet from entrances AND air intakes, and outside hangars and fuel or ordnance spaces — so distance from an entrance alone does not make a spot suitable. Hangars are prohibited outright; smoking is allowed only in DESIGNATED areas, not anywhere 50 feet out; and commands 'may' designate areas, which is not a requirement.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The more powerful a force is, the more effectively it deters.
Two equally capable forces could differ in how well they deter an adversary.
Demonstrations of resolve matter more to deterrence than capable forces do.
Deterrence fails whenever an adversary doubts that a force is capable.
questions.passage: Deterrence depends not only on possessing capable forces but on an adversary's belief that those forces will be used. A capability that an adversary judges will never be employed deters little, however powerful it may be. For this reason, demonstrations of readiness and resolve are as much a part of deterrence as the forces themselves.
questions.explain: Deterrence also depends on 'an adversary's belief that those forces will be used', so equal capability can deter unequally. Power alone 'deters little' if never expected to be used, which defeats the first choice; resolve is 'as much a part' as forces — equal, not greater; and the passage concerns doubt about USE, not about capability, and makes no 'whenever' rule.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: The ordnance officer may permit loading during a nearby electrical storm if the mission is urgent.
Loading may resume as soon as the storm stops producing lightning.
Armament switches must be verified safe after the ordnance has been loaded.
Loading halted for a storm four miles away could resume once the storm was six miles away.
questions.passage: Before ordnance is loaded on an aircraft, the aircraft shall be grounded and its armament switches verified in the safe position. Loading shall stop immediately if an electrical storm is reported within five miles of the loading area and shall not resume until the storm has moved beyond that distance. The ordnance officer may not waive these requirements.
questions.explain: Loading 'shall not resume until the storm has moved beyond' five miles; at six miles it has. The ordnance officer 'may not waive these requirements'; the passage ties resumption to distance, not to whether lightning stops; and switches are verified safe BEFORE loading.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Intelligence revealed the exact position of the Japanese carriers before the battle.
The United States won at Midway because its carriers outnumbered the Japanese carriers.
Advance knowledge of the enemy's plans did not by itself locate the enemy carriers.
Patrol aircraft were unnecessary once intelligence had identified the Japanese objective.
questions.passage: At the Battle of Midway in June 1942, American commanders had intelligence indicating the Japanese objective and approximate timing, which allowed US carriers to be positioned in advance northeast of the atoll. Intelligence could not, however, give the exact position of the Japanese carriers on the morning of the battle; that information came from patrol aircraft that sighted them at sea.
questions.explain: Intelligence gave the objective and timing but 'could not… give the exact position of the Japanese carriers'; that came from patrol aircraft. The first choice contradicts this, the last choice contradicts the role of the patrol sightings, and carrier numbers are never mentioned.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The person who conducts the fitness assessment is not the person who decides whether a failing member is processed for separation.
The command fitness leader is elected by the members of the command.
A member who fails the assessment is automatically processed for separation.
The commanding officer conducts the physical fitness assessment and maintains its records.
questions.passage: The command fitness leader is appointed in writing by the commanding officer and advises the command on all matters relating to physical readiness. The fitness leader conducts the physical fitness assessment and maintains its records, but does not determine whether a member who fails the assessment will be processed for separation; that decision rests with the commanding officer.
questions.explain: The fitness leader 'conducts the physical fitness assessment' but the separation decision 'rests with the commanding officer' — two different people. The fitness leader is 'appointed in writing', not elected; nothing says processing is automatic — it is a decision; and the fitness leader, not the CO, conducts the assessment and keeps the records.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: In a head-on meeting, the smaller vessel alters course to starboard while the larger holds its course.
An overtaking vessel must always alter course to starboard.
In a head-on meeting, each vessel alters course to port.
Two power-driven vessels meeting head-on will pass port side to port side if both follow the rule.
questions.passage: When two power-driven vessels meet on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses so as to involve risk of collision, each shall alter course to starboard so that each passes on the port side of the other. This rule applies only when the vessels are meeting nearly head-on; it does not govern a vessel that is overtaking another.
questions.explain: 'Each shall alter course to starboard so that each passes on the port side of the other.' The rule applies to EACH vessel regardless of size; it 'does not govern' overtaking, so nothing about overtaking can be inferred from it; and turning to port reverses the rule.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Members may drive a government vehicle home whenever they work past normal hours.
Without written authorization, using a government vehicle to commute is not permitted.
Emergency-response personnel may always use government vehicles to commute.
The installation commander may authorize a member to use a government vehicle for personal errands.
questions.passage: Government vehicles shall be used for official purposes only. Transportation between a member's residence and place of duty is not an official purpose, except when it is authorized in writing by the installation commander for personnel whose duties require them to respond to emergencies outside normal working hours.
questions.explain: Commuting 'is not an official purpose, except when it is authorized in writing', and vehicles are for 'official purposes only' — so no written authorization, no commuting. Working late is not the exception; emergency personnel still need the written authorization; and the exception covers commuting for emergency duties, not personal errands.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A pilot climbing through an inversion could find visibility improving above it.
Air temperature normally increases with height.
An inversion prevents clouds from forming at any altitude.
Air beneath an inversion rises rapidly, carrying smoke upward.
questions.passage: A temperature inversion occurs when a layer of warm air lies above cooler air near the ground, reversing the usual decrease of temperature with height. Because the cool surface air is denser than the air above it, it resists rising, and smoke, haze and moisture can become trapped beneath the inversion. Visibility near the surface may therefore be poor even when the sky above the inversion is clear.
questions.explain: Visibility near the surface 'may… be poor even when the sky above the inversion is clear', so climbing above it could bring better visibility. The usual pattern is a DECREASE with height (the inversion reverses it); clouds at other altitudes are never discussed; and the cool surface air 'resists rising'.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: During normal operations, a department head may approve a 20-day leave request.
The executive officer may approve leave during an increased state of readiness.
During an increased state of readiness, a 10-day leave request would need the commanding officer's approval.
Leave may not be granted during an increased state of readiness.
questions.passage: Leave requests of more than 14 days require the approval of the executive officer. Requests of 14 days or fewer may be approved by the department head. During any period in which the command has been ordered to an increased state of readiness, only the commanding officer may approve leave of any length.
questions.explain: During increased readiness 'only the commanding officer may approve leave of any length', including 10 days. Twenty days exceeds the department head's 14-day limit; 'only the commanding officer' excludes the executive officer; and leave can still be approved — by the CO — so it is not banned.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Carbon monoxide can be detected by its distinctive smell.
A pilot's own sense of feeling normal is not a reliable sign that there has been no carbon monoxide exposure.
Cabin heaters are the only source of carbon monoxide in small aircraft.
Opening the fresh-air vents increases the amount of carbon monoxide in the cabin.
questions.passage: Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless, so a pilot exposed to it may not notice its effects until judgment is already impaired. Heater systems that draw warm air from around the engine exhaust are a common source of exposure in small aircraft. Pilots who suspect contamination should shut off the heater and open the fresh-air vents.
questions.explain: A pilot 'may not notice its effects until judgment is already impaired', so feeling normal proves little. The gas is 'odorless'; heaters are 'a common source', not the only one; and opening fresh-air vents is the recommended remedy, not a cause.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A navy that has established sea control in one area controls the sea everywhere.
Once established, sea control is permanent.
Sea control cannot be established until the adversary's fleet has been destroyed.
A navy might hold sea control in an area during an operation and no longer hold it afterward.
questions.passage: Sea control is the condition in which a navy can use an area of the sea for its own purposes for a period of time and, if necessary, deny its use to an adversary. Sea control is seldom absolute or permanent; it is usually established in a specific area for as long as an operation requires.
questions.explain: Sea control is 'seldom absolute or permanent' and is held 'for as long as an operation requires', so it can lapse afterward. It is 'established in a specific area', not everywhere; 'permanent' contradicts 'seldom… permanent'; and destroying the enemy fleet is never named as a precondition.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Once a space has been certified safe, personnel may reenter it at any time while the certificate is in force.
Any member of the work party may certify a confined space safe for entry.
A certificate issued for a ventilated space may no longer be valid if the ventilation fails.
Retesting is required only when vapors have actually been detected.
questions.passage: Personnel shall enter a confined space, such as a fuel tank or void, only after the space has been tested by a gas-free engineer and certified safe for entry. The certificate is valid only for the conditions under which it was issued. If ventilation stops or work that could release vapors begins, the space shall be vacated and retested before personnel reenter.
questions.explain: The certificate 'is valid only for the conditions under which it was issued', and if ventilation stops the space is vacated and retested. Changed conditions require retesting before reentry, so 'at any time' fails; certification is by 'a gas-free engineer'; and retesting is triggered by ventilation stopping or vapor-producing work, not only by detected vapors.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The pilot's salute is not, by itself, enough for the aircraft to be launched.
A pilot who shakes his or her head is signaling readiness to launch.
Once a ready signal has been given, it cannot be withdrawn.
The deck-edge operator decides when the aircraft is launched.
questions.passage: An aircraft shall not be launched from the catapult unless the catapult officer has received both a ready signal from the pilot and a final check signal from the deck-edge operator. If either signal is withdrawn after it has been given, the launch sequence shall be suspended. The pilot signals readiness with a salute; a pilot who is not ready shakes his or her head.
questions.explain: Launch requires 'both a ready signal from the pilot and a final check signal from the deck-edge operator', so the salute alone is not enough. A head shake means NOT ready; 'if either signal is withdrawn' shows signals can be withdrawn; and the deck-edge operator gives one required signal — the passage never says that person decides the launch.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Ely was a naval officer when he made these flights.
Ely's shipboard landing took place after his takeoff from a ship.
Ely took off from and landed on the same ship.
The Navy commissioned its first aircraft carrier soon after Ely's flights.
questions.passage: In November 1910, civilian pilot Eugene Ely flew a Curtiss biplane off a wooden platform built over the bow of the cruiser USS Birmingham. Two months later he landed on a platform fitted to the stern of the armored cruiser USS Pennsylvania, using ropes weighted with sandbags to stop the aircraft. These flights showed that aircraft could operate from ships, although years passed before the Navy commissioned its first aircraft carrier.
questions.explain: The takeoff was in November 1910 and the landing came 'two months later'. Ely is called a 'civilian pilot'; the takeoff was from Birmingham and the landing on Pennsylvania; and 'years passed' before the first carrier was commissioned.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Navy aircraft shall conduct all search and rescue operations near naval installations.
The Navy may provide search and rescue support where civilian capability is adequate, provided the command's mission permits.
Civilian search and rescue resources are generally insufficient.
A request for Navy search and rescue support could properly be declined if meeting it would interfere with the command's primary mission.
questions.passage: Navy aircraft and crews may support civil search and rescue operations when civilian resources are insufficient. Such support shall not interfere with the command's primary mission and shall not be provided where an adequate civilian capability exists.
questions.explain: Support 'shall not interfere with the command's primary mission', so a request that would interfere can be declined. Support is permitted only when civilian resources are insufficient — never 'all' operations; it 'shall not be provided where an adequate civilian capability exists', whatever the mission; and the passage never rates civilian resources in general.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Of two otherwise identical gyroscopes, the faster-spinning one resists a change in axis direction more strongly.
A gyroscope responds to a force at the exact point where the force is applied.
A gyroscope gains rigidity in space as its rotor slows down.
Precession appears 180 degrees from the point where the force is applied.
questions.passage: A gyroscope's spinning rotor resists any change in the direction of its axis, a property called rigidity in space. Rigidity increases with the mass of the rotor and with its speed of rotation. When a force is applied to the rim, the gyroscope responds not at the point where the force is applied but at a point 90 degrees farther along in the direction of rotation, an effect called precession.
questions.explain: 'Rigidity increases with the mass of the rotor and with its speed of rotation', so with mass equal, the faster rotor is more rigid. The response comes '90 degrees farther along', which defeats both the 'exact point' and the '180 degrees' choices; and slowing the rotor would reduce rigidity, not increase it.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The executive officer is responsible for the ship's safe navigation while the officer of the deck is on watch.
A senior officer who arrives on the bridge automatically takes charge of the watch.
The officer of the deck answers to different officers for different aspects of the watch.
The officer of the deck is designated by the navigator.
questions.passage: The officer of the deck underway is the officer on watch designated by the commanding officer to be in charge of the ship. The officer of the deck reports directly to the commanding officer for the safe navigation and general operation of the ship, and to the executive officer for carrying out the ship's routine. Unless relieved by the commanding officer or another officer authorized to do so, the officer of the deck remains in charge of the watch even when senior officers are present on the bridge.
questions.explain: The OOD reports 'to the commanding officer for the safe navigation… and to the executive officer for carrying out the ship's routine' — two officers, two areas. The XO's link is to the routine, not navigation; the OOD stays in charge 'even when senior officers are present' unless properly relieved; and the OOD is 'designated by the commanding officer'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Spatial disorientation occurs only on dark nights over water.
The inner ear gives accurate attitude information during sustained turns.
Spatial disorientation is the leading cause of military aviation accidents.
A pilot flying in cloud may sense that the aircraft is level when it is not.
questions.passage: Spatial disorientation occurs when a pilot's perception of the aircraft's attitude differs from its actual attitude. It is most likely when outside visual references are lost, as in cloud or on a dark night over water, because the inner ear can be fooled by sustained turns and accelerations. Pilots are therefore trained to trust their flight instruments over their bodily sensations.
questions.explain: Disorientation is a mismatch between perceived and actual attitude, most likely in cloud because 'the inner ear can be fooled by sustained turns'. A dark night over water is one example, not the only case; the inner ear can be FOOLED, not accurate; and accident rankings are never mentioned — a true-sounding outside claim.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Only one foreign object damage walkdown is required on each flying day.
A period of heavy weather is not always followed by an additional walkdown.
The air officer may waive the walkdown required after maintenance on the flight deck surface.
Walkdowns are required only when debris has been seen on the flight deck.
questions.passage: A foreign object damage walkdown of the flight deck shall be conducted before the first launch of each flying day. An additional walkdown is required after any maintenance on the flight deck surface. A walkdown is also required after a period of heavy weather, unless the air officer determines that the affected area was sheltered from windblown debris.
questions.explain: The heavy-weather walkdown is required 'unless the air officer determines that the affected area was sheltered', so it can be skipped. Additional walkdowns after maintenance and weather make 'only one' wrong; the air officer's exception is attached to the weather sentence only, not to maintenance; and walkdowns are scheduled events, not triggered by sighted debris.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Effective orders specify every action that subordinates are to take.
Orders that state only the desired result are the most effective kind.
Some limits on a subordinate's freedom of action can be justified by the need for coordination.
Subordinates should be given no constraints at all so that they can adapt.
questions.passage: Orders that specify every action leave subordinates unable to adapt when circumstances change, while orders that state only the desired result can leave units working at cross-purposes. Effective orders therefore state the purpose of the operation and the commander's intent, and they limit subordinates' freedom of action only as much as coordination requires.
questions.explain: Effective orders 'limit subordinates' freedom of action only as much as coordination requires', so coordination justifies some limits. Specifying every action leaves units 'unable to adapt'; stating only the result risks 'cross-purposes'; and 'no constraints at all' contradicts the limits the passage endorses.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Aircraft operating from ships are exposed to conditions that speed corrosion more than inland conditions do.
When two different metals touch in salt water, both corrode at the same rate.
The less active of two metals in contact is the one that corrodes.
Frequent washing eliminates corrosion on shipboard aircraft.
questions.passage: Corrosion of aircraft aluminum is accelerated by salt, moisture and contact with dissimilar metals. When two different metals touch in the presence of an electrolyte such as salt water, the more active metal corrodes while the less active one is protected. For this reason, aircraft operating from ships are washed frequently and inspected for corrosion more often than aircraft based inland.
questions.explain: Corrosion is 'accelerated by salt, moisture', and 'for this reason' ship-based aircraft are washed and inspected more often than inland ones — linking the shipboard environment to faster corrosion. The MORE active metal corrodes while the other is protected, which defeats both metal choices; and the passage never claims washing eliminates corrosion.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A phone that has been switched off may be carried into a space where classified information is processed.
All personal electronic devices are prohibited throughout the command.
A medical device with a transmitter is allowed in a classified space as long as it is switched off.
A member with a transmitter-equipped medical device might be allowed to bring it into a classified processing space.
questions.passage: Personal electronic devices may be carried in the command's general work spaces. In spaces designated for processing classified information, devices with cameras, microphones or wireless transmitters are prohibited, whether or not they are switched on. A medical device that contains a transmitter may be permitted in such a space with the written approval of the security manager.
questions.explain: Such a medical device 'may be permitted… with the written approval of the security manager'. The prohibition applies 'whether or not they are switched on', which defeats both 'switched off' choices — the medical exception depends on approval, not on the power switch; and devices are allowed in general work spaces.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The witness to a man overboard is responsible for maneuvering the ship.
The duty of pointing at the person in the water can pass from the original witness to someone else.
The witness must throw a life ring before calling out the alarm.
The witness must throw a life ring in every case.
questions.passage: Any person who sees someone fall overboard shall immediately call out 'Man overboard,' giving the side, and throw a life ring toward the person if one is within reach. The witness shall keep the individual in sight and point continuously until relieved of that duty by a lookout or other watchstander. The officer of the deck will maneuver the ship as appropriate to recover the person.
questions.explain: The witness points 'until relieved of that duty by a lookout or other watchstander', so the duty can pass to someone else. The OOD maneuvers the ship; the alarm is called out 'immediately', and nothing puts the life ring first; and a ring is thrown only 'if one is within reach'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Some water droplets in clouds stay liquid even though their temperature is below freezing.
Rime ice forms from large droplets that freeze slowly.
Clear ice is lighter and easier to remove than rime ice.
Icing occurs only in clouds that contain large droplets.
questions.passage: Icing is most severe in clouds containing large supercooled water droplets, which remain liquid below freezing until they strike a surface and freeze on contact. Clear ice formed this way is heavy, hard to remove and spreads back along the wing before it freezes. Rime ice, formed from small droplets that freeze instantly on impact, is rough and milky but generally easier to remove.
questions.explain: Supercooled droplets 'remain liquid below freezing until they strike a surface'. Rime ice comes from SMALL droplets that freeze instantly; clear ice is 'heavy, hard to remove' while rime is 'easier to remove'; and icing is 'most severe' with large droplets — rime ice shows it also occurs with small ones.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Members may accept any contractor gift worth less than a set dollar amount.
Members must report every item they receive from a contractor, including pens.
A contractor's offer of an expensive item to a single member should be reported to the ethics counselor.
Refreshments provided by contractors may not be accepted in any circumstances.
questions.passage: Members shall not accept gifts from contractors doing business with the command. The prohibition does not apply to unsolicited items of nominal value, such as pens or calendars, that are offered to the general public, nor to refreshments served at events open to all attendees. Any gift not covered by these exceptions shall be declined or returned, and the offer shall be reported to the ethics counselor.
questions.explain: An expensive item offered to one member fits neither exception, so it is declined and 'the offer shall be reported to the ethics counselor'. The passage gives no dollar figure, and the nominal-value exception also requires the item to be offered to the general public; only gifts NOT covered by the exceptions are reported; and refreshments at events open to all attendees are expressly excepted.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The endurance of its ships is the main factor limiting a naval force's range.
Two forces with identical warships could have very different ranges depending on their replenishment support.
Underway replenishment allows a force to remain on station indefinitely.
A force with replenishment ships never needs to enter port.
questions.passage: The range of a naval force is limited less by the endurance of its ships than by the fuel, ammunition and stores that can be delivered to it. Underway replenishment, the transfer of supplies between ships at sea, allows a force to remain on station far longer than it could if it had to return to port to resupply. A force without replenishment ships must therefore plan its operations around the nearest available port.
questions.explain: Range depends 'less by the endurance of its ships than by the fuel, ammunition and stores that can be delivered', so identical ships with different supply could reach differently. The first choice reverses that priority; 'far longer' is not 'indefinitely'; and nothing says replenished forces never need port.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: On most aircraft the rudder controls roll.
Adverse yaw swings the nose toward the direction of the turn.
The upward-deflected aileron produces more drag than the downward-deflected one.
Without rudder, the nose of an aircraft rolling into a left turn would tend to swing to the right.
questions.passage: On most aircraft, the ailerons control roll, the elevator controls pitch and the rudder controls yaw. When a pilot rolls into a turn, the aileron that deflects downward produces more drag than the one that deflects upward, which tends to yaw the nose away from the direction of the turn. Pilots apply rudder in the direction of the turn to counter this adverse yaw.
questions.explain: Adverse yaw turns the nose 'away from the direction of the turn' — in a left turn, to the right — and rudder is what counters it. The rudder controls yaw, not roll; 'toward the turn' reverses the effect; and it is the DOWNWARD aileron that makes more drag.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A command may revoke a member's clearance eligibility when it has a security concern.
Suspension of access by a command automatically revokes the member's eligibility.
A member could keep clearance eligibility while being denied access to classified information.
A command must obtain the facility's approval before suspending a member's access.
questions.passage: A member's eligibility for a security clearance is determined by the central adjudication facility, not by the member's command. A command may, however, suspend a member's access to classified information at any time when it has information raising a security concern, pending the facility's review. Suspension of access does not by itself revoke eligibility.
questions.explain: 'Suspension of access does not by itself revoke eligibility', so a member can be eligible but without access. Eligibility is decided by the facility, 'not by the member's command'; 'automatically revokes' contradicts the last sentence; and the command may suspend 'at any time… pending the facility's review' — review comes after, not approval before.

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: The bonding cable between the truck and the aircraft is disconnected before the grounding cables.
Grounding and bonding serve the same purpose during fueling.
The nozzle may be opened before bonding, provided both the truck and the aircraft are grounded.
The bonding cable may be disconnected while fuel is still flowing.
questions.passage: During aircraft fueling, the fuel truck and the aircraft shall each be grounded, and they shall then be bonded to each other before the fuel nozzle is opened. Bonding equalizes static charge between the truck and the aircraft; grounding drains charge to the earth. After the nozzle has been closed and removed, the bonding and grounding cables shall be disconnected in the reverse order of their connection.
questions.explain: Grounding is connected first and bonding 'then'; reversing that order means bonding comes off first, then grounding. Bonding 'equalizes' charge while grounding 'drains charge to the earth' — different purposes; bonding comes 'before the fuel nozzle is opened'; and cables come off only 'after the nozzle has been closed and removed'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The fleet was painted white to make it harder to see at sea.
The Great White Fleet completed its voyage in less than a year.
The cruise showed that the fleet was self-sufficient in fuel.
The voyage revealed a weakness as well as a capability.
questions.passage: In December 1907, sixteen US battleships departed Hampton Roads, Virginia, on a voyage around the world that would last fourteen months. Painted white in the peacetime fashion of the day, the force became known as the Great White Fleet. The cruise demonstrated that the United States could deploy a large battle fleet far from home, and it also exposed the fleet's dependence on foreign colliers for coal.
questions.explain: It 'demonstrated that the United States could deploy a large battle fleet far from home' (capability) and 'exposed the fleet's dependence on foreign colliers' (weakness). White paint followed 'peacetime fashion', not concealment; the voyage lasted 'fourteen months'; and dependence on foreign colliers is the opposite of self-sufficiency.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Once a hazard has been reported, the person who found it has no further duty regarding it.
A sailor who has reported a hazard may still be expected to act on it personally.
Only supervisors are responsible for reporting safety hazards.
A person must act to prevent damage even when doing so would be unsafe.
questions.passage: Every person in the naval service is responsible for reporting a safety hazard to a superior as soon as it is discovered. Reporting a hazard does not relieve the person of the duty to take immediate action to prevent injury or damage when he or she is able to do so safely.
questions.explain: Reporting 'does not relieve the person of the duty to take immediate action', so the reporter may still have to act. 'No further duty' contradicts that; 'every person in the naval service' must report, not only supervisors; and the duty to act applies only 'when he or she is able to do so safely'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: At some depth between the surface layer and deep water, sound speed may reach a minimum.
Sound travels faster through air than through seawater.
Sound speed increases steadily from the surface to the sea floor.
Near the surface, salinity has the greatest effect on sound speed.
questions.passage: Sound travels through seawater roughly four times faster than through air, and its speed increases with water temperature, pressure and salinity. Near the surface, where temperature usually has the greatest effect, sound speed tends to fall as depth increases and the water cools. In deeper water, where temperature changes little, rising pressure becomes the dominant factor and sound speed increases again with depth.
questions.explain: Sound speed 'tends to fall as depth increases' near the surface and 'increases again with depth' in deeper water — falling then rising implies a lowest point in between. Seawater is 'roughly four times faster' than air; the speed first falls, so it does not rise steadily; and near the surface it is TEMPERATURE that 'usually has the greatest effect'.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: Aircrew may fly once 12 hours have passed since drinking, whatever their condition.
Aircrew may use any over-the-counter medication up to 12 hours before a flight.
With a flight surgeon's approval, an aircrew member could take an over-the-counter medication on the morning of a flight.
Prescription medications never restrict aircrew from flying.
questions.passage: Aircrew shall not fly within 12 hours of consuming alcohol and in no case while under its influence. Flight surgeons may further restrict aircrew from flying after the use of certain prescription medications. Aircrew shall not use over-the-counter medications within 24 hours before a flight unless a flight surgeon has approved their use.
questions.explain: Over-the-counter medications are barred within 24 hours of flight 'unless a flight surgeon has approved their use', so approved use on the morning of a flight is possible. Aircrew may never fly 'while under its influence', whatever the hours; the OTC limit is 24 hours, not 12; and flight surgeons 'may further restrict' flying after certain prescriptions.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Surprise is lost as soon as the enemy learns that an attack is coming.
Deception is the only reliable means of achieving surprise.
Surprise can be achieved only by attacking at an unexpected place.
An enemy that detects an attack shortly before it arrives may still be surprised.
questions.passage: Surprise is achieved by striking an enemy at a time or place, or in a manner, for which it is unprepared. It does not require that the enemy be wholly unaware of an attack, only that it become aware too late to react effectively. Speed, deception and security all contribute to achieving surprise.
questions.explain: Surprise requires only that the enemy 'become aware too late to react effectively', not that it be 'wholly unaware'. 'Lost as soon as the enemy learns' contradicts that; deception is one of three contributors, not the only one; and surprise can come from time, place OR manner, not place alone.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Ordnance handlers wear purple jerseys.
Jersey color alone does not show whether a red-jersey sailor handles ordnance or works on a crash and salvage crew.
Personnel wearing the correct jersey may enter the flight deck during flight operations without flotation gear.
Jersey colors on the flight deck are assigned by rank.
questions.passage: Flight deck personnel wear jerseys whose colors identify their duties. Purple jerseys are worn by aviation fuel handlers, and red jerseys are worn by ordnance handlers and by crash and salvage crews. Personnel who are not wearing the proper jersey and flotation gear are not permitted on the flight deck during flight operations.
questions.explain: Red is worn 'by ordnance handlers and by crash and salvage crews', so the color alone cannot tell the two apart. Purple is for fuel handlers; flight operations require 'the proper jersey AND flotation gear'; and colors 'identify their duties', not rank.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A detachment deployed aboard ship is exempt from this instruction.
On every matter, the ship's instructions take priority over this instruction for embarked detachments.
An embarked detachment could follow the ship's instructions on one matter and the wing's instruction on another.
Aviation units ashore must follow ships' instructions on matters of shipboard routine.
questions.passage: This instruction applies to all aviation units of the wing, including detachments deployed aboard ship. Where this instruction and a ship's instructions differ, detachments aboard ship shall comply with the ship's instructions on matters of shipboard routine and with this instruction on matters of aircraft maintenance.
questions.explain: Embarked detachments follow 'the ship's instructions on matters of shipboard routine and… this instruction on matters of aircraft maintenance' — different authorities for different matters. Shipboard detachments are expressly INCLUDED; the ship's priority covers routine only, not maintenance; and the ship's-instructions rule applies to 'detachments aboard ship', not units ashore.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: A two-hour flight in an unpressurized aircraft at a cabin altitude of 12,000 feet would not require supplemental oxygen.
Supplemental oxygen is required at every cabin altitude above 10,000 feet, regardless of time.
A flight at a cabin altitude of 14,000 feet may be made without oxygen for up to three hours.
Pressurized aircraft never require supplemental oxygen.
questions.passage: Occupants of an unpressurized aircraft shall use supplemental oxygen at all times at cabin altitudes above 13,000 feet. At cabin altitudes from 10,000 to 13,000 feet, oxygen is required for any portion of the flight at those altitudes that exceeds three hours. Below 10,000 feet, no supplemental oxygen is required.
questions.explain: Between 10,000 and 13,000 feet, oxygen is required only for the portion 'that exceeds three hours'; two hours at 12,000 feet does not. The three-hour allowance makes 'regardless of time' wrong; above 13,000 feet oxygen is required 'at all times'; and the passage covers only unpressurized aircraft, so it says nothing about pressurized ones.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Air pressure at 36,000 feet is zero.
More of the atmosphere's mass lies below 18,000 feet than above 25,000 feet.
Temperature in the lowest layer of the atmosphere decreases at a constant rate with altitude.
Air pressure increases as altitude increases.
questions.passage: Air pressure decreases with altitude because there is less air above to press down. At about 18,000 feet, pressure is roughly half of its sea-level value, meaning that about half of the mass of the atmosphere lies below that altitude. Temperature also generally decreases with altitude in the lowest layer of the atmosphere, though not at a uniform rate.
questions.explain: About half of the atmosphere's mass lies below 18,000 feet, so the other half lies above it; the mass above 25,000 feet is only part of that upper half, so it is less. the passage gives no pressure figure for 36,000 feet, so 'zero' is unsupported; temperature falls 'not at a uniform rate'; and pressure DECREASES with altitude.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Sponsors are chosen by the newly reporting member.
A sponsor must always be of the same rank as the new member.
Sponsors are assigned after the new member has completed check-in.
A new member could be assigned a sponsor of a different rank.
questions.passage: The command sponsor program assigns an experienced member to each newly reporting member before that member arrives. The sponsor answers questions about the command and the local area and helps the new member through check-in. Sponsors are selected by the gaining department and should, when possible, be of similar rank and family status to the new member.
questions.explain: Sponsors 'should, when possible, be of similar rank', so a different rank is possible when matching is not. Sponsors are 'selected by the gaining department'; 'when possible' is not 'always'; and sponsors are assigned 'before that member arrives' and help 'through check-in'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Crew rest rules do not depend on aircrew judging their own fatigue.
A commanding officer may reduce crew rest periods whenever circumstances warrant.
Fatigued individuals usually recognize their fatigue before their performance suffers.
Reducing a crew rest period adds no risk once the commanding officer has approved it.
questions.passage: Fatigue degrades performance gradually, and the fatigued individual is often the last to recognize it. For this reason, crew rest requirements are stated as minimum periods of rest rather than left to individual judgment. A commanding officer may extend required rest periods when circumstances warrant, but may reduce them only when operational necessity outweighs the added risk, and only after that risk has been assessed.
questions.explain: Rest requirements are minimums 'rather than left to individual judgment', because individuals are 'often the last to recognize' fatigue. 'When circumstances warrant' is the test for EXTENDING rest — reducing it requires operational necessity and a risk assessment; the third choice reverses 'last to recognize'; and the passage names 'the added risk' of a reduction.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A runway that is adequate on a hot afternoon may be too short on a cool morning.
A high density altitude reduces engine power but has no effect on lift.
The same aircraft at the same airfield may need a longer takeoff run on a hot afternoon than on a cool morning.
Pressure altitude increases as air temperature rises.
questions.passage: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. As air temperature rises, air density falls and density altitude increases. An aircraft operating at a high density altitude produces less lift and less engine power and therefore needs a longer takeoff run, so a runway that is adequate on a cool morning may be marginal on a hot afternoon.
questions.explain: Higher temperature raises density altitude, which reduces lift and power and 'therefore needs a longer takeoff run' — so the hot afternoon may need more runway. The first choice reverses morning and afternoon; a high density altitude brings 'less lift and less engine power' — both, not power alone; and it is DENSITY altitude, not pressure altitude, that rises with temperature.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: An aircraft may be released for flight while some discrepancies remain uncorrected.
Any maintenance supervisor may defer a discrepancy that does not affect safety of flight.
The pilot must approve each deferral before it is recorded in the aircraft's logbook.
A safety-of-flight discrepancy may be deferred if a correction date is logged.
questions.passage: Aircraft shall not be released for flight with an open discrepancy that affects safety of flight. A discrepancy that does not affect safety of flight may be deferred, but only by the maintenance control supervisor, and the deferral shall be recorded in the aircraft's logbook with a scheduled date for correction. The pilot shall review all deferred discrepancies before accepting the aircraft.
questions.explain: A discrepancy that does not affect safety of flight 'may be deferred', and the pilot reviews 'all deferred discrepancies before accepting the aircraft' — so an aircraft can fly with some discrepancies still uncorrected. Deferral is limited to 'the maintenance control supervisor', not any supervisor; the pilot REVIEWS deferrals before accepting the aircraft but is never said to approve them; and a safety-of-flight discrepancy cannot be carried into flight at all — logging a correction date applies only to deferrable ones.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The move director may begin the move once both wingtip walkers are in position.
A walker may signal a stop only after the director has confirmed that clearance is inadequate.
At least four people take part in moving an aircraft into a hangar.
Wingtip and tail walkers are required whenever an aircraft is moved on the flight line.
questions.passage: When an aircraft is to be moved into or out of a hangar, a walker shall be posted at each wingtip and at the tail, in addition to the move director. Each walker shall watch the clearance between the aircraft and nearby objects and shall signal the director to stop if the clearance becomes inadequate. The move shall not begin until all walkers are in position.
questions.explain: A walker at 'each wingtip and at the tail' makes three, and they are 'in addition to the move director' — at least four people. The move waits until ALL walkers are in position, so the tail walker counts too; the walker judges the clearance and signals the director, not the other way round; and the rule covers moves 'into or out of a hangar', not every move on the flight line.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: Sound levels of 85 decibels or more will damage the hearing of unprotected personnel.
A space that regularly reaches 90 decibels must be labeled at each entrance.
Personnel who work in hazardous noise areas must wear hearing protection at all times.
