Any space in which the sound level has once reached 85 decibels is a hazardous noise area.
questions.passage: A hazardous noise area is any space in which the sound level regularly reaches 85 decibels or more. Such spaces shall be marked with warning labels at each entrance, and personnel who work in them shall be enrolled in the hearing conservation program and receive an annual hearing test.
questions.explain: A space that 'regularly reaches 85 decibels or more' is a hazardous noise area, 90 is more than 85, and such spaces 'shall be marked with warning labels at each entrance'. Hearing damage may be real-world fact, but the passage never states it; hearing protection is never mentioned — only enrollment and an annual test; and the definition needs the level to be reached 'regularly', not once.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A waiver also extends the following year's due date by up to 60 days.
Any aircrew member who is deployed may be granted a waiver of up to 60 days by the wing commander.
Aircrew who receive a waiver complete the check in a simulator instead of an aircraft.
A check completed under a waiver can leave less than a year until the next is due.
questions.passage: Aircrew shall complete the annual instrument flight check before the end of their birth month. The wing commander may waive the requirement for up to 60 days for aircrew who are deployed to locations without suitable aircraft or simulators. A waiver does not change the date on which the following year's check falls due.
questions.explain: A waived check is done up to 60 days after the birth month, yet 'a waiver does not change the date on which the following year's check falls due' — so the next check can come due in less than a year. The first choice reverses that last sentence; the waiver is only for aircrew deployed 'to locations without suitable aircraft or simulators', not every deployed member; and nothing says the waived check is flown in a simulator — the waiver exists because none is available.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: Aircraft may wait on the taxiway when the designated holding area is already full.
Wash crews must wear chemical-resistant gloves and eye protection whenever they are on the wash rack.
When two aircraft are on the wash rack, a third awaiting a wash belongs in the holding area.
No more than two aircraft may be washed at the station on any one day.
questions.passage: No more than two aircraft may occupy the wash rack at one time. Aircraft awaiting a wash shall be parked in the designated holding area, not on the taxiway. Wash crews shall wear chemical-resistant gloves and eye protection whenever cleaning compounds are in use.
questions.explain: With two aircraft on the rack, a third cannot join them ('no more than two… at one time'), so it is awaiting a wash and 'shall be parked in the designated holding area'. No overflow exception allows the taxiway; protective equipment is required 'whenever cleaning compounds are in use', not whenever crews are on the rack; and the limit is two 'at one time', not two per day.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A person whose certification has lapsed may be present during an ordnance operation.
Personnel certified for one type of ordnance may handle any other type under supervision.
Recertification requires only a new written examination, not further training.
Personnel who have completed formal training may handle ordnance while awaiting their examination.
questions.passage: Ordnance shall be handled only by personnel who are certified for the specific type of ordnance involved. Certification requires completion of formal training, a practical demonstration under supervision and a written examination, and it expires after one year. Personnel whose certification has expired may observe ordnance operations but shall not perform any handling task until they have been recertified.
questions.explain: Personnel whose certification has expired 'may observe ordnance operations', so they may be present without handling anything. Certification is 'for the specific type of ordnance involved', and supervision is part of earning it, not a way round it; the passage never says what recertification involves; and certification needs training, a demonstration AND an examination, so training alone does not permit handling.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Devices containing lithium batteries must not be carried in checked baggage.
Overcharging is the most common cause of lithium battery fires.
Spare lithium batteries may be placed in a cargo compartment if their terminals are protected.
Spare batteries are kept out of cargo holds partly because a fire there might go unseen.
questions.passage: Lithium batteries in portable electronic devices can overheat and ignite if they are damaged, overcharged or exposed to high temperatures, and the resulting fire is difficult to extinguish. For this reason, spare lithium batteries carried aboard aircraft shall be kept in carry-on baggage with their terminals protected against short circuit, and shall not be placed in checked baggage or cargo compartments, where a fire might go undetected.
questions.explain: Spare batteries 'shall not be placed in checked baggage or cargo compartments, where a fire might go undetected' — the risk of an unseen fire is one stated reason. The rule covers SPARE batteries, not devices; overcharging is one of three causes and is never ranked; and protected terminals are required IN ADDITION to carry-on stowage, not as a substitute that opens the cargo compartment.

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: The operations officer must approve every change to the flight schedule.
A change made at 1700 on the day before flying needs the operations officer's agreement.
Changes made before 1600 on the day before flying must be reported to the maintenance department.
The schedules officer need not inform crews of changes made before 1600.
questions.passage: Changes to the squadron flight schedule made after 1600 on the day before flying require the concurrence of the operations officer. The schedules officer may make changes before that time without further approval but shall inform the affected crews. Changes made on the day of flight shall also be reported to the maintenance department so that aircraft assignments can be adjusted.
questions.explain: 1700 is 'after 1600 on the day before flying', so the change requires 'the concurrence of the operations officer' — his agreement. Changes before 1600 need no 'further approval', so 'every change' over-claims; maintenance is told of changes made 'on the day of flight', not the day before; and the schedules officer 'shall inform the affected crews' — the last choice reverses that.

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: Survival radios must be tested on the distress frequency before each flight.
A radio that fails its test may be flown if no spare is available at the flight equipment shop.
A test on the distress frequency could set off an unneeded rescue response.
Each aircrew member is responsible for keeping a spare survival radio of his or her own.
questions.passage: Survival radios shall be tested before each flight by transmitting a short test signal on the designated test frequency. Transmissions on the distress frequency are prohibited during testing, since they can trigger a search and rescue response. A radio that fails its test shall be replaced before flight; consequently, each squadron shall maintain a supply of spare radios at the flight equipment shop.
questions.explain: Distress-frequency transmissions during testing 'can trigger a search and rescue response' — a response to a test, when no one is in distress. Testing uses 'the designated test frequency', and the distress frequency is prohibited, so the first choice reverses the rule; a failed radio 'shall be replaced before flight' with no exception; and the spares are held by 'each squadron… at the flight equipment shop', not by individuals.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A temporary duty member cannot stand a watch before completing safety indoctrination.
Personnel arriving for temporary duty must have their orders endorsed on the day they arrive.
All personnel reporting aboard, permanent or temporary, must complete these same steps.
Temporary duty personnel are assigned a watch station and a berthing space on arrival.
questions.passage: Personnel arriving aboard for temporary duty shall report to the ship's personnel office within 24 hours to have their orders endorsed. They shall be assigned a berthing space and a muster station, and they shall complete the ship's general safety indoctrination before standing any watch. On departure, they shall return all issued equipment and have their orders endorsed again.
questions.explain: They 'shall complete the ship's general safety indoctrination before standing any watch', so no watch comes first. 'Within 24 hours' can run into the next calendar day, so 'the day they arrive' tightens the rule; the passage covers only temporary duty personnel; and they are assigned a MUSTER station, not a watch station — a close paraphrase with one word changed.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Water collects faster in the tanks of idle aircraft than in those that fly every day.
An idle aircraft on the flight line still needs a fuel sample drawn each day.
Daily fuel samples are needed only for aircraft that are scheduled to fly that day.
Every aircraft assigned to the command, including those in the hangar, must be sampled each day.
questions.passage: Some commands have interpreted the requirement for a daily fuel sample as applying only to aircraft scheduled to fly that day. This interpretation is incorrect. A sample shall be drawn from each aircraft on the flight line each day, whether or not it is scheduled to fly, because water that collects in the tanks of an idle aircraft will still be present when the aircraft is next flown.
questions.explain: 'A sample shall be drawn from each aircraft on the flight line each day, whether or not it is scheduled to fly.' The passage says water collects in idle tanks but compares no rates; the third choice is the very interpretation the passage calls 'incorrect'; and the rule covers aircraft 'on the flight line', not every aircraft the command holds.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Personnel at replenishment stations must stay on the engaged side until the evolution is secured.
The replenishment evolution begins when the two ships come alongside each other.
Uninvolved personnel may return to the weather decks once the last line has been passed.
Uninvolved personnel may not use the weather decks on either side during the evolution.
questions.passage: During any replenishment evolution, only personnel assigned to the replenishment stations are permitted on the weather decks on the engaged side. The evolution begins when the first line is passed and ends when the last line has been cleared. Personnel who are not involved shall remain inside the skin of the ship until the evolution has been secured.
questions.explain: The first sentence restricts only the engaged side, but the last requires uninvolved personnel to 'remain inside the skin of the ship' — which excludes every weather deck, engaged or not. Nothing confines station personnel to the engaged side; the evolution begins 'when the first line is passed', not on coming alongside; and it ends when the last line 'has been cleared', not passed — uninvolved personnel wait until it is secured.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Engine runs can sometimes take place somewhere other than the run-up area.
When the run-up area is closed, engines may be run in the hangar if its doors are open.
The maintenance officer may designate any spot on the apron as a temporary run-up site.
A fire bottle need not be manned for an engine run at a temporary site on the apron.
questions.passage: Aircraft engines shall not be run in the hangar under any circumstances. Engine runs shall be conducted only at the designated run-up area, with the aircraft tied down and chocked and a fire bottle manned. Where the run-up area is closed for construction, the maintenance officer may designate a temporary site on the parking apron, provided it is at least 200 feet from any building.
questions.explain: While the run-up area is 'closed for construction', the maintenance officer may designate 'a temporary site on the parking apron' — so runs can sometimes happen elsewhere. The hangar ban applies 'under any circumstances'; the apron site must be 'at least 200 feet from any building', so not any spot qualifies; and nothing relaxes the tie-down, chock and fire-bottle requirements at the temporary site.

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: Crews who are familiar with a checklist make more errors than crews who are new to it.
A checklist that is used as written protects against every kind of crew error.
Reading a checklist item aloud does not by itself show that the item has been checked.
A crew member may answer a challenge from memory if the item was checked earlier in the flight.
questions.passage: A checklist protects against omission only if it is used as written. Crews who become familiar with a checklist tend to read items aloud while their attention is elsewhere, responding to each challenge from habit rather than from a check of the actual switch or gauge. For this reason, each response shall be given only after the crew member has looked at or touched the item being checked.
questions.explain: Familiar crews 'tend to read items aloud while their attention is elsewhere', so an item can be read aloud without being checked. The passage says familiar crews 'tend to' respond from habit but compares no error rates; a checklist protects 'against omission', not every kind of error; and every response comes 'only after' looking at or touching the item — an earlier check does not count.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: Only junior officers of the squadron may stand the squadron duty.
Officers in a flight status are excused from standing the duty.
An officer relieved from the duty at 0800 may be scheduled for a flight beginning at 1500 that day.
An officer in a flight status may still stand the squadron duty.
questions.passage: Squadron duty officers are normally drawn from among the junior officers of the squadron. Officers in a flight status shall not stand the duty on a day on which they are scheduled to fly, and an officer who has stood the duty shall not be scheduled for a flight that begins within eight hours after being relieved.
questions.explain: Flight-status officers are barred from the duty only 'on a day on which they are scheduled to fly', so on other days they may stand it. 'Normally' describes the usual source of duty officers, not an 'only' rule; flight status brings a limit, not a general excusal; and 1500 is seven hours after 0800 — 'within eight hours after being relieved'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Wind shear is most often caused by thunderstorms near airfields.
A sudden loss of headwind is more dangerous on final approach than in cruise.
An aircraft that flies into a sudden increase in headwind loses airspeed.
Pilots who meet shear at low altitude should confirm the trend before adding power.
questions.passage: Wind shear is a sudden change in wind speed or direction over a short distance. An aircraft flying into a shear that suddenly reduces its headwind loses airspeed and may lose altitude before the pilot can respond, which makes shear most dangerous during takeoff and landing, when the aircraft is slow and close to the ground. Pilots who encounter shear at low altitude are trained to apply maximum power immediately rather than wait to confirm the trend.
questions.explain: Shear is 'most dangerous during takeoff and landing, when the aircraft is slow and close to the ground' — final approach is part of landing, cruise is neither. Thunderstorms may cause shear in the real world but are never mentioned; airspeed is lost when the shear 'suddenly reduces its headwind', not increases it; and pilots apply power immediately 'rather than wait to confirm the trend'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Once its engines are shut down, a parked aircraft is safe for anyone to approach.
No one may approach a parked aircraft until its seat and canopy safety pins are installed.
Stored hydraulic pressure can still be present in an aircraft after its engines stop.
Ejection seat cartridges are removed from an aircraft whenever its engines are shut down.
questions.passage: Personnel sometimes assume that an aircraft parked with its engines shut down presents no hazard to people walking nearby. In fact, ejection seat cartridges, explosive canopy systems and stored hydraulic pressure remain active after shutdown. For this reason, only personnel with a specific need shall approach a parked aircraft, and no one shall enter a cockpit until the seat and canopy safety pins have been confirmed installed.
questions.explain: 'Stored hydraulic pressure remain[s] active after shutdown.' The first choice is the mistaken assumption the passage corrects ('In fact…'); the safety-pin check applies to entering a COCKPIT, while approaching needs only 'a specific need'; and the cartridges 'remain active after shutdown' — they are not removed.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: If the risks cannot be made acceptable, the period is not flown with reduced margins.
A night qualification period must be cancelled whenever the risks to deck personnel are high.
Commanding officers must eliminate all risk before a night qualification period is conducted.
Only the risks to aircrew, not to deck personnel, are weighed before each period.
questions.passage: Commanding officers shall weigh the benefits of each night carrier qualification period against the attendant risks to aircrew and deck personnel. Where the risks cannot be reduced to an acceptable level, the period shall be postponed rather than conducted with reduced margins.
questions.explain: Where risks 'cannot be reduced to an acceptable level, the period shall be postponed rather than conducted with reduced margins'. The remedy is postponement, not cancellation, and the trigger is risk that cannot be made acceptable, not merely 'high' risk; risks are reduced to an acceptable level, not eliminated; and the risks weighed are those 'to aircrew and deck personnel' — both.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: All of the taxiway sign lights at the north end of the field have failed.
Aircraft taxiing at the north end of the field must use the taxi light at all times.
Vegetation is the main reason that aircrew have had difficulty seeing the signs.
Some taxiway signs at the north end were blocked from view by vegetation.
questions.passage: Aircrew have reported difficulty seeing taxiway signs at the north end of the field at night. An inspection found that several sign lights had failed and that vegetation had grown in front of others. Until the lights are repaired and the vegetation is cut back, aircraft taxiing at night in that area shall use the taxi light and proceed at no more than a fast walk.
questions.explain: The inspection found 'vegetation had grown in front of others' — some signs were blocked by plants. 'Several' lights failed, not all; the taxi-light rule applies to aircraft taxiing 'at night in that area', not at all times; and the passage lists two causes without ranking either as the main one.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Only maintenance control personnel may isolate a fuel leak on an aircraft.
Absorbent used to clean up a fuel spill is disposed of as hazardous waste.
An engine may be started to move the aircraft from the leak once maintenance control is told.
Electrical power may be applied to a leaking aircraft provided its engines are not started.
questions.passage: Personnel who discover a fuel leak on an aircraft shall stop all work in the area and notify maintenance control. No electrical power shall be applied to the aircraft and no engine shall be started until the leak has been isolated and the spilled fuel has been cleaned up. Fuel-soaked rags and absorbent shall be placed in a sealed container for disposal as hazardous waste.
questions.explain: 'Fuel-soaked rags and absorbent shall be placed in a sealed container for disposal as hazardous waste.' Maintenance control is NOTIFIED, and the passage never says who isolates the leak; no engine start is allowed until the leak is isolated and cleaned up, whoever has been told; and power and engine starts are BOTH barred — avoiding one does not permit the other.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A safety stand-down is required within 30 days after every mishap.
The individuals involved in the mishap may not be mentioned during the stand-down.
Those involved may be discussed if needed to explain the sequence of events.
The stand-down must be held within 30 days, and its purpose is to establish who was at fault.
questions.passage: Commands shall conduct a safety stand-down within 30 days after any Class A mishap. The stand-down is intended to review the lessons of the mishap with all hands, not to assign blame; accordingly, discussion of the individuals involved shall be limited to what is necessary to explain the sequence of events.
questions.explain: Discussion of the individuals is 'limited to what is necessary to explain the sequence of events', so it is allowed to that extent. The 30-day rule follows a 'Class A mishap', not every mishap; 'limited' is not a total ban; and the stand-down is 'not to assign blame' — the last choice reverses its purpose.

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: The wing maintenance office may approve a deviation when the cognizant activity is unknown.
A squadron may deviate from an approved procedure if the deviation improves safety.
Every deviation request must be forwarded through the wing maintenance office.
A squadron may not authorize its own deviation from an approved maintenance procedure.
questions.passage: Requests to deviate from an approved maintenance procedure shall be submitted to the cognizant engineering activity, which alone may authorize the deviation. A squadron that cannot identify the cognizant activity for a particular aircraft system shall forward the request through the wing maintenance office.
questions.explain: The cognizant engineering activity 'alone may authorize the deviation', and the squadron submits requests to it — so the squadron cannot authorize its own. The wing office only FORWARDS requests and gains no authority to approve them; no safety-improvement exception exists; and only a squadron that 'cannot identify the cognizant activity' routes through the wing office.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A float coat with a damaged inflation system is not to be used.
Cranial helmets and goggles must be worn on the flight deck at all times.
Float coats are inspected by the flight deck supervisor before each flight operation.
The float coat's light and whistle keep the wearer afloat if he or she is unconscious.
questions.passage: All personnel on the flight deck during flight operations shall wear a cranial helmet, goggles and a float coat. The float coat is fitted with a light and a whistle so that a person who falls overboard can be located, and its inflation system keeps the wearer afloat even if he or she is unconscious. Personnel shall inspect their float coats before each use and turn in any coat with a damaged inflation system.
questions.explain: Personnel 'turn in any coat with a damaged inflation system', so such a coat is taken out of use. The protective equipment is required 'during flight operations', not at all times; each person inspects 'their' own coat; and it is the INFLATION SYSTEM that keeps the wearer afloat — the light and whistle are for locating him or her.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Every 'should' in this instruction must be followed unless the commanding officer approves otherwise.
In quoted material, 'should' takes its meaning from the source directive.
'May' indicates a recommended practice that can be departed from when circumstances warrant.
'Will' indicates a future action rather than a requirement.
questions.passage: The terms 'shall' and 'will' are used in this instruction to indicate mandatory requirements. 'Should' indicates a recommended practice that may be departed from when circumstances warrant, and 'may' indicates an action that is permitted but not required. Where these terms appear in material quoted from other directives, they retain the meaning given in the source directive.
questions.explain: Terms in material 'quoted from other directives… retain the meaning given in the source directive' — 'should' included. A 'should' 'may be departed from when circumstances warrant', and no commanding-officer approval is mentioned; the third choice gives 'may' the definition of 'should'; and 'will', like 'shall', indicates 'mandatory requirements'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Exactly two qualified personnel are assigned to each aircraft fueling.
The fueling supervisor may reduce the crew to one person when a fire watch is posted.
A fire watch must be posted whenever an aircraft is being fueled.
A fueling crew may include more than two people.
questions.passage: A minimum of two qualified personnel shall be present whenever an aircraft is being fueled. One shall operate the fuel nozzle and the other shall man the emergency shutoff. Additional personnel may be assigned as fire watch at the discretion of the fueling supervisor.
questions.explain: Two is 'a minimum', and 'additional personnel may be assigned as fire watch' — so more than two may be present. 'Exactly two' turns a floor into a fixed number; the supervisor's discretion covers adding a fire watch, never going below two; and the fire watch is optional ('may be assigned'), not required.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Even a patrol dealing with a danger to personnel must report it before moving on.
A patrol that removes a danger to personnel need not report it afterward.
A patrol must report every abnormal condition before taking any action on it.
A patrol that finds an abnormal condition must wait in that space for the petty officer.
questions.passage: Roving patrol watchstanders shall inspect each space on their route at least once every hour and record the time of each inspection in the patrol log. Any abnormal condition shall be reported to the petty officer of the watch before the patrol continues on its route. If the condition presents an immediate danger to personnel, the patrol shall first take whatever action is needed to protect personnel and then make the report.
questions.explain: Any abnormal condition 'shall be reported… before the patrol continues on its route', and the danger exception changes only the ORDER: the patrol 'shall first take whatever action is needed… and then make the report'. So the report still comes before the patrol moves on. Skipping the report once the danger is removed ignores 'and then make the report'; reporting before any action ignores the exception; and waiting for the petty officer is never stated.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: An E-6 going ashore in a foreign port need not carry a liberty card.
An E-4 may go ashore alone in a foreign port if back aboard before midnight.
Members in grade E-5 and above must be back aboard by midnight in every port.
An E-3 ashore in a foreign port might be allowed to stay out past midnight.
questions.passage: While the ship is in a foreign port, enlisted members below the grade of E-5 shall go on liberty with at least one other member of the command. Liberty for these members expires at midnight unless the commanding officer has authorized an extended liberty period for that port. Members in grade E-5 and above may go ashore alone, but all members, regardless of grade, shall carry their liberty cards while ashore.
questions.explain: Midnight is the limit for members below E-5 'unless the commanding officer has authorized an extended liberty period', so an E-3 could stay later in such a port. Liberty cards are required of 'all members, regardless of grade'; the companion rule for members below E-5 has no early-return exception; and the midnight rule is stated only for members below E-5, so applying it to E-5 and above is a scope shift.

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: Advance leave may be granted for any reason if the balance stays within 30 days.
A newly enlisted member may take advance leave only if there is an emergency.
A member who separates owing leave must stay on duty until the days are earned back.
A member at the 30-day limit must serve a full year to earn the balance back to zero.
questions.passage: A member may request advance leave, which is leave taken before it has been earned, up to a maximum negative balance of 30 days. Members earn leave at a rate of 2.5 days for each month of active service. Advance leave is intended for emergencies and for situations in which a member has not yet had time to earn enough leave, such as shortly after enlistment. A member who separates from the service with a negative leave balance shall repay the value of the unearned days.
questions.explain: Leave is earned at 2.5 days per month, so a negative balance of 30 days takes 30 ÷ 2.5 = 12 months of service to earn back. 'Any reason' is tempting, but the passage says only what advance leave is 'intended for', not that every reason qualifies; new members are named as a separate case from emergencies, so 'only if there is an emergency' is wrong; and a member who separates 'shall repay the value' of the days, not stay on to earn them.

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: A face shield worn over the eyes during grinding may be worn in place of safety glasses.
Ordinary prescription eyeglasses meet the requirement once side shields have been fitted to them.
A sailor grinding in safety-rated prescription glasses with side shields still needs a face shield.
Safety glasses must be worn in the machine shop at all times, even when no machine runs.
questions.passage: Safety glasses with side shields shall be worn by all personnel in the machine shop while any machine is operating, including personnel who are only passing through. A full face shield shall be worn over the safety glasses during grinding. Prescription eyeglasses do not satisfy the requirement unless they are rated as safety eyewear and fitted with side shields.
questions.explain: Rated prescription glasses with side shields count as the safety glasses, but grinding requires 'a full face shield… over the safety glasses' as well. The shield goes OVER the glasses, not in place of them; ordinary glasses must be 'rated as safety eyewear' as well as fitted with side shields; and the rule applies 'while any machine is operating', not at all times (over-claim).

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: The pilot signals the deck crew when the chocks and chains may be removed.
An aircraft being moved on the flight deck must stay secured by six chains.
Once the director signals, all chains may come off before the brakes are set.
In forecast heavy weather, eight chains on a parked aircraft are not enough.
questions.passage: On the flight deck, an aircraft that is not being moved shall be secured with chocks and at least six tie-down chains. When heavy weather is forecast, the number of chains shall be increased to at least twelve. Chocks and chains may be removed only on the signal of the aircraft director, and the final chains shall not be removed until the pilot has set the brakes.
questions.explain: In forecast heavy weather a parked aircraft needs 'at least twelve' chains, so eight falls short. Removal is 'on the signal of the aircraft director', not the pilot; the six-chain rule covers an aircraft 'that is not being moved' (scope shift); and 'the final chains shall not be removed until the pilot has set the brakes', whatever the director signals.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: A vehicle doing 8 mph 15 feet from a parked aircraft is over the limit.
A vehicle may pass under an aircraft's wing if a spotter is guiding it.
Within 25 feet of a parked aircraft, vehicles may travel at up to 10 miles per hour.
A spotter must guide every vehicle that moves within 25 feet of an aircraft.
questions.passage: Vehicles operating on the flight line shall not exceed 10 miles per hour, or 5 miles per hour within 25 feet of any aircraft. Vehicles shall not be driven under any part of an aircraft, and a vehicle backing toward an aircraft shall be guided by a spotter. Only vehicles with a current flight line permit may be driven past the entry control point.
questions.explain: Within 25 feet of 'any aircraft' the limit is 5 miles per hour, and 8 exceeds it. No vehicle may be driven 'under any part of an aircraft', spotter or not; 'any aircraft' includes parked ones, so 10 mph is wrong there; and a spotter is required only for a vehicle 'backing toward an aircraft' (over-claim).

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Every maintenance task must be inspected by a collateral duty inspector.
Inspectors may check their own work when no other qualified inspector is available on shift.
An inspector who does a quality assurance task needs another inspector to check it.
The inspection may be completed after the maintenance action is signed off.
questions.passage: Certain maintenance tasks are designated as quality assurance items because an error in them could endanger the aircraft. Each such task shall be inspected by a collateral duty inspector before the maintenance action is signed off. The inspector may not be the person who performed the task, even if that person is also qualified as an inspector. The inspector's signature certifies that the task was completed correctly.
questions.explain: The task must be inspected, and the inspector 'may not be the person who performed the task, even if that person is also qualified' — so a second person is needed. Only 'certain' tasks are quality assurance items (over-claim); no 'unavailable' exception exists; and the inspection comes 'before the maintenance action is signed off' (reversed order).

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: An aircraft could be released even though the missing tool is never found.
A broken tool is not counted as missing if its largest piece is recovered.
Tool containers need to be inventoried only when they are returned.
All aircraft on the flight line are held when any tool is reported missing.
questions.passage: Each tool container shall be inventoried before it is issued and again when it is returned. If a tool is found missing on return, the aircraft on which the container was used shall not be released for flight until the tool has been found or the aircraft has been inspected and certified free of it. A broken tool counts as missing unless all of its pieces are recovered.
questions.explain: The aircraft is held 'until the tool has been found OR the aircraft has been inspected and certified free of it' — the second route releases it without finding the tool. A broken tool counts as missing 'unless ALL of its pieces are recovered'; inventories happen before issue AND on return; and only 'the aircraft on which the container was used' is held (scope shift).

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: Noncritical actions are completed before the critical actions are begun.
Not every step of an emergency procedure must be performed from memory.
Pilots must recite every step of each emergency procedure before a flight check.
Critical actions are performed by reading them aloud from the checklist.
questions.passage: Emergency procedures in the aircraft checklist are divided into critical actions, which are printed in bold type and must be performed from memory, and noncritical actions, which may be performed by reading the checklist. Pilots shall be able to recite every critical action word for word before a flight check. Once the critical actions are complete, the crew shall refer to the checklist to finish the remaining steps.
questions.explain: Only critical actions 'must be performed from memory'; noncritical ones 'may be performed by reading the checklist', so not every step is memorized. The checklist is consulted 'once the critical actions are complete' (reversed order); word-for-word recital covers 'every critical action', not every step (scope shift); and critical actions are done 'from memory', not read.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Any crew member may depart from the manual when he or she judges it necessary.
The aircraft commander may depart from the manual whenever a quicker method exists.
A departure from the manual can be justified and still have to be reported.
A departure from the manual must be approved before the aircraft commander makes it.
questions.passage: The flight manual sets the standard procedures against which crews are trained and evaluated, but it is not a substitute for sound judgment. Compound emergencies, weather or other unforeseen circumstances may make it necessary to deviate from its procedures. In such cases the aircraft commander may depart from the manual to the extent necessary to protect the aircraft and crew, but shall report any such departure after landing.
questions.explain: The aircraft commander 'may depart from the manual' when circumstances require it, 'but shall report any such departure after landing' — permitted, yet reported. The authority belongs to 'the aircraft commander', not any crew member; it extends only 'to the extent necessary to protect the aircraft and crew', not to convenience; and the report comes 'after landing', with no prior approval mentioned.

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: Confidential material must be destroyed in the presence of two cleared persons.
Secret material may be destroyed in any available office shredder or by burning.
A destruction record must be kept for all classified material that is destroyed.
The minimum team for destroying Secret material is larger than for Confidential.
questions.passage: Secret material shall be destroyed by an approved method, such as burning or shredding in an approved shredder, in the presence of two cleared persons. Both persons shall sign the destruction record. Confidential material may be destroyed by a single cleared person, and no destruction record is required for it. Material awaiting destruction shall be safeguarded in the same way as other material of its classification.
questions.explain: Secret destruction needs 'two cleared persons', while Confidential 'may be destroyed by a single cleared person' — so the Secret minimum is larger. The two-person rule is for Secret only (scope shift); the shredder must be 'approved'; and 'no destruction record is required' for Confidential material, so 'all classified material' over-claims.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Combinations must be changed on a fixed annual schedule as well as on these occasions.
A member's transfer from the command could make a combination change necessary.
The combination record may be kept inside the container it opens if the envelope is sealed.
A combination needs to be changed only once a compromise has actually been confirmed.
questions.passage: The combination of a security container shall be changed when the container is first placed in use, when any person who knows the combination no longer requires access, and when the combination is suspected of being compromised. A record of the combination shall be kept in a sealed envelope stored in a separate container that is cleared to the same level as the material it protects.
questions.explain: A transferring member who knew the combination 'no longer requires access', which is one of the listed triggers. A yearly change may be common practice, but the passage never states it; the record goes in 'a separate container'; and a change follows a SUSPECTED compromise and other events, not only a confirmed one.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: A force gains tempo whenever it slows down at some point in an operation.
Two forces moving at the same speed can still differ in tempo.
A force raises its tempo only by acting faster than its enemy at every stage.
A force with a higher tempo than its enemy will win the engagement.
questions.passage: Tempo is the rate at which a force acts relative to its enemy, not simply the speed at which it moves. A force that acts faster than its enemy can respond forces the enemy to react to situations that have already changed. Tempo may therefore be gained by slowing down at one point in order to act more quickly at a decisive one.
questions.explain: Tempo is 'the rate at which a force acts relative to its enemy, not simply the speed at which it moves', so equal speed does not mean equal tempo: what counts is acting faster than the enemy can respond. 'Whenever it slows down' over-claims: slowing gains tempo only 'in order to act more quickly at a decisive' point. 'At every stage' contradicts the last sentence, which allows slowing at one point. Winning the engagement is never stated; the passage says only that the enemy is forced to react to situations that have already changed.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: Settling a member's problem does not let a division officer cancel the mast.
A member must tell the division officer the subject before the request is forwarded.
The executive officer may deny the request once the matter has been resolved.
A request for mast goes straight to the commanding officer, bypassing the chain.
questions.passage: Any member may request mast to speak personally with the commanding officer about a matter of concern. The request shall be forwarded through the chain of command without delay, and each person in the chain may try to resolve the matter. However, no one in the chain may deny the request or require the member to state its subject, and the member may still see the commanding officer even if the matter appears to have been resolved.
questions.explain: Each person 'may try to resolve the matter', but 'no one in the chain may deny the request', and the member may see the CO 'even if the matter appears to have been resolved'. No one may 'require the member to state its subject'; the executive officer is part of the chain and has no power to deny; and the request is 'forwarded through the chain of command', not around it.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Whenever two orders conflict, the member must report it to the first superior.
The first superior need not be told of a conflict if the new order is withdrawn.
A member who obeys the new order without raising the conflict is not responsible for it.
The member must get the first superior's consent before obeying the new order.
questions.passage: A member who receives an order that conflicts with an earlier order from another superior shall inform the person giving the new order of the conflict. If that person withdraws the new order, the earlier order stands and nothing further is required. If that person directs that the new order be carried out, the member shall obey it and, as soon as practicable, report the matter to the superior who gave the earlier order. Responsibility for the conflict then rests with the person who insisted on the new order.
questions.explain: If the new order is withdrawn, 'the earlier order stands and nothing further is required'; the report to the earlier superior is required only when the new order is insisted upon. 'Whenever… must report' ignores that withdrawal case. Responsibility shifts only after the member has informed the new superior and that person 'insisted', so the passage never relieves a member who skipped that step; and the first superior is told 'as soon as practicable' after obeying, not asked for consent beforehand.

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: In condition Yoke, opening a Z closure needs no permission from damage control central.
At general quarters, opening a Y closure needs damage control central's permission.
In condition Zebra, closures marked X may be opened without damage control central's permission.
Closures marked Z are shut in every material condition the ship sets.
questions.passage: Watertight closures aboard ship are marked to show when they must be shut. Closures marked X are shut in every material condition. Closures marked Y are shut in condition Yoke and condition Zebra, and closures marked Z are shut only in condition Zebra, which is set for general quarters. Opening any closure that is required to be shut requires the permission of damage control central.
questions.explain: General quarters is condition Zebra, Y closures are shut 'in condition Yoke and condition Zebra', and opening any closure 'required to be shut requires the permission of damage control central', so a Y closure at general quarters needs permission. The Yoke/Z option is tempting, but the passage states only when permission IS needed; it never says other closures need none (denying the antecedent). X closures are shut in every condition, so opening one always needs permission; and 'every condition' describes X, not Z (swapped).

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The reflash watch is secured as soon as the fire has been reported out.
Personnel may need to stay at a fire scene for some time after the fire is out.
Once the reflash watch is secured, the space may be entered without breathing apparatus.
The reflash watch is responsible for testing the space for oxygen and toxic gases.
questions.passage: After a fire has been reported out, a reflash watch shall be posted at the scene with a charged hose or a ready extinguisher. The watch shall remain until the on-scene leader confirms that the space has cooled and that all smoldering material has been removed. The space shall then be ventilated and tested for oxygen and toxic gases before anyone enters it without breathing apparatus.
questions.explain: The reflash watch is posted 'after a fire has been reported out' and remains until the space has cooled and smoldering material is gone — personnel stay after the fire is out. Securing on report reverses that; after the watch, the space must still be 'ventilated and tested' before entry without breathing apparatus; and the passage never says who does the testing.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: With 55-knot winds forecast, the lines are doubled and the commanding officer is informed.
With 40-knot winds forecast, the commanding officer must decide whether to get underway.
The officer of the deck gets the ship underway whenever winds above 50 knots are forecast.
Mooring lines are doubled up only after winds above 35 knots have actually arrived.
questions.passage: When the ship is moored and winds above 35 knots are forecast, the officer of the deck shall have the mooring lines doubled up and shall station a line-handling party on deck. An additional anchor shall be made ready for letting go. If the winds are forecast to exceed 50 knots, the commanding officer shall also be informed so that a decision can be made whether to get underway.
questions.explain: A 55-knot forecast is above 35 knots, so the lines are doubled, and above 50 knots, so the CO 'shall also be informed'. Forty knots does not pass the 50-knot trigger; the CO is informed so 'a decision can be made', and the OOD is never given that decision; and the action follows the FORECAST, not the arrival of the wind.

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: Passengers may remove their life jackets once the boat officer has inspected them.
When a boat officer is embarked, the boat officer takes over handling the boat.
A boat officer is required on every trip made more than two miles from the ship.
A boat six miles from the ship carries someone responsible for passenger conduct.
questions.passage: Every person embarked in a ship's boat shall wear a life jacket while the boat is underway. A boat officer shall be assigned whenever the boat operates at night, in restricted visibility or more than five miles from the ship. The coxswain remains responsible for handling the boat, but the boat officer is responsible for its safety and for the conduct of the passengers.
questions.explain: Six miles is 'more than five miles from the ship', so a boat officer is assigned, and the boat officer 'is responsible… for the conduct of the passengers'. Life jackets are worn 'while the boat is underway' with no inspection exception; 'the coxswain remains responsible for handling the boat'; and the distance trigger is five miles, not two.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: The chairman of the qualification board signs the final qualification letter.
Any qualified petty officer may sign off any item in the qualification standard.
A member with all items signed off is not yet qualified to stand watch alone.
A member may go before the qualification board once most items are signed off.
questions.passage: A qualification standard lists the knowledge and practical factors a member must demonstrate before standing a watch alone. Each item shall be signed off by a person who is already qualified in that watch station or a higher one. After all items are signed, the member appears before a qualification board, and only the commanding officer may sign the final qualification letter.
questions.explain: Signing off all items is followed by a qualification board and a final letter that 'only the commanding officer may sign', so the member is not yet qualified. The board chairman is not the CO; the signer must be qualified 'in that watch station or a higher one', not merely any qualified petty officer; and the board comes 'after all items are signed'.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: After 200 days without an arrested landing, a pilot needs only two daylight landings before night ones.
After 60 days without an arrested landing, a pilot needs two daylight landings before night ones.
After 120 days without an arrested landing, a pilot needs no practice ashore before night landings.
After 100 days without an arrested landing, a pilot needs four daylight landings before night ones.
questions.passage: A pilot who has not made an arrested landing aboard ship within the past 90 days shall complete at least two arrested landings in daylight before making any at night. A pilot who has not made one within 180 days shall first complete a period of practice landings ashore, followed by at least four daylight arrested landings, before making any at night.
questions.explain: At 120 days the pilot is past 90 but within 180, so only the first rule applies: two daylight arrested landings, with no ashore practice. At 200 days the 180-day rule requires ashore practice plus four daylight landings; at 60 days neither rule applies; and at 100 days the requirement is two daylight landings, not four.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: Aircrew with expired training may fly over water if the commanding officer approves.
Aircrew whose training has expired may still fly some missions if their CO approves.
Aircrew who fail the swimming portion may retake it as often as needed within 30 days.
Aircrew must complete water survival training at least once in every year of flight duty.
questions.passage: All personnel assigned to flight duties shall complete water survival training, which includes a swim test and underwater egress, every four years. Personnel whose training has expired shall not fly over water, but they may continue to fly over land until they are retrained, provided their commanding officer approves. Personnel who fail the swimming portion may retake it once within 30 days.
questions.explain: Personnel whose training has expired 'may continue to fly over land… provided their commanding officer approves'. The CO's approval covers flying over LAND only — over water is barred outright; the swim may be retaken 'once', not repeatedly; and the cycle is 'every four years', not yearly.

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: A medical waiver excuses the member from the body composition assessment as well.
A waiver granted in one cycle also covers the cycle that follows it.
A member waived in any two cycles is referred to a medical officer for review.
A member holding a medical waiver may still be measured during that cycle.
questions.passage: A member who receives a medical waiver for the physical readiness test is excused from that test but shall still complete the body composition assessment. A waiver applies only to the current test cycle. Members who are waived in two consecutive cycles shall be referred to a medical officer for a review of their fitness for continued duty.
questions.explain: A waived member is excused from the test 'but shall still complete the body composition assessment' — so is still measured. The first choice reverses that; a waiver covers 'only the current test cycle'; and referral follows waivers in two CONSECUTIVE cycles, not any two.

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: A Marine could go over a year between rifle qualifications without breaking the rule.
A Marine who fails to qualify may make a second attempt only after 60 days have passed.
Deployed Marines are exempt from qualifying for the whole year of their deployment.
A Marine returning from deployment must qualify within 60 days of returning.
questions.passage: Marines shall qualify with the service rifle once each fiscal year. A Marine who fails to qualify shall be scheduled for remedial training and a second attempt within 60 days. Marines deployed where no qualified range is available are exempt until they return, but they must qualify within 90 days of returning. Qualification scores are entered in each Marine's training record.
questions.explain: A Marine deployed where no range is available is exempt 'until they return' and then has '90 days of returning' to qualify, so the gap can exceed a year. The second attempt comes 'within 60 days', not after; the exemption depends on no qualified range being available and lasts only until return; and the post-deployment window is 90 days, not 60.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A statement arriving on 10 April from a member shown the report on 1 March is returned unread.
A member who signs the report shares responsibility with the reporting senior for its accuracy.
A member who agrees with the report must sign it within 30 days of being shown it.
A member who submits a statement in time will have the report's marks reconsidered.
questions.passage: The reporting senior signs each evaluation and is responsible for its accuracy. Before signing, the reporting senior shall show the completed report to the member being evaluated and give the member the opportunity to sign it. The member's signature acknowledges only that he or she has seen the report, not agreement with it. A member who disagrees may submit a written statement within 30 days of being shown the report; a statement received after that is returned unread. A member who declines to sign may still submit a statement within the same period.
questions.explain: A statement must arrive 'within 30 days of being shown the report', which runs out on 31 March, and 'a statement received after that is returned unread', so one arriving on 10 April is returned. Responsibility for accuracy belongs to 'the reporting senior', and the member's signature acknowledges 'only' having seen the report; the 30-day limit applies to statements, not to signing; and the passage never says what is done with a timely statement (unstated).

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: A report is adverse only if most of its trait marks are below the standard.
A member's statement is removed from the report once the reporting senior endorses it.
A member's statement on an adverse report is added only after the report is filed.
A report with acceptable marks in every trait can still be adverse.
questions.passage: A fitness report is adverse if it contains a mark below the standard in any performance trait or a comment describing substandard performance. Before an adverse report is filed, the member shall be given the report and allowed to submit a statement. The statement, together with any endorsement the reporting senior adds to it, becomes a permanent part of the report.
questions.explain: A report is adverse if it has a below-standard mark 'OR a comment describing substandard performance', so a comment alone makes it adverse. One mark below standard in 'any' trait is enough, not most; the statement and endorsement become 'a permanent part of the report'; and the member is allowed to submit a statement 'before an adverse report is filed'.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: The working uniform may be worn into any business off the installation.
Service uniforms may never be worn to a restaurant where meals are served at the table.
In some places a member may not be free to wear service uniform off base.
The working uniform may be worn to a table-service restaurant at lunch.
questions.passage: Members may wear the working uniform while commuting and while making brief stops at businesses on the way to or from work, such as for fuel or groceries. The working uniform shall not be worn to restaurants where meals are served at the table, to bars or to entertainment venues. Service and dress uniforms may be worn off the installation at any time unless a local commander has restricted their wear.
questions.explain: Service uniforms may be worn off the installation 'unless a local commander has restricted their wear', so a local restriction can bar them. The working uniform is limited to brief stops and barred from table-service restaurants, bars and entertainment venues; the restaurant ban applies to the WORKING uniform, not service uniforms (scope shift); and lunch breaks are not an exception.

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: An officer's unduly familiar relationship with a sailor at another command is prohibited.
Unduly familiar ties between chiefs and junior sailors are banned even across different commands.
Officers and enlisted members may not have any personal friendship with each other.
The officer and enlisted prohibition applies only when one member supervises the other.
questions.passage: Personal relationships between officers and enlisted members that are unduly familiar and do not respect differences in grade are prohibited. This prohibition applies whether or not the members are in the same chain of command. Relationships between chief petty officers and junior enlisted members assigned to the same command are prohibited on the same basis, since such relationships can create the appearance of favoritism.
questions.explain: The officer and enlisted prohibition 'applies whether or not the members are in the same chain of command', so a sailor at another command is covered. The chief and junior-sailor rule is limited to members 'assigned to the same command'; only relationships that are 'unduly familiar' are barred, not all friendship; and the chain-of-command sentence rules out a supervision-only reading.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: Members may not speak to reporters at all without public affairs authorization.
The public affairs officer may authorize the release of classified information.
Public affairs approval cannot clear a member to discuss future operations.
Members may discuss future operations as long as the details are unclassified.
questions.passage: Members may discuss their personal experiences with the news media, but they may not speak on behalf of the command unless authorized by the public affairs officer. Information that is classified or that relates to future operations shall not be discussed under any circumstances. Members who are uncertain whether information may be released shall refer the question to the public affairs officer.
questions.explain: Future operations 'shall not be discussed under any circumstances', and authorization does not lift that. Members 'may discuss their personal experiences' without authorization, which defeats the first choice; classified information is also barred 'under any circumstances'; and the future-operations ban is separate from classification ('classified OR… future operations').

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: A qualified sailor not on the current watch bill would not be issued a watch weapon.
A weapon is cleared at the clearing barrel only when it is returned to the armory.
Any member listed on the current watch bill may draw a watch weapon from the armory.
Ammunition is issued already loaded in the weapon so it can be counted with it.
questions.passage: Weapons for watchstanders shall be issued from the armory only to personnel listed on the current watch bill who also hold a current weapons qualification. Each weapon shall be cleared at the clearing barrel under the armorer's supervision when it is issued and again when it is returned. Ammunition shall be issued separately and counted in the presence of the watchstander.
questions.explain: Weapons go 'only to personnel listed on the current watch bill who also hold a current weapons qualification' — both conditions — so a qualified sailor off the watch bill fails one. Clearing happens on issue AND return; a listed member without a current qualification fails the other condition; and ammunition is 'issued separately'.

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: Essential personnel may approach from any side once the pilot gives a thumbs-up.
All personnel must stay at least 50 feet away while the rotors are turning.
The tail rotor area may be approached once the pilot has given a thumbs-up.
Even an essential crew member may not approach a turning helicopter from behind.
questions.passage: Before rotors are engaged on the flight deck, all personnel except those essential to the evolution shall clear the area within 50 feet of the helicopter. Essential personnel shall approach or leave the helicopter only from the front, within the pilot's field of view, and only after receiving a thumbs-up from the pilot. No one shall approach the tail rotor area while the rotors are turning.
questions.explain: Essential personnel approach 'only from the front, within the pilot's field of view', and no one approaches the tail rotor area while rotors turn. The thumbs-up is an additional condition, not a substitute for approaching from the front; the 50-foot rule excludes 'those essential to the evolution'; and 'no one' may approach the tail rotor area, thumbs-up or not.

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: An aircraft outdoors not facing into the wind may be jacked in a 20-knot wind.
A mechanic may stay in the cockpit during jacking to watch the aircraft's attitude.
The jacks are raised one at a time, and the aircraft is leveled afterward.
Wind alone would not stop jacking an outdoor aircraft facing into a 20-knot wind.
questions.passage: An aircraft shall not be jacked when the wind exceeds 25 knots, or 15 knots if the aircraft is outdoors and not facing into the wind. During jacking, no one shall be in the cockpit or under the aircraft except the jack operators, and the jacks shall be raised evenly so that the aircraft remains level throughout. A jacked aircraft shall never be left unattended.
questions.explain: The 15-knot limit applies only to an aircraft 'outdoors and NOT facing into the wind'; one facing into the wind falls under the 25-knot limit, and 20 is below it. An aircraft not facing into the wind is limited to 15 knots, so 20 is too much; no one but the jack operators may be in the cockpit or under the aircraft; and the jacks are raised 'evenly so that the aircraft remains level throughout'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Any damage found in a borescope inspection requires the engine to be removed.
An engine with confirmed foreign object damage could still be flown.
An engine found undamaged must be reinspected after its next 10 flight hours.
A borescope inspection is needed only when an ingestion is known to have occurred.
questions.passage: Any engine suspected of ingesting a foreign object shall be inspected with a borescope before further flight. If damage is found that is within the limits given in the maintenance manual, the engine may remain in service but shall be reinspected after the next 10 flight hours. Damage beyond those limits requires removal of the engine. The results of every inspection shall be entered in the engine's logbook.
questions.explain: Damage 'within the limits… may remain in service', so a damaged engine can keep flying. Removal is required only for damage 'beyond those limits'; the 10-hour reinspection applies to engines with within-limits damage, not undamaged ones; and the inspection follows a SUSPECTED ingestion, not only a known one.

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: A higher heat stress index calls for a longer rest in a cool space before re-entering.
After resting for a full stay time, a member who had symptoms may go back in later that day.
Stay-time limits apply in every working space, whatever its heat stress index.
The minimum rest after a full stay time is shorter when the index is higher.
questions.passage: In any space where the heat stress index exceeds the posted limit, personnel shall work only for the stay time shown on the heat stress chart for that index, and stay times are shorter at higher index values. A member who has used up a stay time must rest in a cool space for at least that long before re-entering. A member who shows symptoms of heat illness shall be removed immediately, regardless of how much of the stay time remains, and shall not re-enter a hot space for the rest of the day.
questions.explain: After a full stay time the member must rest 'for at least that long', so the minimum rest equals the stay time, and stay times 'are shorter at higher index values'; so a higher index means a shorter minimum rest. The 'longer rest' option matches common sense but reverses what the passage sets out; a member with symptoms 'shall not re-enter a hot space for the rest of the day', whatever rest is taken; and the limits apply only where the index 'exceeds the posted limit'.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: In an in-port emergency, the duty officer may act before telling the commanding officer.
The command duty officer may grant leave while the commanding officer is ashore.
The duty officer must reach the commanding officer before taking emergency action.
The command duty officer may impose nonjudicial punishment during an in-port emergency.
questions.passage: In port, the command duty officer is the commanding officer's direct representative and is responsible for the safety and security of the ship. The command duty officer may take any action the commanding officer would take in an emergency, but shall inform the commanding officer of the situation as soon as possible. The command duty officer may not grant leave or impose nonjudicial punishment.
questions.explain: The duty officer 'may take any action the commanding officer would take in an emergency' and informs the CO 'as soon as possible' — action can come first. Granting leave and imposing nonjudicial punishment are barred outright, with no exception for the CO's absence or an emergency; and informing the CO is not a precondition for acting.

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: Restriction imposed before a hearing is a form of punishment in itself.
Time spent on pre-hearing restriction must be deducted from any later punishment.
A restricted member chooses the times at which to muster with the duty officer.
Time already spent on restriction might lighten a member's later punishment.
questions.passage: A member placed on restriction shall not go beyond the limits specified in the restriction order and shall muster with the duty officer at the times the order sets. Restriction imposed before a hearing is not a punishment in itself; it is used to ensure the member's presence. Time spent on such pre-hearing restriction may be taken into account when punishment is later decided.
questions.explain: Pre-hearing restriction time 'may be taken into account when punishment is later decided', so it can lighten the result. Pre-hearing restriction 'is not a punishment in itself' (reversed); 'may be taken into account' is not 'must be deducted' (over-claim); and the muster times are those 'the order sets'.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: Any member of the team may take command if the boarding officer becomes incapacitated.
A team with two qualified boarding officers could continue if one is incapacitated.
A boarding team must consist of exactly two members, one of them its leader.
The pre-boarding brief may be skipped for a vessel that has been boarded before.
questions.passage: A boarding team shall consist of at least two members, one of whom is a qualified boarding officer who leads the team. Before boarding, the team shall be briefed on the vessel's description and any known hazards. If the boarding officer becomes incapacitated during the boarding, the team shall withdraw unless another qualified boarding officer is present to assume command.
questions.explain: The team withdraws 'unless another qualified boarding officer is present to assume command', and a second qualified officer is exactly that. Only a QUALIFIED boarding officer can assume command; 'at least two members' is a minimum, not an exact number; and the brief is required 'before boarding' with no exception for earlier boardings.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: An aircraft that flies twice in one day needs a new daily inspection before its second flight.
After exposure to heavy weather, a turnaround inspection alone cannot clear the aircraft to fly.
The 72-hour period starts again each time a turnaround inspection is completed.
A turnaround inspection may replace a daily inspection if there has been no heavy weather.
questions.passage: A daily inspection remains valid for 72 hours unless the aircraft is exposed to conditions listed in the maintenance manual, such as heavy weather, in which case a new daily inspection is required before flight. Between flights in that period, a less detailed turnaround inspection shall be completed. A daily inspection may be done in place of a turnaround inspection, but a turnaround inspection may never be done in place of a daily inspection.
questions.explain: Heavy weather is one of the listed conditions, so 'a new daily inspection is required before flight', and 'a turnaround inspection may never be done in place of a daily inspection'; together, a turnaround alone cannot clear the aircraft. Two flights inside the 72-hour period need only a turnaround between them; nothing says a turnaround restarts the 72 hours (unstated); and a turnaround 'may never' replace a daily inspection, weather or not.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The tidal range at a new moon is smaller than at a full moon.
The tidal range at a first-quarter moon is smaller than at a new moon.
Spring tides recur at intervals of about two weeks, once at each new and full moon.
The sun's pull on the oceans is stronger than the moon's pull on them.
questions.passage: Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the moon, with a smaller contribution from the sun. When the sun and moon are aligned, at new moon and at full moon, their pulls combine to produce spring tides, which have the greatest range between high and low water. When the sun and moon are at right angles to each other, at the first-quarter and last-quarter moons, their pulls partly cancel, producing neap tides with the smallest range.
questions.explain: A first-quarter moon gives neap tides with 'the smallest range', while a new moon gives spring tides with 'the greatest range', so the quarter-moon range is smaller. New moon and full moon are grouped together as spring tides, with no comparison between them (scope shift); the two-week interval may be true in life but the passage never gives it; and the moon is the main cause with the sun's contribution 'smaller' (reversed).

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: A wind that keeps blowing at the same speed will make the waves grow higher without limit.
The same wind may raise smaller waves on a small lake than on the open ocean.
Swell is raised by the local wind at the coast where it arrives.
Wind speed matters more than fetch or duration in setting the height of the waves.
questions.passage: The height of wind-driven waves depends on three factors: the speed of the wind, the length of time it has blown, and the fetch, which is the distance of open water over which it blows. Increasing any one factor tends to build larger waves, but only up to a point; once the sea is fully developed for a given wind speed, the waves stop growing however much longer the wind blows. Swell consists of waves that have traveled out of the area where they were generated, and it can reach a coast under a calm sky.
questions.explain: Fetch is 'the distance of open water over which it blows', and a larger fetch tends to build larger waves, so a small lake can limit wave height compared with the ocean. Waves 'stop growing however much longer the wind blows' once the sea is fully developed (over-claim); swell has 'traveled out of the area where [it was] generated' and can arrive under a calm sky (reversed); and the passage never ranks the three factors (true-sounding but unstated).

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: A target may know it is being searched for before the searcher detects it.
Passive sonar finds a target's range from the time an echo takes to return to the ship.
A submarine making no sound at all would be easy to find with passive sonar.
Active sonar can detect targets at longer ranges than passive sonar is able to.
questions.passage: Active sonar transmits a pulse of sound and listens for the echo returned by a target; the time the echo takes to return gives the target's range. Passive sonar transmits nothing and simply listens for sounds the target itself makes, such as machinery or propeller noise. An active pulse can be heard by the target at a greater distance than the one at which its echo can be detected by the ship that sent it.
questions.explain: The target can hear the pulse 'at a greater distance' than the searcher can detect the echo, so at some ranges the target knows it is being searched for while the searcher still has nothing. Echo timing belongs to ACTIVE sonar, since passive 'transmits nothing' (swapped); passive sonar listens for sounds 'the target itself makes', so a silent target would be hard, not easy, to find (reversed); and the passage never compares the detection ranges of the two methods (unstated).

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: In the Northern Hemisphere, air moving south is deflected to the left of its path.
The Coriolis effect is stronger at 40 degrees north than at 10 degrees north.
Water draining from a sink swirls in opposite directions in the two hemispheres.
Hurricanes almost never form anywhere in the Southern Hemisphere.
questions.passage: Because the earth rotates, moving air and water are deflected from a straight path, an effect named after the scientist Coriolis. In the Northern Hemisphere the deflection is to the right of the direction of motion, and in the Southern Hemisphere it is to the left. The effect is zero at the equator and grows stronger toward the poles, which is one reason hurricanes almost never form within about five degrees of the equator.
questions.explain: The effect 'grows stronger toward the poles', and 40 degrees north is closer to the pole than 10 degrees north. In the Northern Hemisphere the deflection is to the right whatever the direction of motion (logic twist); the sink claim is a popular belief the passage never mentions; and 'almost never form' applies only 'within about five degrees of the equator' (scope shift).

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Lightning occurs only during the mature stage, when updrafts and downdrafts coexist.
A storm with rain falling from its base has moved beyond the cumulus stage.
Updrafts dominate a thunderstorm during its dissipating stage.
Most thunderstorm cells complete all three stages in about an hour.
questions.passage: A thunderstorm passes through three stages. In the cumulus stage, the cloud is dominated by updrafts and grows rapidly upward. The mature stage begins when precipitation starts to fall from the base of the cloud; falling rain drags air down with it, so updrafts and downdrafts exist side by side, and turbulence, lightning and hail are usually at their worst. In the dissipating stage, downdrafts dominate and the storm gradually rains itself out.
