questions.explain: The mature stage 'begins when precipitation starts to fall from the base of the cloud', so rain from the base means the cumulus stage is over. Lightning is 'usually at [its] worst' in the mature stage, not confined to it (over-claim); DOWNDRAFTS dominate the dissipating stage (reversed); and the passage gives no duration (true-sounding but unstated).

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: Rain may begin at a place well before a warm front's surface position reaches it.
Warm fronts typically bring a narrow band of showers or thunderstorms that passes quickly.
At any one place, cold-front showers usually last longer than warm-front rain.
Cold fronts are most common during the winter months.
questions.passage: A cold front forms where a mass of cold air advances and wedges under warmer air, lifting it sharply. Because the lifting is abrupt, a cold front tends to produce a narrow band of showers or thunderstorms that passes quickly. At a warm front, warm air slides gradually up over retreating cold air, producing a broad area of layered cloud and steady precipitation that can extend hundreds of miles ahead of the front's position at the surface.
questions.explain: Warm-front precipitation 'can extend hundreds of miles ahead of the front's position at the surface', so it can start long before the front arrives. The narrow band of storms belongs to the COLD front (swapped); cold-front weather 'passes quickly' while warm-front rain is broad and steady (reversed); and no season is mentioned (unstated).

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Mountain waves form on the upwind side of the ridge.
Smooth lens-shaped clouds downwind of a ridge are a sign that the air is dry.
Even a light wind blowing across a ridge will set up a series of mountain waves.
Clear skies downwind of a ridge do not show that rotor turbulence is absent.
questions.passage: When strong winds blow roughly at right angles across a mountain ridge, the air flowing over the crest can set up a series of waves extending many miles downwind. Beneath the wave crests, rotors of violently turbulent air may form near the level of the ridge tops. If the air is moist, smooth lens-shaped clouds may mark the wave crests and ragged roll clouds may mark the rotors; in dry air, the same waves and rotors can be present with no clouds at all.
questions.explain: 'In dry air, the same waves and rotors can be present with no clouds at all', so a cloudless sky is no guarantee of smooth air. The waves extend 'downwind' (reversed); lens-shaped clouds appear 'if the air is moist' (reversed); and the passage requires 'strong winds' (over-claim that drops the condition).

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: A pilot who holds a steady indicated altitude into lower pressure without resetting is descending.
Flying from lower into higher pressure without resetting makes the altimeter read too high.
An altimeter measures the aircraft's height above the ground directly, without using pressure.
A setting made correctly before takeoff remains correct for the whole flight, wherever the aircraft goes.
questions.passage: A pressure altimeter measures the pressure of the surrounding air and displays it as an altitude, using the sea-level pressure that the pilot has set in its window as a reference. If an aircraft flies from an area of higher pressure into one of lower pressure without the setting being updated, the altimeter will read higher than the aircraft's true altitude. Pilots therefore update the setting from nearby reporting stations as they fly.
questions.explain: As pressure falls the altimeter reads 'higher than the aircraft's true altitude'; if the indicated figure is held steady, the true altitude must be dropping below it. Check: indicated stays the same, error grows, so true altitude falls. The passage describes only the high-to-low case, so the reverse case is unsupported (reversed condition); the instrument 'measures the pressure of the surrounding air', not height above ground; and pilots must update the setting in flight, so a pre-takeoff setting does not stay correct.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: Clear air turbulence is most likely where the wind is strong and steady with height.
Clear air turbulence is usually worst in the jet stream's core, where the wind is fastest.
A clear weather radar display is no assurance of smooth air near the jet stream.
Turbulence that weather radar cannot detect occurs only near the jet stream.
questions.passage: The jet stream is a narrow band of strong wind found near the top of the lower atmosphere. Clear air turbulence often occurs near the jet stream, especially where wind speed changes sharply with height or across a short horizontal distance. Because it occurs in cloudless air, it cannot be seen by the pilot, and it is not detected by ordinary weather radar, which senses precipitation rather than the motion of the air.
questions.explain: Clear air turbulence 'often occurs near the jet stream' and 'is not detected by ordinary weather radar', so a clear radar picture does not rule it out there. It is most likely 'where wind speed changes sharply with height', the opposite of steady wind; the passage never says where in the jet stream it is worst, and 'fastest wind' is not the same as sharply changing wind; and 'often occurs near' does not mean 'only near'.

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: An observer at 60 degrees north sees Polaris lower in the sky than an observer at 40 degrees north does.
A navigator can find longitude as well as latitude from the angle of Polaris.
An observer who sees Polaris 30 degrees up is about a third of the way from the equator to the pole.
Polaris is the brightest star visible from the Northern Hemisphere.
questions.passage: In the Northern Hemisphere, a navigator can find latitude from the North Star, Polaris, which lies almost directly above the earth's North Pole. The angle of Polaris above the horizon is approximately equal to the observer's latitude: an observer at the North Pole sees it nearly overhead, 90 degrees up, while an observer at the equator sees it on the horizon. South of the equator, Polaris stays below the horizon and cannot be used.
questions.explain: Polaris's angle equals latitude, running from 0 degrees at the equator to 90 degrees at the pole; 30 is one-third of 90. Check: 30 / 90 = 1/3. A higher latitude means a HIGHER angle, so 60 degrees north sees it higher (reversed); the passage speaks only of latitude, never longitude (unstated); and brightness is never mentioned (a common belief, not stated).

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: A satellite orbiting 10,000 miles up takes less than a day to complete one orbit.
A satellite 22,000 miles above the North Pole would appear motionless from the ground.
A satellite in a low orbit appears to stay fixed over one point on the ground.
Satellites in high orbits travel through space more slowly than low-orbit satellites.
questions.passage: The higher a satellite orbits, the longer it takes to complete one orbit. Satellites in low orbits a few hundred miles up circle the earth in about an hour and a half. At about 22,000 miles above the equator, a satellite takes the same time to complete an orbit as the earth takes to turn once, so it keeps pace with the earth's rotation and appears to hang motionless over one point. Communications and weather satellites are often placed in this orbit so that ground antennas need not track them.
questions.explain: Higher orbits take longer, and at about 22,000 miles the period equals one rotation of the earth (one day), so a satellite at a lower 10,000 miles needs less than a day. The fixed-point effect is stated for an orbit 'above the equator', not above a pole (scope shift); low-orbit satellites circle in about 90 minutes, so they cannot stay fixed (contradicted); and orbital SPEED is never discussed, only time per orbit (true-sounding but unstated).

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A part that has never carried a load near its breaking load cannot fail from fatigue.
Inspections at set intervals will find every fatigue crack before the part breaks.
Two identical parts that have carried the same loads can be in different condition if one has gone through more load cycles.
A part that reaches its set number of cycles must already be cracked.
questions.passage: Metal fatigue is the gradual weakening of a part under repeated cycles of loading, even when each individual load is well below the load that would break the part in a single application. Fatigue usually begins as a microscopic crack at a point where stress is concentrated, such as a rivet hole or a sharp corner, and the crack grows a little with each cycle until, if it is not found, the part eventually breaks. Because a part may show no visible damage until the crack is large, fatigue-critical parts are inspected at set intervals and retired after a set number of cycles.
questions.explain: The crack 'grows a little with each cycle', so more cycles under the same loads means a larger crack and a weaker part. The first option is the trap the passage warns against: fatigue happens 'even when each individual load is well below' the breaking load. Inspection catching every crack over-claims: the passage says only that parts are inspected at intervals, and that cracks may not be visible until large. Retiring a part after a set number of cycles is a precaution; the passage never says such a part is already cracked.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: Composite structures are stronger than aluminum structures of the same weight and size.
Delamination always leaves a visible dent in the panel's surface.
Composite structures never require any form of corrosion inspection.
A visual inspection alone may miss damage that has weakened a composite panel.
questions.passage: Composite structures made of carbon fibers set in resin are lighter than comparable aluminum structures and do not corrode in the same way. However, an impact that leaves only a small dent, or no mark at all, on the surface of a composite panel can separate its internal layers, a condition called delamination that reduces the panel's strength. Technicians therefore inspect suspect panels with ultrasonic or tap testing rather than relying on what they can see.
questions.explain: An impact leaving 'no mark at all' can still cause delamination that 'reduces the panel's strength', which is why technicians do not rely 'on what they can see'. The passage says composites are LIGHTER, not stronger (true-sounding but unstated); damage may leave 'no mark at all' (contradicted); and composites do not corrode 'in the same way', which is not the same as never needing a check (over-claim).

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: A sound source that is moving away from a listener actually produces a lower pitch.
The pitch shift is the same whatever the speed of the source.
Of two identical sources closing on a listener, the faster sounds higher-pitched.
The Doppler effect occurs with sound waves but does not occur with radar waves.
questions.passage: When a source of sound moves toward a listener, the sound waves are crowded together and the listener hears a higher pitch than the source actually produces; when the source moves away, the waves are spread out and the pitch heard is lower. The size of the shift increases with the speed of the source relative to the listener. Sonar operators use this effect, called the Doppler effect, to judge whether a contact is closing or opening.
questions.explain: Both approaching sources are heard higher than they produce, and the shift 'increases with the speed of the source', so the faster one sounds higher. The listener HEARS a lower pitch than the source 'actually produces' (one-word twist from heard to produced); the shift grows with speed (contradicted); and the passage says nothing about radar either way (unstated).

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The same supersonic flight flown lower would put a stronger boom along its whole path.
A supersonic aircraft flying high enough produces no boom at all on the ground.
A listener directly beneath the aircraft hears the boom just as it passes overhead.
A boom is heard only at the spot where the aircraft first exceeds the speed of sound.
questions.passage: An aircraft flying faster than sound continuously trails a cone-shaped shock wave behind it. A sonic boom is heard on the ground wherever this cone sweeps past, so it occurs not just once, at the moment the aircraft passes the speed of sound, but along the entire path of its supersonic flight. The strength of the boom on the ground decreases as the altitude of the aircraft increases.
questions.explain: The boom is heard 'along the entire path of its supersonic flight', and its strength 'decreases as the altitude of the aircraft increases', so flying lower makes it stronger all along the track. 'Decreases' is not 'disappears', so high altitude does not remove the boom; when a listener hears it relative to the aircraft passing overhead is never stated; and 'only where it first exceeds' is the misconception the passage corrects.

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: Vortices can remain over a runway after the aircraft that shed them has gone.
Wingtip vortices rise slowly behind the aircraft that produced them.
A strong crosswind holds a vortex over the runway longer than a light crosswind does.
Only large transport aircraft produce wingtip vortices.
questions.passage: Every wing producing lift sheds a pair of counter-rotating vortices from its tips. The vortices are strongest when the generating aircraft is heavy, slow and in a clean configuration with the flaps up, because the wing must then work at a high angle of attack. Vortices sink slowly behind the aircraft and, near the ground, spread sideways; a light crosswind can hold one vortex over the runway for several minutes.
questions.explain: A light crosswind 'can hold one vortex over the runway for several minutes', long after the generating aircraft has moved on. Vortices 'sink' (reversed); the passage mentions only a LIGHT crosswind and says nothing about a strong one (scope shift); and 'every wing producing lift' sheds vortices (over-claim to 'only large').

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: Ground effect increases the induced drag on an aircraft flying close to the ground surface.
Ground effect is at its strongest at a height of about one wingspan.
Ground effect occurs over hard runways but not over open water.
A plane with a 40-foot wingspan flying 20 feet above a runway has reduced induced drag.
questions.passage: When an aircraft flies within about one wingspan of the ground, the ground interferes with the wing's downwash and wingtip vortices, reducing induced drag. This ground effect allows an aircraft to fly at a lower speed than it could at altitude. An aircraft that lifts off at too low an airspeed may therefore climb a few feet and then sink back, because it cannot sustain flight once it leaves ground effect.
questions.explain: Twenty feet is within one 40-foot wingspan of the ground, and within that height the ground reduces induced drag. Check: 20 < 40 ✓. Ground effect REDUCES induced drag (reversed); 'within about one wingspan' sets the limit of the effect, not where it peaks (misread qualifier); and surfaces are never compared (unstated).

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: A turbojet develops more thrust at high altitude than at sea level because the air there is colder.
Burning more fuel always raises a turbojet's thrust without any limit.
The compressor blades are the part of the engine most limited by heat.
Other things being equal, a turbojet develops more thrust on a cold day than on a hot day.
questions.passage: A turbojet produces thrust by accelerating a mass of air rearward. The thrust it develops depends partly on the mass of air passing through the engine each second, and cold, dense air contains more mass in a given volume than hot, thin air. The temperature of the gases entering the turbine is the main limit on how much fuel can be burned, because the turbine blades weaken if they become too hot.
questions.explain: Thrust depends on the mass of air passing through each second, and cold, dense air carries more mass in a given volume, so a cold day helps. High-altitude air is colder but also thinner, and the passage gives no basis for more thrust there (half-reasoned trap); turbine temperature limits how much fuel can be burned (contradicted); and it is the TURBINE blades that weaken with heat (swapped part).

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: Carburetor ice cannot form when the outside air is above freezing.
Carburetor ice is most likely at full power, with the throttle valve held wide open.
Engines with fuel injection cannot develop carburetor ice.
A pilot flying through humid air at 70°F cannot rule out carburetor ice.
questions.passage: In a float-type carburetor, fuel vaporization and the drop in pressure through the venturi can cool the incoming air by as much as 60°F in a fraction of a second. If the air is moist, ice can form in the venturi and on the throttle valve even when the outside air temperature is well above freezing. Ice is most likely at reduced power settings, when the partly closed throttle valve restricts the flow. In an aircraft with a fixed-pitch propeller, the first sign is usually a drop in engine rpm.
questions.explain: Ice can form in moist air 'even when the outside air temperature is well above freezing', and cooling of up to 60°F can take 70°F air below 32°F. Check: 70 − 60 = 10°F. The first wrong choice contradicts that sentence; ice is most likely at 'reduced power settings' with the throttle partly closed (reversed); and fuel injection is never mentioned (true in life but not stated).

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: Signals from three satellites are enough for a fix of latitude, longitude and altitude.
A receiver in a deep, narrow valley might be unable to fix a three-dimensional position.
GPS signals reach the earth too strong to be overpowered by another transmitter's signal.
GPS satellites each complete about two orbits of the earth every day.
questions.passage: A GPS receiver determines its position by measuring the time that signals take to arrive from several satellites. Signals from at least four satellites are needed for a three-dimensional position, because the receiver must solve for its own clock error as well as for latitude, longitude and altitude. The signals are weak by the time they reach the earth and travel in straight lines, so they can be blocked by terrain or buildings and overpowered by a stronger transmitter on the same frequency.
questions.explain: Terrain can block the straight-line signals, and fewer than four satellites in view rules out a three-dimensional position. Three satellites ignore the fourth unknown, the receiver's clock error; the signals are 'weak' and can be 'overpowered' (contradicted); and orbital periods are never mentioned (true in life but not stated).

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: An inertial system relies on signals from satellites to work out where the vehicle is.
Without updates, an inertial system should be less accurate after ten hours than after one.
An inertial system can work out its position without ever being given a starting point.
Inertial navigation is generally less accurate than satellite navigation over long flights.
questions.passage: An inertial navigation system calculates position by measuring every acceleration of the vehicle with gyroscopes and accelerometers and adding up the results from a known starting point. It needs no signals from outside the vehicle, so it cannot be jammed. Small measurement errors, however, accumulate with each calculation, so the reported position drifts further from the true position the longer the system runs without an update.
questions.explain: Errors 'accumulate', so the position 'drifts further from the true position the longer the system runs without an update' — ten hours allows more drift than one. It 'needs no signals from outside the vehicle' (contradicted); it adds up results 'from a known starting point' (contradicted); and no comparison with satellite navigation is made (true-sounding but unstated).

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: With the pitot fully blocked, the airspeed indicator reads zero in every phase of the flight.
Static pressure rises as an aircraft climbs to a higher altitude.
With a fully blocked pitot, slowing down in level flight will not change the airspeed shown.
A blocked static port produces exactly the same airspeed errors as a blocked pitot tube does.
questions.passage: The airspeed indicator works by comparing ram air pressure from the pitot tube with still air pressure from the static ports. If both the pitot tube's opening and its drain hole become blocked by ice, the air trapped in the pitot line stays at a constant pressure. The indicator then responds only to changes in static pressure, which falls as the aircraft climbs, so the indicated airspeed increases in a climb and decreases in a descent regardless of the actual speed.
questions.explain: With pitot pressure trapped, the indicator responds 'only to changes in static pressure'; in level flight static pressure stays the same, so the reading does not change even as the real speed drops. The indication rises and falls with climbs and descents, so it is not stuck at zero (over-claim); static pressure 'falls as the aircraft climbs' (reversed); and a blocked static port is never discussed (unstated).

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: In fast forward flight, the retreating blade has the higher angle of attack.
At high forward speeds, the advancing blade is the first to stall.
Blade flapping increases the angle of attack of the advancing blade.
A helicopter's top speed is limited mainly by the power its engine can deliver.
questions.passage: In forward flight, a helicopter's advancing rotor blade moves into the relative wind and meets the air at a higher speed than the retreating blade, which moves away from it. Without correction, the advancing side would produce more lift than the retreating side. Blade flapping corrects this imbalance by reducing the angle of attack of the advancing blade and increasing that of the retreating blade. At high forward speeds, the retreating blade's angle of attack can become so large that the blade stalls, which limits the helicopter's top speed.
questions.explain: Flapping reduces the advancing blade's angle of attack and increases the retreating blade's, so the retreating blade ends up higher. The RETREATING blade stalls at high speed (reversed); flapping REDUCES the advancing blade's angle (reversed); and the passage names retreating-blade stall, not engine power, as the speed limit (true-sounding substitute).

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: Deviation for each location is printed on the navigation chart for that area.
Variation is caused by magnetic fields from electrical equipment within the aircraft.
Variation has the same value at every location on earth.
Two aircraft side by side could share the same variation but differ in deviation.
questions.passage: A magnetic compass points toward the magnetic north pole, not the geographic North Pole, and the angle between the two directions at any location is called variation. Variation differs from place to place and is printed on navigation charts. Deviation is a separate error caused by magnetic fields within the aircraft itself, such as those from electrical equipment; because it depends on the aircraft rather than the location, it is recorded on a compass correction card mounted in that aircraft.
questions.explain: Variation depends on location, so two aircraft side by side share it, while deviation 'depends on the aircraft rather than the location', so it can differ. Charts carry VARIATION, and electrical equipment causes DEVIATION — the first two wrong choices swap the terms; and variation 'differs from place to place' (contradicted).

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: After losing oxygen at 18,000 feet, a person notices no symptoms of hypoxia for at least 20 minutes.
Every person has the same time of useful consciousness at a given altitude.
A crewmember exerting himself after a rapid decompression at 30,000 feet may have under a minute.
A gradual loss of oxygen leaves less useful time than a rapid decompression.
questions.passage: Time of useful consciousness is the period after the loss of an oxygen supply during which a person can still perform useful flying duties. It shortens sharply with altitude, from roughly 20 to 30 minutes at 18,000 feet to as little as one or two minutes at 30,000 feet. Physical exertion, fatigue and smoking can all shorten it further, and a rapid decompression can cut it by up to half compared with a gradual loss of oxygen at the same altitude.
questions.explain: At 30,000 feet the time can be one or two minutes, a rapid decompression can cut it 'by up to half', and exertion shortens it 'further', so under a minute is possible. Check: half of one to two minutes is 30 to 60 seconds. Time of useful consciousness measures ability to perform duties, not the onset of symptoms (scope shift); exertion, fatigue and smoking make it vary between people (contradicted); and the rapid decompression is the WORSE case (reversed).

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: A pilot who has lost all vision under high G has necessarily lost consciousness as well.
Under rapid G onset, a pilot waiting for vision to dim before straining may already be unconscious.
Because the anti-G suit works automatically, straining adds no protection to a suited pilot.
Under slowly building G, a pilot will always lose vision before losing consciousness.
questions.passage: During high positive-G maneuvers, blood is pulled toward the lower body and away from the head. As blood flow to the eyes falls, a pilot may first lose peripheral vision and then all vision while still conscious; if the G load keeps rising, consciousness is lost. When G builds very rapidly, however, consciousness can be lost before any visual warning appears. The anti-G suit squeezes the legs and abdomen to limit the pooling of blood, while the anti-G straining maneuver, a forceful tensing of the muscles with controlled breathing, raises blood pressure further. The suit works automatically, but the straining maneuver protects the pilot only while he or she is performing it.
questions.explain: When G builds very rapidly, 'consciousness can be lost before any visual warning appears', and the straining maneuver protects 'only while he or she is performing it', so a pilot who holds off straining until vision dims may be unconscious first. A pilot can lose 'all vision while still conscious' (contradicted); straining 'raises blood pressure further', on top of the suit; and the passage says only that a pilot 'may' lose vision first, not 'always'.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Rods provide the sharp color vision that pilots depend on most when flying at night.
Red cockpit lighting helps a pilot preserve dark adaptation.
At night, a pilot may fail to see a dim light he or she looks straight at.
A brief flash of white light does not affect a fully dark-adapted eye.
questions.passage: The center of the retina contains mainly cones, which give sharp, color vision in good light but work poorly in darkness. Rods, which are concentrated away from the center, are far more sensitive to dim light but do not distinguish color. For this reason, a dim object at night is often seen more easily by looking slightly to one side of it than by looking straight at it. Full dark adaptation of the rods takes about 30 minutes and can be lost within seconds by exposure to bright white light.
questions.explain: Looking straight at an object uses the central cones, which 'work poorly in darkness', so a dim light seen head-on can be missed. Rods 'do not distinguish color' and sharp color vision comes from cones (swapped); red lighting is true in practice but never mentioned; and adaptation 'can be lost within seconds' by bright white light (contradicted).

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: Two days after crossing six time zones, a crew's body clock is still hours off local time.
The body clock fully adjusts to a new time zone after a single good night's sleep.
Alertness is normally at its lowest point in the early afternoon.
Flying eastward across time zones disrupts the body clock more than flying westward does.
questions.passage: Human alertness follows a roughly 24-hour cycle governed by an internal body clock. Alertness is normally lowest between about 0200 and 0600, and a smaller dip often occurs in the early afternoon. Because the body clock adjusts to a new time zone by only about one hour per day, a crew that crosses several time zones may be flying during their body's low point even when local time suggests they should be alert.
questions.explain: At about one hour per day, two days of adjustment leave roughly four of the six hours still to go. Check: 6 − 2 = 4 hours. One-night adjustment contradicts 'only about one hour per day'; the early-afternoon dip is the 'smaller' one, with the lowest point between 0200 and 0600 (misread); and direction of travel is never discussed (true-sounding but unstated).

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: Gas trapped in body cavities contracts as an aircraft climbs.
A crewmember with a cold who climbs comfortably may still get an ear block on descent.
Air must flow into the middle ear on the climb to equalize the pressure.
Scuba diving shortly before a flight raises the risk of decompression sickness at altitude.
questions.passage: As an aircraft climbs, the surrounding pressure falls and gas trapped in body cavities expands. Gas in the middle ear and sinuses usually vents without difficulty on the climb, but on descent the pressure must be equalized by air flowing back in, and a cold or congestion can prevent this. For this reason, most ear blocks occur during descent rather than the climb, and aircrew with colds are commonly kept from flying until they recover.
questions.explain: Venting on the climb 'usually' happens without difficulty, but on descent air must flow back in, which 'a cold or congestion can prevent' — so a trouble-free climb does not rule out a descent block. Gas EXPANDS on the climb (reversed); air flows back in on DESCENT, not the climb (reversed phase); and scuba diving is true aviation advice but never mentioned.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: A runway narrower than usual can lead a pilot to fly a higher approach than intended.
A downsloping runway gives the impression that the aircraft is too high.
On an unusually wide runway, a pilot may fly too high an approach.
Pilots judge their approach path mainly by their flight instruments.
questions.passage: Pilots judge their approach path largely by the apparent shape of the runway ahead. An upsloping runway looks steeper than a level one, giving the impression that the aircraft is too high, so the pilot may respond by flying a lower approach than intended. A runway narrower than the pilot is used to creates the same impression of excessive height, while an unusually wide runway can make the pilot feel too low.
questions.explain: A pilot who feels too high corrects by flying lower; a wide runway makes the pilot 'feel too low', so the same response runs the other way, toward a higher approach. A narrow runway gives the 'same impression of excessive height' as an upslope, which leads LOWER (reversed); a downslope is never described (unstated); and the passage says pilots judge 'largely by the apparent shape of the runway' (contradicted).

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: Rapid forward acceleration gives a pilot the false sense that the nose is pitching down.
The false pitch-up sensation occurs only during catapult launches.
The false pitch-up sensation is a greater danger on a dark night than in clear daylight.
A sudden deceleration gives a pilot the false sense that the aircraft's nose is pitching down.
questions.passage: The inner ear's otolith organs cannot tell the difference between tilting the head back and accelerating forward, since both shift the organs in the same way. During a catapult launch or a rapid acceleration on a go-around, a pilot without good outside visual references may therefore feel that the aircraft's nose is pitching up sharply. A pilot who responds to this false sensation by pushing the nose down can fly into the water or the ground.
questions.explain: The illusion grips a pilot 'without good outside visual references', which describes a dark night far better than clear daylight with a visible horizon. Forward acceleration feels like the nose pitching UP (reversed); a go-around acceleration is also named (over-claim to 'only'); and deceleration may produce the opposite illusion in real life but is never mentioned (true but not stated).

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: Monitor sank Virginia during their fight on March 9.
This was the first battle ever fought between two ironclad warships anywhere.
Monitor took no part in the fighting that sank the two wooden warships.
Shot from the wooden warships pierced Virginia's armor.
questions.passage: On March 8, 1862, the Confederate ironclad CSS Virginia attacked the Union blockading squadron at Hampton Roads, Virginia, sinking two wooden warships whose shot bounced off her armor. The Union ironclad USS Monitor arrived during the following night. On March 9 the two ironclads fought for several hours at close range, neither was able to sink the other, and the battle ended in a draw.
questions.explain: The wooden ships were sunk on March 8, and Monitor arrived 'during the following night', so she was not there. Neither ironclad 'was able to sink the other' (contradicted); 'first ironclad battle' is a well-known fact the passage never states; and the wooden ships' shot 'bounced off her armor' (contradicted).

questions.stem: Which choice can be derived solely from the information in the passage?
options: The copper plates corroded where they touched the iron bolts.
Sheathing let ships stay at sea longer between cleanings.
The copper plates covered the whole hull, above as well as below the waterline.
The expression 'copper-bottomed' comes from this practice.
questions.passage: In the 18th century, the hulls of wooden warships were attacked by shipworms and fouled by weed and barnacles, which slowed the ships and forced frequent returns to port for cleaning. The Royal Navy began covering hulls below the waterline with thin copper plates, which resisted both problems. Early sheathing, however, was fastened with iron bolts, and contact between the copper and the iron in seawater made the bolts corrode until bolts of a copper alloy replaced them.
questions.explain: Fouling 'forced frequent returns to port for cleaning', and the copper 'resisted' fouling, so sheathed ships needed fewer cleaning trips. It was the iron BOLTS that corroded, not the copper (reversed); the plates covered hulls 'below the waterline' only (scope shift); and the origin of the expression is true in life but never stated.

questions.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: The battle's outcome reduced the Japanese carrier strength available at Midway.
Japan lost more carriers than the United States at Coral Sea.
Opposing surface ships exchanged gunfire during the battle.
The United States won at Midway because two of Japan's carriers were absent from it.
questions.passage: The Battle of the Coral Sea in May 1942 was the first naval battle in which the opposing ships never came within sight of each other; every attack was made by carrier aircraft. The Japanese sank the US carrier Lexington, while American aircraft sank one Japanese light carrier and damaged a larger one. Afterward, the Japanese called off their planned seaborne invasion of Port Moresby, and the damage and aircraft losses kept two Japanese carriers out of the Battle of Midway a month later.
questions.explain: Damage and aircraft losses 'kept two Japanese carriers out of the Battle of Midway', so fewer Japanese carriers were available there. Each side lost one carrier sunk (Lexington against one light carrier), so Japan did not lose more; the ships 'never came within sight of each other' and every attack was by aircraft (contradicted); and the passage never says why Midway was won, so the 'because' is an unsupported cause.

questions.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Once convoys were introduced in 1917, U-boats sank no further British merchant ships.
Convoys were used from the first months of the war.
A prediction made by some opponents of convoys proved mistaken in practice.
Before convoys were adopted, Britain came close to running out of food.
questions.passage: In the early years of the First World War, British merchant ships sailed independently, and German U-boats sank them in growing numbers. Many naval officers opposed convoys, arguing that a large group of ships would be easier for submarines to find and would offer a bigger target. When convoys were introduced in 1917, losses fell sharply: on the vast ocean a convoy was little easier to find than a single ship, and a U-boat that did find one had to attack in the presence of escorts.
questions.explain: Opponents argued a convoy 'would be easier for submarines to find', yet in practice it 'was little easier to find than a single ship'. Losses 'fell sharply', not to zero (over-claim); ships sailed independently early in the war and convoys came 'in 1917' (contradicted); and the food shortage may be true history but is never stated.

questions.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: The bombers were launched early because bad weather was approaching the task force.
After the raid, some of the bombers landed back aboard Hornet.
The raid did serious damage to Japan's war industry.
The bombers had to fly a longer route than the original plan had assumed.
questions.passage: In April 1942, sixteen Army B-25 bombers took off from the carrier USS Hornet to attack targets in Japan. The bombers could take off from a carrier deck but were too large to land back aboard, so the plan called for them to fly on and land at airfields in China. The task force was sighted by Japanese picket boats earlier than expected, and the bombers were launched farther from Japan than planned; none of the aircraft reached the intended Chinese airfields.
questions.explain: The bombers were 'launched farther from Japan than planned' and still had to reach China beyond it, so the route was longer than assumed. The early launch followed the sighting by 'picket boats', not weather (wrong cause); the bombers were 'too large to land back aboard' (contradicted); and damage to industry is never mentioned (unstated).

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: Nautilus could remain submerged indefinitely, without ever needing to surface.
Wartime diesel-electric boats could run their diesels fully submerged without a snorkel.
Nautilus could stay submerged longer than a typical wartime diesel-electric submarine.
In 1958 Nautilus surfaced through the ice at the North Pole.
questions.passage: Diesel-electric submarines of the Second World War ran on batteries when submerged and had to surface or raise a snorkel at regular intervals to run their air-breathing diesel engines and recharge. USS Nautilus, commissioned in 1954 as the first nuclear-powered submarine, used a reactor that needs no air, allowing her to remain submerged for weeks at a time. In 1958 she became the first vessel to cross the North Pole submerged, passing beneath the Arctic ice.
questions.explain: Diesel-electric boats had to surface or snorkel 'at regular intervals', while Nautilus could stay down 'for weeks at a time'. 'Weeks' is not 'indefinitely' (over-claim); the diesels were 'air-breathing', which is why the boats had to surface or snorkel (contradicted); and Nautilus crossed the pole 'submerged', with no surfacing described (one-word twist).

questions.stem: The open tank shown is filled with still water. At which marked point on the wall is the water pressure greatest?
options: Point A
Point C
Point B
It is the same at all three points, because it is the same water
questions.explain: Pressure in a still liquid depends on depth below the surface (P = ρgh). C is deepest, so it has the most water pressing down from above and the highest pressure. The pressure is not equal throughout: that idea (Pascal's principle) applies to an extra pressure added to a sealed fluid, not to the weight of the fluid itself.

questions.stem: A sealed steel tank is completely full of oil. A small piston in the side wall has a face area of 2 in². When a 30 lb force pushes the piston in, how does the pressure change at the bottom of the tank compared with at the top?
options: It rises more at the bottom, because the oil is deepest there
It rises by the same 15 psi at the top and at the bottom
It rises 15 psi next to the piston and less farther away from it
It rises 30 psi at the bottom and 15 psi at the top
questions.explain: The added pressure is 30 lb ÷ 2 in² = 15 psi, and Pascal's principle says a pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is passed undiminished to every part of it. The bottom is still at a higher total pressure than the top because of depth, but the INCREASE is the same 15 psi everywhere. It does not fade with distance from the piston.

questions.stem: Water flows steadily through a horizontal 90° pipe elbow. Pressure taps are drilled in the inside (short-radius) wall and the outside (long-radius) wall of the bend. Which tap reads the lower pressure?
options: The outside wall of the bend
Neither; an incompressible fluid has the same pressure across the pipe
The inside wall of the bend
They alternate, as eddies form first on one side and then the other
questions.explain: To make the water follow the curve, there must be a net force toward the center of the bend, and in a fluid that force comes from a pressure difference: pressure is higher at the outside wall and lower at the inside wall. (The water also runs faster along the inside of the bend, which by Bernoulli means lower pressure there.) Incompressibility does not make pressure uniform in a moving, turning fluid.

questions.stem: Water flows at 3 ft/s through a pipe 4 inches in diameter, which then narrows to 2 inches in diameter. How fast does the water flow in the narrow section?
options: 6 ft/s
3 ft/s
12 ft/s
questions.explain: The same volume passes every section each second, so area × speed is constant. Area depends on diameter squared: halving the diameter cuts the area to 1/4, so the speed rises 4 times, to 12 ft/s. 6 ft/s uses the diameter ratio instead of the area ratio; 0.75 ft/s has the ratio upside down.

questions.stem: Two ships steam side by side on parallel courses, close together and at the same speed. What tends to happen?
options: They are pushed apart, because water piles up between them
They are drawn toward each other, because the fast-moving water between them is at lower pressure
Nothing sideways, because both ships move at the same speed
They are drawn together only if one ship is much larger than the other
questions.explain: The water squeezed through the narrow gap between the hulls speeds up relative to the ships, and faster-moving fluid has lower pressure (Bernoulli). The higher pressure on the outer sides then pushes the ships together. It happens whatever their sizes, which is why ships alongside for replenishment must steer carefully.

questions.stem: A sealed, flexible bag holds 6 liters of air at the surface. A diver takes it down to a depth of 20 m in seawater. Each 10 m of seawater adds about 1 atmosphere of pressure. Ignoring temperature changes, what is the bag's volume at 20 m?
options: 2 liters
3 liters
6 liters, because the bag is sealed
18 liters
questions.explain: Boyle's law: pressure × volume stays constant. At the surface the pressure is 1 atm; at 20 m it is 1 + 2 = 3 atm absolute. So the volume becomes 6 ÷ 3 = 2 L. 3 L forgets the 1 atm of air already pressing on the surface (it uses gauge pressure). Sealing the bag keeps the amount of air fixed, not its volume.

questions.stem: Gas in a cylinder with a freely sliding piston (so its pressure stays constant) is heated from 27 °C to 327 °C. What happens to its volume?
options: It increases about twelvefold
It stays the same, because the pressure is constant
It doubles
It increases by about 50%
questions.explain: At constant pressure, volume is proportional to ABSOLUTE temperature. 27 °C = 300 K and 327 °C = 600 K, so the volume doubles. Dividing the Celsius numbers (327 ÷ 27 ≈ 12) is the classic error: gas laws only work in kelvins. Constant pressure is exactly the condition that lets the volume change.

questions.stem: A rigid, sealed tank holds air at 27 °C and an absolute pressure of 30 psi. The tank is heated to 127 °C. What is the new absolute pressure?
options: about 141 psi
30 psi, because the tank is sealed and rigid
22.5 psi
40 psi
questions.topic: Pressure and temperature of a gas
questions.explain: With the volume fixed, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature: 300 K → 400 K is a factor of 4/3, so 30 × 4/3 = 40 psi. 141 psi scales by the Celsius ratio (127 ÷ 27). 22.5 psi applies the ratio upside down. A rigid tank keeps the volume fixed, not the pressure.

questions.stem: Blocks A and B have equal volumes. Block A floats with part of it above the surface; block B has sunk and rests on the bottom. Which block has the greater buoyant force acting on it?
options: Block A, because the water is holding it up
Both are the same, because their volumes are equal
Block B
Neither; B has no buoyant force because it rests on the bottom
questions.explain: Buoyant force = weight of water displaced. B is fully under water, so it displaces its whole volume; A displaces only the part below the surface. So B gets the larger upward push. It still sinks because its weight is even larger. Resting on the bottom does not switch the buoyant force off; the floor simply supplies the rest of B's support.

questions.stem: A hydrometer floats in fresh water with the 1.000 mark exactly at the surface. It is then placed in battery acid with a specific gravity of 1.25. The hydrometer will —
options: float higher, with less of its stem under the surface
sink lower, with more of its stem under the surface
float at the same level, because its weight has not changed
sink to the bottom, because acid is heavier
questions.explain: A floating object always displaces its own weight of liquid. Denser liquid weighs more per cubic inch, so less volume needs to be displaced and the hydrometer rides higher. That is why the higher specific-gravity marks are LOWER on the stem. Its weight is unchanged, but the volume needed to balance it is not.

questions.stem: A loaded cargo ship sails from a freshwater river out into the ocean. What happens to its draft (how deep the hull sits) and to the buoyant force on it?
options: The draft decreases; the buoyant force stays the same
The draft decreases; the buoyant force increases
The draft stays the same; the buoyant force increases
The draft increases; the buoyant force stays the same
questions.topic: Floating in fresh and salt water
questions.explain: A floating ship's buoyant force always equals its weight, which has not changed, so the force is the same in both. Seawater is denser, so it supplies that force with LESS displaced volume and the hull rises (smaller draft). That is why load lines carry separate fresh-water and salt-water marks. An increased buoyant force would make the ship accelerate upward out of the water.

questions.stem: An ice cube floats in a glass of fresh water filled exactly to the brim. When the ice has completely melted, the water —
options: overflows, because the part of the ice above the surface melts into extra water
drops below the brim, because ice takes up more space than water
is still exactly at the brim; none spills
It depends on how much of the cube was above the surface
questions.explain: Floating ice displaces exactly its own weight of water. When it melts it becomes that same weight of water, which fills exactly the volume it was already displacing. So the level does not change. The ice above the surface is the extra volume ice has as a solid, and it disappears on melting.

questions.stem: A rowboat carrying a heavy iron anchor floats in a small, closed swimming pool. The anchor is thrown overboard and sinks to the bottom. What happens to the water level in the pool?
options: It rises slightly
It stays exactly the same
It rises, then returns to its original level once the anchor settles
It falls slightly
questions.explain: In the boat, the anchor is floating, so it displaces its WEIGHT of water: iron is about 8 times denser than water, so that is about 8 times its own volume. On the bottom it displaces only its own VOLUME. Less water is displaced overall, so the level falls. Expecting a rise ignores the difference between floating (weight) and sunk (volume).

questions.stem: A 30 lb force pushes the 2 in² piston of this hydraulic press. Ignoring friction, what force does the 40 in² piston exert, and how far must the small piston move to raise the load 1 inch?
options: 600 lb; 0.05 inch
1.5 lb; 20 inches
60 lb; 2 inches
600 lb; 20 inches
questions.explain: Pressure = 30 ÷ 2 = 15 psi everywhere in the fluid, so the large piston gets 15 × 40 = 600 lb (area ratio 20). The fluid pushed out of the small cylinder spreads under a piston 20 times larger, so the small piston travels 20 × 1 = 20 in. Force × 20, distance ÷ 20: work in equals work out. 0.05 in would mean getting extra force for free.

questions.stem: Three containers have the same base area but different shapes: one flares wide at the top, one has straight sides and one narrows to a thin neck. All are filled with water to the same depth. On which base is the water pressure greatest?
options: It is the same on all three bases
The flared one, because it holds the most water
The narrow-necked one, because the water is squeezed into a smaller space
The straight-sided one, because only its walls are vertical
questions.explain: Pressure at a point in still water depends only on the depth (and the liquid's density), not on how much water is in the container or its shape. Same depth, same pressure, and with equal base areas, the same force on each base. The extra water in the flared container is held up by its sloping walls.

questions.stem: A hose is used as a siphon to drain water from a tank over its rim into a bucket. Which change will stop the flow?
options: Raising the top of the hose loop a few inches higher above the tank rim
Using a hose with a narrower outlet end than inlet end
Letting the tank level fall to less than half full
Raising the hose outlet to the same height as the water surface in the tank
questions.explain: A siphon runs because the outlet is below the surface it draws from: the longer column of water on the outlet side outweighs the shorter one, and air pressure on the tank surface keeps the column unbroken. Once the outlet is level with the tank's surface there is no height difference to drive the flow. The loop always rises above the rim; that is normal (up to about 30 ft for water).

questions.stem: A household outlet is rated at 120 V AC. What does the 120 V figure represent?
options: The peak voltage; the effective voltage is about 85 V
The average voltage over a complete cycle
The effective (rms) voltage; the peak voltage is about 170 V
The peak-to-peak voltage
questions.explain: AC ratings are effective (rms) values: the DC voltage that would heat a resistor equally. Peak = effective × 1.414 ≈ 170 V. The average over a full sine cycle is zero, because the positive and negative halves cancel, so 'average' cannot be the rating.

questions.stem: An AC supply has a peak voltage of 200 V. Approximately what steady DC voltage would deliver the same power to a resistor?
questions.explain: The DC voltage with the same heating effect is the effective (rms) value: 0.707 × peak = 0.707 × 200 ≈ 141 V. 200 V treats the peak as the working value; 283 V multiplies by 1.414 instead of dividing; 100 V simply halves the peak.

questions.stem: An ideal transformer has 200 turns on its primary and 1,000 turns on its secondary. The primary is fed 120 V AC and draws 5 A. What are the secondary voltage and current?
options: 600 V at 5 A
24 V at 25 A
600 V at 25 A
600 V at 1 A
questions.explain: Voltage follows the turns ratio: 120 × 1,000 ÷ 200 = 600 V. An ideal transformer cannot create power, so power in (120 × 5 = 600 W) equals power out: 600 W ÷ 600 V = 1 A. Stepping voltage up steps current down by the same factor. 600 V at 5 A or 25 A would mean more power out than in.

questions.stem: A 12 V car battery is connected across the primary winding of a step-up transformer. Once the current has settled, what does the secondary winding deliver?
options: A higher DC voltage set by the turns ratio
Nothing; a steady current does not induce a voltage
The same 12 V, because DC passes straight through
A lower DC voltage at a higher current
questions.explain: A transformer works by electromagnetic induction: only a CHANGING magnetic field induces a voltage in the secondary. Steady DC makes a steady field, so after a brief pulse at switch-on the secondary output is zero. The windings are not connected to each other, so nothing 'passes through'.

questions.stem: Compared with its primary winding, the secondary winding of a step-up transformer has —
options: more turns, with higher voltage and higher current
fewer turns, with higher voltage and lower current
more turns, with higher voltage and lower current
the same number of turns, but a larger iron core
questions.explain: Voltage is proportional to the number of turns, so stepping up needs MORE turns on the secondary. Power is (ideally) conserved, so the higher voltage comes with lower current. Higher voltage AND higher current would create energy from nothing.

questions.stem: A 24 V supply drives 3 A through a heater element. The element is replaced with one of twice the resistance, on the same 24 V supply. What happens?
options: The current falls to 1.5 A and the power stays the same
The current rises to 6 A and the power doubles
The current falls to 1.5 A and the power falls to a quarter
The current falls to 1.5 A and the power is halved
questions.explain: Original resistance = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 Ω; doubled = 16 Ω, so I = 24 ÷ 16 = 1.5 A. Power = V × I: 24 × 3 = 72 W before and 24 × 1.5 = 36 W after, which is half. With the voltage fixed, P = V² ÷ R, so doubling R halves the power. 'A quarter' wrongly squares the change; unchanged power ignores the lower current.

questions.stem: Two identical lamps are connected in parallel across an ideal battery. A third identical lamp is added in parallel. What happens to the brightness of the original two lamps and to the current from the battery?
options: The lamps dim, because the current is now shared three ways
The lamps brighten, because the total resistance has dropped
The lamps stay equally bright, and the battery current increases
The lamps stay equally bright, and the battery current stays the same
questions.explain: Each parallel branch sits directly across the battery, so each lamp still gets the full battery voltage and the same current: no change in brightness. The new branch adds its own current, so the battery supplies more in total (total resistance falls). Dimming would happen if the lamp were added in SERIES.

questions.stem: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor are connected in parallel, and this pair is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor across a 12 V battery. What current does the battery supply?
options: about 0.92 A
3 A
1 A
2 A
questions.explain: The parallel pair: (6 × 3) ÷ (6 + 3) = 2 Ω. Add the series 4 Ω: total 6 Ω. Current = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 A. 0.92 A adds all three resistors as if in series (13 Ω); 3 A uses only the 4 Ω resistor.

questions.stem: To measure the current flowing through a lamp in a circuit, an ammeter must be connected —
options: in parallel across the lamp's terminals
in series with the lamp, so the lamp's current flows through the meter
directly across the battery terminals
either in series or in parallel, since the reading is the same
questions.explain: Current must pass THROUGH the meter to be measured, so an ammeter goes in series. An ammeter has very low resistance: placed in parallel, or across the battery, it would act almost like a short circuit, draw a large current and probably blow its fuse. Voltmeters are the ones that go in parallel.

questions.stem: A 1,200 W space heater runs on a 120 V supply. What current does it draw, and what is its resistance while running?
options: 10 A and 120 Ω
12 A and 10 Ω
10 A and 12 Ω

questions.stem: A bar magnet is cut in half across its middle. Each piece —
options: has only one pole: one piece is north, the other south
loses its magnetism, because the poles have been separated
becomes a complete magnet with its own north and south poles
keeps a pole at its old end, while the cut face is neutral
questions.explain: Magnetism comes from countless tiny aligned domains, each with its own north and south. Cutting the bar just leaves two shorter magnets, each with a new pole at the cut face. A single isolated pole has never been found, however many times a magnet is cut.

questions.stem: An electromagnet is made by winding insulated wire around a soft-iron core and passing a current through it. Which change would WEAKEN it?
options: Winding more turns of wire on the same core
Increasing the current through the coil
Replacing the soft-iron core with a copper core of the same size
Pushing the turns closer together on a shorter core
questions.explain: Soft iron is ferromagnetic: its domains line up with the coil's field and multiply it hundreds of times. Copper is not magnetic, so a copper core behaves almost like air and the magnet becomes much weaker. More turns, more current, or the same turns packed more tightly (more turns per inch) all strengthen the field.

questions.stem: A strong magnet is dropped down a long vertical copper pipe and, separately, down an identical plastic pipe. Compared with its fall through the plastic pipe, the magnet falls through the copper pipe —
options: more slowly, because currents induced in the copper oppose its motion
at the same rate, because copper is not attracted to magnets
faster, because the copper pulls the magnet down
in a series of jerks, because it sticks to the wall and slips
questions.explain: The falling magnet's changing field induces eddy currents in the conducting copper, and by Lenz's law those currents make a magnetic field that OPPOSES the change causing them, which acts as a brake. It is true that copper is not attracted to a stationary magnet, which is exactly why the slow fall surprises people. Plastic does not conduct, so no braking currents form.

questions.stem: Two long parallel wires close together both carry current in the same direction. The wires —
options: repel each other
attract each other
feel no force, because neither wire is a magnet
twist until they are at right angles to each other
questions.explain: Every current makes a magnetic field, and a current in a magnetic field feels a force. For parallel currents in the SAME direction the forces pull the wires together; opposite currents push them apart. (Unlike electric charges, where like repels like.)

questions.stem: The ACTUAL mechanical advantage of a machine is found by —
options: dividing the output force the machine really delivers by the input force really applied
dividing the distance the effort moves by the distance the load moves
counting the rope strands that support the moving block
dividing the useful work out by the work put in
questions.explain: Actual MA is measured: real output force ÷ real input force (for rotating machines, the ratio of output torque to input torque achieved). It includes friction losses. The distance ratio and the strand count give the IDEAL mechanical advantage, from geometry alone. Work out ÷ work in is efficiency, which also equals actual MA ÷ ideal MA.

questions.stem: A block and tackle has 4 rope strands supporting the moving block. A pull of 120 lb is needed to raise a 360 lb load. What is the system's efficiency?
questions.explain: Ideal MA = 4 strands. Actual MA = 360 ÷ 120 = 3. Efficiency = actual ÷ ideal = 3 ÷ 4 = 75%. 33% divides the effort by the load; 133% has the ratio upside down, and no real machine can exceed 100%.

questions.stem: Ignoring friction and the weight of the pulleys, what pull F on the free end holds the 270 lb load shown?
options: 135 lb
270 lb
90 lb
questions.explain: Three strands support the moving block, so they share the load equally: 270 ÷ 3 = 90 lb in each strand, including the one you pull. 135 lb counts only 2 strands; 67.5 lb counts 4.

questions.stem: The 80 lb load hangs from a single movable pulley, as shown. Ignoring friction and the pulley's weight, what upward pull holds the load, and how much rope must be pulled to raise it 3 ft?
options: 40 lb; 3 ft
40 lb; 6 ft
80 lb; 3 ft
40 lb; 1.5 ft
questions.explain: Two strands hold the pulley (the anchored strand and the one you pull), so each carries 80 ÷ 2 = 40 lb. To lift the pulley 3 ft, BOTH strands must shorten by 3 ft, so you pull 6 ft of rope. Half the force always costs twice the distance; '40 lb; 3 ft' would be getting work for free.

questions.stem: Gear A (16 teeth) turns at 240 rpm and drives gear B (48 teeth). How does gear B turn?
options: 80 rpm, in the same direction as A
80 rpm, in the opposite direction to A
720 rpm, in the opposite direction to A
240 rpm, in the opposite direction to A
questions.explain: Teeth × rpm is shared: 16 × 240 = 3,840 teeth per minute, so B turns 3,840 ÷ 48 = 80 rpm. Directly meshed gears always turn opposite ways. 720 rpm multiplies by the ratio instead of dividing; the bigger gear must be slower.

questions.stem: In the gear train shown, gear A turns clockwise at 180 rpm. How does gear C turn?
options: 90 rpm, counterclockwise
60 rpm, clockwise
360 rpm, clockwise
90 rpm, clockwise
questions.explain: B is an idler: it does not change the overall ratio, so C behaves as if it meshed with A: 180 × 12 ÷ 24 = 90 rpm. Each mesh reverses direction; two meshes bring C back to A's direction, clockwise. 60 rpm is B's speed, not C's.

questions.stem: A 15-tooth pinion delivers 40 lb-ft of torque to the 45-tooth gear it meshes with. Ignoring losses, what torque does the 45-tooth gear deliver?
options: 13.3 lb-ft
40 lb-ft, because torque passes straight through
120 lb-ft
600 lb-ft
questions.explain: The larger gear turns 3 times slower (45 ÷ 15), and since power (torque × speed) is conserved, it delivers 3 times the torque: 40 × 3 = 120 lb-ft. 13.3 lb-ft divides instead of multiplying. This is why reduction gearing is used where high turning force is needed.

questions.stem: A cam that is a perfectly round disk mounted off-center on its shaft (an eccentric) turns at a steady speed. A follower rests on its edge. How does the follower move?
options: Up and down smoothly, once for each revolution of the shaft
Up and down twice for each revolution of the shaft
It stays still, because the cam is perfectly round
Up for half a revolution, then it stays still for the other half
questions.explain: Because the disk is off-center, its edge is farther from the shaft on one side than the other, so the follower rises to a single high point and falls to a single low point each turn: one smooth rise and fall per revolution. A round cam only gives no motion if it is centered on its shaft. Pauses (dwells) need a cam with flat or constant-radius sections.

questions.stem: What weight placed 6 ft to the right of the fulcrum balances the 90 lb weight 4 ft to the left?
options: 135 lb
90 lb
360 lb
60 lb
questions.explain: Balance when moments are equal: 90 × 4 = 360 lb-ft, so ? × 6 = 360 and ? = 60 lb. The farther weight needs less force. 135 lb puts the distances the wrong way round; 360 is the moment, not a weight.

questions.stem: The wheelbarrow carries 180 lb whose weight acts 1.5 ft from the wheel axle. The handles are 4.5 ft from the axle. What lifting force F at the handles holds it level, and how much of the load does the wheel carry?
options: 60 lb; 120 lb
60 lb; 180 lb
540 lb; 0 lb
90 lb; 90 lb
questions.explain: Moments about the axle: F × 4.5 = 180 × 1.5 = 270, so F = 60 lb. Vertical forces must balance too: the wheel supplies the rest, 180 − 60 = 120 lb. The wheel does not carry the full 180 lb, because the handles help. 540 lb puts the distances the wrong way round.

questions.stem: In a third-class lever, such as a pair of tweezers or a fishing rod, the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load. Which statement is true?
options: Its mechanical advantage is always greater than 1, because the effort is close to the fulcrum
Its mechanical advantage is exactly 1, like a fixed pulley
Its mechanical advantage is less than 1, but the load end moves farther and faster than the effort
It cannot be balanced, because the load and effort are on the same side of the fulcrum
questions.explain: The effort arm (fulcrum to effort) is shorter than the load arm (fulcrum to load), so MA = effort arm ÷ load arm is below 1: you push harder than the load. In return, the load end moves a larger distance in the same time, gaining speed and range. Forces on the same side of the pivot can still balance, as long as they act in opposite directions.

questions.stem: A 200 lb load hangs from a rope wound on the 3-inch-radius axle. The effort rope is wound on the 12-inch-radius wheel. Ignoring friction, what effort holds the load?
options: 800 lb
200 lb
50 lb
questions.explain: Torques balance: effort × 12 = 200 × 3 = 600 lb-in, so effort = 50 lb. Ideal MA = R ÷ r = 12 ÷ 3 = 4. 800 lb has the radii the wrong way round; 66.7 lb divides by 3 instead of 4.

questions.stem: A 240 lb load sits on a light beam 3 ft from the left support; the supports are 12 ft apart. How much of the load does the LEFT support carry?
options: 180 lb
60 lb
120 lb
240 lb
questions.explain: Take moments about the right support: left force × 12 = 240 × 9 (the load is 9 ft from the right support), so the left support carries 180 lb and the right carries 60 lb. The support NEARER the load carries more. 60 lb swaps the two; 120 lb assumes an even split.

questions.stem: The spring shown (20 lb/in) stretches under the 60 lb load. If the same 60 lb load hung instead from two of these springs hooked end to end, how far would the pair stretch in total?
options: 1.5 in
3 in
12 in
6 in
questions.explain: One spring stretches 60 ÷ 20 = 3 in. Hooked end to end (in series), EACH spring carries the full 60 lb and stretches 3 in, so the pair stretches 6 in. 1.5 in is the answer for two springs side by side, sharing the load; 3 in assumes the second spring changes nothing.

questions.stem: A 90 lb load hangs from a rigid bar held up by two vertical springs side by side, one with a stiffness of 20 lb/in and one of 10 lb/in. The load is positioned so that the bar hangs level. How much of the load does the stiffer spring carry?
options: 60 lb
45 lb
30 lb
90 lb
questions.explain: A level bar means both springs stretch the same distance x. Together they give 20x + 10x = 30x = 90 lb, so x = 3 in. The stiffer spring carries 20 × 3 = 60 lb and the softer 10 × 3 = 30 lb. Equal stretch, unequal force: the stiffer spring takes the larger share, not half.

questions.stem: Pulley A (6-inch diameter) turns at 900 rpm and drives pulley B (18-inch diameter) through the open belt shown. How does B turn?
options: 300 rpm, in the opposite direction to A
300 rpm, in the same direction as A
2,700 rpm, in the same direction as A
900 rpm, in the same direction as A
questions.explain: The belt moves both rims at the same speed, so diameter × rpm is equal: 6 × 900 = 18 × rpm, giving 300 rpm. An open (uncrossed) belt keeps the same direction; only a crossed belt reverses it. 2,700 rpm has the ratio upside down.

questions.stem: A wheel rolls without slipping to the right along a level road. At that instant, which point on the rim is moving fastest relative to the road?
options: Every point on the rim moves at the same speed
The bottom point, where the tire grips the road
The front point, level with the axle
The top of the wheel, at twice the speed of the axle
questions.explain: Each rim point combines the axle's forward speed v with the rim's rotation (also speed v). At the top both point forward: 2v. At the contact point they cancel: the bottom is momentarily at rest, which is what 'without slipping' means. The front point moves at about 1.4v, forward and downward. Equal rim speeds are true only relative to the axle, not to the road.

questions.stem: A wheel rolls without slipping to the right at a steady speed. At the instant shown, the point on the rim at the front of the wheel, level with the axle, is moving —
options: straight down, at the axle's speed
forward and downward, at about 1.4 times the axle's speed
forward, at the axle's speed
forward and upward, at about 1.4 times the axle's speed
questions.explain: Rolling right means turning clockwise, so relative to the axle the front point moves straight DOWN at speed v. Add the axle's forward speed v: the result points forward and down at √2 × v ≈ 1.4v. 'Straight down' forgets the forward motion of the whole wheel; 'upward' gets the rotation backward (that is the rear point).

questions.stem: A rifle is held level 5 ft above flat ground. At the same instant one bullet is fired horizontally and another is simply dropped from the same height. Ignoring air resistance, which reaches the ground first?
options: The dropped bullet, because the fired one has to travel much farther
They reach the ground at the same time
The fired bullet, because it is moving much faster
It depends on the fired bullet's muzzle speed
questions.explain: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent. Both bullets start with zero VERTICAL speed and fall with the same gravitational acceleration, so they fall 5 ft in the same time. The fired bullet just covers a lot of horizontal ground while it falls.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top of its flight, what are its velocity and its acceleration?
options: Both zero for an instant
Velocity zero; acceleration about 9.8 m/s² downward
Velocity zero; acceleration upward until it turns around
Velocity 9.8 m/s; acceleration zero
questions.topic: Motion at the top of a throw
questions.explain: At the top, the ball stops for an instant, so its velocity is zero. But gravity never switches off: the acceleration is 9.8 m/s² downward the whole time, going up, at the top and coming down. If the acceleration really were zero at the top, the ball would stay hanging there.

questions.stem: A pendulum bob is pulled aside to point A and released from rest. It swings through its lowest point B and up to point C on the other side. Ignoring friction and air resistance, where is its kinetic energy greatest, and how high is C?
options: Greatest at A; C is lower than A
Greatest at B; C is at the same height as A
Greatest at B; C is lower than A, because energy is used up at the bottom
The same everywhere; C is higher than A
questions.explain: With no losses, total energy is constant. At A it is all potential (the bob is at rest); at B, the lowest point, the most potential energy has turned into kinetic, so the bob moves fastest. Climbing again, it turns the kinetic energy back into potential, stopping at exactly the starting height. Real pendulums swing lower over time only because of friction and drag.

questions.stem: Which change doubles the time a simple pendulum takes for one complete swing (its period)?
options: Making the string four times as long
Doubling the mass of the bob
Making the string twice as long
Doubling the starting angle from 5° to 10°
questions.explain: The period depends on the square root of the length (T = 2π√(L/g)), so doubling T needs 4 × the length. Doubling the length only raises the period by about 41%. Mass has no effect, and for small swings the angle has almost none either: that is why pendulums keep good time.

questions.stem: A 2,000 kg truck moving at 10 m/s hits a stationary 3,000 kg car, and the two lock together. Ignoring friction, how fast do they move just after the collision?
options: about 6.7 m/s
5 m/s
10 m/s
4 m/s
questions.explain: Momentum is conserved: 2,000 × 10 = 20,000 kg·m/s before. Afterward the combined 5,000 kg carries the same momentum: 20,000 ÷ 5,000 = 4 m/s. 6.7 m/s divides by the car's mass only; 5 m/s averages the speeds. (Kinetic energy is not conserved here: much becomes heat and crumpled metal.)

questions.stem: A moving steel ball strikes an identical stationary steel ball head-on, and the collision is perfectly elastic. What happens?
options: The first ball stops and the second moves off at the first ball's speed
Both balls move off together at half the original speed
The first ball bounces straight back at full speed and the second stays put
The first ball bounces back at half speed and the second moves forward at half speed
questions.explain: An elastic collision conserves both momentum and kinetic energy. For equal masses the only way to do both is a complete swap: the striker stops and the target takes all its velocity, as in Newton's cradle. Moving off at half speed conserves momentum but loses half the kinetic energy, so it cannot be elastic.

questions.stem: A 4 kg rifle, free to move, fires a 0.01 kg bullet at 800 m/s. What is the rifle's recoil speed?
options: 8 m/s
2 m/s
questions.explain: Total momentum starts at zero, so the rifle's backward momentum equals the bullet's forward momentum: 0.01 × 800 = 8 kg·m/s. Rifle speed = 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s. 8 m/s stops at the momentum without dividing by the rifle's mass; 3,200 m/s multiplies the wrong numbers.

questions.stem: A car takes a flat curve at a steady speed. If it takes the same curve at twice the speed, the sideways friction force needed to hold it on the curve is —
options: twice as large
four times as large
the same, because the curve has not changed
half as large, because the car spends half as long in the curve
questions.explain: Centripetal force = mv² ÷ r, so it grows with the SQUARE of speed: twice the speed needs 2² = 4 times the force. That is why a small increase in speed through a bend greatly raises the risk of skidding.

questions.stem: A ball on a string is whirled in a horizontal circle. At the instant the ball is at the most northerly point of the circle, moving due east, the string breaks. Seen from above, the ball then moves —
options: due north, straight outward along the line of the string
on around the curve for a while, then straightens out
northeast, between the tangent and the outward direction
due east, in a straight line along the tangent
questions.explain: The string supplied the only inward (centripetal) force. With it gone there is no sideways force at all, so by Newton's first law the ball carries on in a straight line in the direction it was already moving: due east along the tangent. There is no outward 'centrifugal' push to fling it north.

questions.stem: A 2 kg object is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², how fast is it moving just before it hits the ground?
options: 40 m/s
20 m/s
10 m/s
questions.explain: Potential energy becomes kinetic: mgh = ½mv², and the mass cancels, so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 20) = √400 = 20 m/s. 200 m/s is g × h with no square root; 40 m/s is 2 × 20. A heavier object would land at the same speed.

questions.stem: The 100 lb block rests on a frictionless ramp inclined at 30°. What force, pushing parallel to the ramp surface, holds it still?
options: about 87 lb
100 lb
about 58 lb
50 lb
questions.explain: Only the part of the weight along the slope must be held: W × sin 30° = 100 × 0.5 = 50 lb. About 87 lb (W × cos 30°) is the part pressing INTO the ramp, balanced by the surface. Needing the full 100 lb would mean the ramp gives no help at all.

questions.stem: A 100 lb lamp hangs from two cables attached to the ceiling. One cable makes an angle of 30° with the vertical, the other 60° with the vertical. Which cable has the greater tension?
options: The 30° cable, at about 87 lb
The 60° cable, at about 87 lb
Neither; both carry 50 lb
The 30° cable, carrying the full 100 lb
questions.explain: The sideways pulls must cancel and the upward parts must add to 100 lb. Solving: the cable nearer to vertical (30°) carries 100 × cos 30° ≈ 87 lb and the other 100 × cos 60° = 50 lb. The steeper (more vertical) cable does most of the lifting. The two tensions add to more than 100 lb because part of each pull is sideways.

questions.stem: In a four-stroke gasoline engine, during which two strokes are BOTH the intake and exhaust valves closed?
options: Compression and power
Intake and exhaust
Intake and compression
Power and exhaust
questions.explain: Intake: intake valve open, piston drawing in mixture. Compression: both closed so the mixture can be squeezed. Power: both closed so the burning gas pushes the piston down. Exhaust: exhaust valve open, piston pushing burned gas out. Any open valve during compression or power would let the pressure escape.

questions.stem: In a four-stroke engine, how fast does the camshaft turn compared with the crankshaft?
options: At half the crankshaft speed
At the same speed as the crankshaft
At twice the crankshaft speed
At one quarter of the crankshaft speed
questions.explain: A full four-stroke cycle takes two crankshaft revolutions (each stroke is half a turn), but each valve opens only once per cycle. The cam that opens it must therefore turn once for every two crank turns: half speed, set by a 2 : 1 gear or belt drive.

questions.stem: In normal running, a diesel engine ignites its fuel by —
options: a spark plug fired near the top of the compression stroke
spraying fuel into air that has been heated by being compressed to a high ratio
glow plugs that stay red-hot all the time the engine runs
