a magneto that sends a high-voltage pulse to each cylinder
questions.explain: Diesels are compression-ignition engines: squeezing air to roughly 15-22 times smaller makes it hot enough to ignite fuel the moment it is injected. Glow plugs only help with cold starting. Spark plugs and magnetos belong to spark-ignition (gasoline) engines.

questions.stem: In a carburetor, fuel is drawn from the float bowl into the airstream at the narrow venturi throat. This happens because, at the throat, the air has —
options: a lower speed and a higher pressure than the air above the fuel in the bowl
a higher speed and a higher pressure, which sprays the fuel
the same pressure as the bowl, but a higher temperature that vaporizes the fuel
a higher speed and a lower pressure than the air above the fuel in the bowl
questions.explain: Air must speed up to get through the narrow throat (continuity), and faster air has lower pressure (Bernoulli). The bowl is vented to the higher pressure of the incoming air, so fuel is pushed up the jet into the low-pressure throat. Air actually COOLS as it speeds up and its pressure drops, which is why carburetor icing can occur.

questions.stem: On a cold morning, a steel wrench and a wooden tool handle have both been in the same unheated garage all night. The steel feels much colder to the touch because —
options: the steel is at a lower temperature than the wood
the wood generates a small amount of its own heat
steel conducts heat away from your hand much faster than wood
steel radiates cold into your hand
questions.explain: After a night in the same room, both are at the same temperature. Your skin senses how quickly it LOSES heat, and steel is a good conductor that draws heat out of your hand quickly, while wood is an insulator. 'Cold' is not a thing that flows; heat flows from warmer to cooler.

questions.stem: A vacuum flask has double glass walls with a vacuum between them, and the facing surfaces are silvered. The vacuum mainly stops heat transfer by ______, while the silvering mainly stops heat transfer by ______.
options: conduction and convection; radiation
radiation; conduction and convection
convection only; conduction
conduction only; convection
questions.explain: Conduction and convection both need matter (touching particles, or a moving fluid), so a vacuum blocks them. Radiation crosses a vacuum easily (that is how sunlight reaches Earth), so the shiny silvered surfaces are added to reflect it back. Silvering cannot stop conduction or convection.

questions.stem: A steel collar is stuck tight on a steel shaft. Which method is most likely to loosen it?
options: Cool the collar only; the metal shrinks back away from the shaft
Heat the shaft only; hot metal slides more easily
Heat the collar only; the hole in it grows as the collar expands
Heat both equally; they expand together and the fit eases
questions.explain: When a ring is heated, every dimension grows, including the hole: it expands as if the hole were made of the same metal. Heating the collar alone therefore opens up the gap. Cooling the collar shrinks the hole and grips tighter; heating the shaft makes it fatter; heating both equally keeps the fit just as tight.

questions.stem: A bimetallic strip is made of brass bonded to steel; brass expands more than steel when heated. When the strip is heated, it —
options: bends so that the brass is on the outside of the curve
bends so that the brass is on the inside of the curve
stays straight but grows longer
bends toward the brass side at first, then straightens
questions.explain: Heated, the brass becomes longer than the steel it is bonded to. The only way a longer strip and a shorter one can stay joined is to curve, with the longer (brass) side on the outside of the arc. Thermostats use this bending to open or close a contact.

questions.stem: In a nuclear reactor, pushing the control rods farther into the core —
options: absorbs more neutrons, slowing the chain reaction
adds extra fuel, speeding up the chain reaction
slows the neutrons down, so they cause more fissions
absorbs heat directly, cooling the core while the reaction continues unchanged
questions.explain: Control rods contain neutron absorbers such as boron or cadmium. Each absorbed neutron cannot trigger another fission, so inserting rods reduces the reaction rate and fully inserting them shuts the reactor down. Slowing neutrons to make fission more likely is the job of the MODERATOR (such as water or graphite), and removing heat is the coolant's job.

questions.stem: Why is an engine's liquid cooling system sealed with a pressure cap?
options: The pressure pumps the coolant around the engine faster
Raising the pressure raises the coolant's boiling point, so it can run hotter without boiling
Raising the pressure lowers the boiling point, so the coolant carries away more heat as steam
It keeps the coolant at exactly atmospheric pressure so it cannot boil over
questions.explain: A liquid's boiling point rises with the pressure on it. Holding the coolant at around 15 psi above atmospheric lifts its boiling point well above 212 °F, so the engine can run hot (efficiently) without the coolant flashing to steam. The water pump, not the cap, circulates the coolant. A pressure cooker uses the same idea.

questions.stem: A cannonball is fired over level ground at an angle above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, how does its horizontal velocity change during the flight?
options: It decreases steadily until the cannonball lands
It drops to zero at the top of the arc
It decreases on the way up and increases on the way down
It stays the same from launch to landing
questions.explain: Once the cannonball leaves the barrel, the only force on it (ignoring air) is gravity, which acts straight down. With no horizontal force there is no horizontal acceleration, so the horizontal velocity is constant for the whole flight. It is the VERTICAL velocity that shrinks to zero at the top and then grows downward.

questions.stem: A ball is kicked at 30° above level ground. At the highest point of its path, which statement is true?
options: Its velocity and its acceleration are both zero
Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is g, downward
Its velocity is horizontal and its acceleration is g, downward
Its velocity is horizontal and its acceleration is zero for an instant
questions.topic: Projectile at the top of its arc
questions.explain: At the top the vertical part of the velocity is momentarily zero, but the horizontal part is unchanged, so the ball is still moving, horizontally. Gravity never switches off, so the acceleration is g downward throughout. Zero velocity at the top is true only for a ball thrown straight up.

questions.stem: Fired over level ground at 30° above the horizontal, a shell lands 2,000 m away. Ignoring air resistance, at what other launch angle, with the same muzzle speed, would it again land 2,000 m away?
options: None; every angle gives a different range
questions.explain: Over level ground, angles that add up to 90° give the same range: 30° and 60° (the 60° shot goes higher and stays up longer, but moves forward more slowly). 45° gives the MAXIMUM range, so it would land beyond 2,000 m. 15° gives a shorter range, the same as 75°.

questions.stem: A stone is thrown horizontally at 12 m/s from the top of a cliff 20 m high. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², how far from the base of the cliff does it land?
questions.explain: Fall time comes from the height alone: 20 = ½ × 10 × t², so t² = 4 and t = 2 s. The horizontal speed stays 12 m/s, so it lands 12 × 2 = 24 m out. 12 m assumes 1 s; 48 m multiplies by t² instead of t; 240 m multiplies the speed by the height.

questions.stem: A supply crate is released from an aircraft flying level at a constant speed. Ignoring air resistance, where is the crate relative to the aircraft as it falls?
options: Directly below the aircraft the whole way down
Falling farther and farther behind the aircraft
Directly below the point where it was released
Ahead of the aircraft, because of its forward momentum
questions.topic: Object released from a moving aircraft
questions.explain: At release the crate already has the aircraft's forward speed, and with no air resistance nothing changes that horizontal speed. Crate and aircraft therefore keep moving forward together, and the crate stays directly beneath the aircraft while it falls. In real life, air resistance makes it trail behind, which is why drops are released well before the target.

questions.stem: Two balls are thrown horizontally from the same rooftop at the same moment, one at 5 m/s and one at 15 m/s. Ignoring air resistance, which statement is true?
options: The faster one lands first, three times as far out
The slower one lands first, because it has a shorter path to cover
They land together, the faster one nine times as far out
They land together, the faster one three times as far out
questions.topic: Time of flight and horizontal speed
questions.explain: Both start with zero vertical speed and fall the same height under the same g, so they take the same time to land. Horizontal distance = horizontal speed × time, so three times the speed gives three times the distance. Nine times would square the speed, which applies to kinetic energy, not to distance here.

questions.stem: A jet cruises in level flight at a constant 500 knots. Which statement about the forces on it is true?
options: Thrust is greater than drag, or it would slow down
Thrust equals drag, and lift equals weight
No forces act on it, so it keeps moving
Lift is greater than weight, or it would sink
questions.explain: Constant speed in a straight line means zero acceleration, so by Newton's first and second laws the net force is zero: thrust balances drag and lift balances weight. An object does not need a net force to KEEP moving, only to change its motion. The forces are still there; they just cancel.

questions.stem: A 2,000 kg truck accelerates at 1.5 m/s² while friction and air resistance oppose it with a total of 1,000 N. What forward driving force must the wheels supply?
questions.explain: The NET force must be m × a = 2,000 × 1.5 = 3,000 N. The driving force has to supply that and also overcome the 1,000 N of resistance: 3,000 + 1,000 = 4,000 N. 3,000 N forgets the resistance; 2,000 N subtracts it instead of adding; 1,000 N would only balance the resistance, giving constant speed with no acceleration.

questions.stem: A horse pulls a cart, and by Newton's third law the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. How can the horse and cart speed up?
options: The horse pulls the cart a little harder than the cart pulls the horse back
The ground pushes the horse forward harder than the cart pulls it back
The two pulls cancel, so the cart moves only on its own momentum
It cannot; equal and opposite forces always mean zero net force
questions.explain: The equal and opposite pulls act on DIFFERENT objects (one on the cart, one on the horse), so they never cancel each other. To find whether the horse accelerates, add only the forces ON the horse: its hooves push back on the ground, and the ground pushes it forward. When that forward push is bigger than the cart's backward pull, the horse speeds up, and the cart, pulled forward harder than friction holds it back, speeds up with it.

questions.stem: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg on Earth. On the Moon, where gravity is about one sixth as strong, her mass is —
options: 80 kg, but her weight is about a sixth
about 13 kg, and her weight is about a sixth
80 kg, and her weight is unchanged
about 13 kg, but her weight is unchanged
questions.explain: Mass is the amount of matter, and it is the same everywhere: 80 kg. Weight is the gravitational force on that mass (m × g), so it falls to about a sixth of its Earth value. She would be just as hard to start or stop moving on the Moon, but much easier to lift.

questions.stem: A car traveling north brakes hard and slows down. In which direction is its acceleration?
options: South
North, the direction it is moving
Zero, because it is slowing, not speeding up
Straight down, because the brakes press on the road
questions.explain: Acceleration points the way the velocity is CHANGING, which is the direction of the net force. The car's northward velocity is shrinking, and the braking (friction) force on the car points south, so the acceleration is southward. Slowing down is still acceleration, just opposite to the motion.

questions.stem: A sailor walks 30 m east along a deck, then 40 m north. What are the distance walked and the size of the displacement?
options: 70 m walked; 70 m displacement
70 m walked; 50 m displacement
50 m walked; 70 m displacement
70 m walked; 10 m displacement
questions.explain: Distance is the whole path: 30 + 40 = 70 m. Displacement is the straight line from start to finish: a right triangle with legs 30 and 40, so √(900 + 1,600) = √2,500 = 50 m (a 3-4-5 triangle). 10 m subtracts the legs, which only works if the second leg doubles back.

questions.stem: The same net force acts on a 2 kg cart and on a 6 kg cart. Compared with the 2 kg cart, the 6 kg cart's acceleration is —
options: three times as large
the same, because the force is the same
one ninth as large
one third as large
questions.explain: a = F ÷ m, so with the same force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass. Three times the mass gives a third of the acceleration. One ninth wrongly squares the ratio; the same acceleration would need three times the force.

questions.stem: A skydiver falls at a steady terminal speed before opening her parachute. At that moment, the air resistance on her is —
options: zero
equal to her weight
less than her weight
greater than her weight
questions.explain: A steady speed means zero acceleration, so the net force is zero: air resistance exactly balances her weight. If it were less she would still be speeding up; if it were greater she would be slowing down (which is what happens for a moment when the parachute opens).

questions.stem: Ignoring friction, what push along the 16 ft ramp shown moves a 480 lb load up to the 4 ft platform?
options: 120 lb
30 lb
480 lb
questions.explain: Ideal MA of a ramp = slope length ÷ height = 16 ÷ 4 = 4, so the push is 480 ÷ 4 = 120 lb. 30 lb divides by the length alone; 480 lb ignores the ramp; 1,920 lb multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A 12 ft ramp rises 2 ft. Because of friction, a 100 lb push is needed to slide a 450 lb crate up it. What is the ramp's efficiency?
questions.explain: Ideal MA = 12 ÷ 2 = 6. Actual MA = 450 ÷ 100 = 4.5. Efficiency = actual ÷ ideal = 4.5 ÷ 6 = 75%. 133% divides the wrong way round (no machine beats 100%); 22% divides the push by the load; 17% is just height ÷ length.

questions.stem: A 200 lb barrel is rolled up a 10 ft ramp onto a platform 2.5 ft high. Ignoring friction, how much work is done, and what push is needed?
options: 2,000 ft-lb; 200 lb push
500 ft-lb; 50 lb push
500 ft-lb; 200 lb push
2,000 ft-lb; 50 lb push
questions.explain: The useful work is lifting 200 lb by 2.5 ft: 500 ft-lb. A ramp does not change the work, only how it is delivered, so push × 10 ft = 500 ft-lb and the push is 50 lb. 2,000 ft-lb multiplies the weight by the ramp's length, as if the barrel were lifted 10 ft.

questions.stem: Ignoring friction, which ramp needs the SMALLEST push to move a 600 lb load up it?
options: 10 ft long, 2 ft high
18 ft long, 3 ft high
12 ft long, 3 ft high
20 ft long, 5 ft high
questions.explain: The push depends on the ratio length ÷ height, not on length alone. Ratios: 18 ÷ 3 = 6, 10 ÷ 2 = 5, 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and 20 ÷ 5 = 4. The highest MA (6) needs the smallest push, 600 ÷ 6 = 100 lb. The 20 ft ramp is the longest but also the steepest of the long ones.

questions.stem: A splitting wedge is 8 in long and 2 in thick at its back end. Ignoring friction, what driving force produces a 1,200 lb splitting force?
options: 300 lb
150 lb
600 lb
questions.explain: A wedge's ideal MA = length of slope ÷ thickness = 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so the driving force is 1,200 ÷ 4 = 300 lb. 150 lb divides by the length alone; 600 lb divides by the thickness alone; 4,800 lb multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A screw jack, a wood screw and a driven-in doorstop wedge all hold their loads without slipping back when you let go. This is mainly because —
options: their ideal mechanical advantage is less than 1
they are made of harder material than the load
the load always acts straight down, never along the slope of the thread
friction is large enough to stop the load driving them backward
questions.explain: In wedges and screws, the sliding surfaces are pressed together hard, so friction is very large compared with the small part of the load's force that acts along the slope. That friction stops the load from driving them backward. The same friction is why their efficiency is low. Their ideal MA is far ABOVE 1, not below it.

questions.stem: A bolt has 16 threads per inch. How many full turns drive it 3/4 in into a threaded hole?
options: about 21
questions.explain: Pitch = 1 ÷ 16 in, so each turn advances it 1/16 in. Turns = 3/4 ÷ 1/16 = 3/4 × 16 = 12. 16 turns would drive it a full inch; about 21 divides 16 by 3/4 instead of multiplying; 64 multiplies 16 by 4.

questions.stem: Two screw clamps are identical except that clamp X has 10 threads per inch and clamp Y has 20 threads per inch. With the same handle and the same effort, clamp Y —
options: clamps about twice as hard and closes twice as far per turn
clamps half as hard, but closes twice as far per turn
clamps just as hard, because the handle is the same
clamps about twice as hard, but closes half as far per turn
questions.explain: Y's pitch is 1/20 in against X's 1/10 in, so for the same circle of the handle, Y's ideal MA (circle ÷ pitch) is twice as large: about twice the clamping force for the same effort. The price is distance: Y closes only half as far each turn. More force AND more distance would break the work rule.

questions.stem: A screw jack has a pitch of 0.2 in, and its handle end travels 44 in around on each full turn. Ignoring friction, what effort lifts a 2,200 lb load?
options: 50 lb
440 lb
10 lb
about 1.6 lb
questions.explain: Each turn the hand moves 44 in while the load rises 0.2 in, so the ideal MA = 44 ÷ 0.2 = 220 and the effort is 2,200 ÷ 220 = 10 lb. 50 lb ignores the pitch (2,200 ÷ 44); 440 lb multiplies the load by the pitch; about 1.6 lb treats 44 in as the handle's length and multiplies by 2π again.

questions.stem: A screw jack has an ideal mechanical advantage of 300 but is only 25% efficient. What effort raises a 3,000 lb load?
options: 10 lb
2.5 lb
40 lb
750 lb
questions.explain: Actual MA = efficiency × ideal MA = 0.25 × 300 = 75, so the effort is 3,000 ÷ 75 = 40 lb. 10 lb is the ideal (frictionless) effort; 2.5 lb divides the MA by the efficiency, as if friction helped; 750 lb is just 25% of the load.

questions.stem: A micrometer's screw has a pitch of 0.5 mm, and its thimble is marked with 50 equal divisions around its edge. How far does the spindle move when the thimble turns by one division?
options: 0.5 mm
25 mm
questions.explain: One full turn (50 divisions) advances the spindle one pitch, 0.5 mm, so one division moves it 0.5 ÷ 50 = 0.01 mm. That fine screw is what lets a micrometer measure to a hundredth of a millimeter. 0.5 mm is a whole turn; 0.05 mm is a tenth of a turn; 25 mm multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A ray of light strikes a flat mirror at 25° to the mirror's surface. What is the angle of reflection, measured from the normal?
questions.explain: Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the surface. The incoming ray is 90 − 25 = 65° from the normal, so it reflects at 65°. 25° measures from the surface; 50° and 130° are angles between the two rays, not the angle of reflection.

questions.stem: A simple periscope has two flat mirrors, each set at 45° in a vertical tube and facing each other. Light enters the top opening horizontally. How does it leave through the bottom opening?
options: Horizontally, but traveling back the way it came in
Vertically, straight down the tube
Horizontally, in the same direction it entered
At 45° below the horizontal
questions.explain: Each 45° mirror turns the light through 90°. The top mirror turns it straight down the tube; the bottom mirror turns it horizontal again, traveling in its original direction, just lower. So the viewer sees an upright scene, as if looking straight through the tube.

questions.stem: Which of these images could be caught on a sheet of paper held in the right place?
options: Your reflection in a flat bathroom mirror
The image seen through a magnifying glass held close to a stamp
A magnifying glass's image of a distant window
The image of a car in a convex side-view mirror
questions.explain: Only a real image, where light rays actually meet, can be caught on a screen. A converging lens forms a real (inverted) image of a distant object near its focal point. A flat mirror, a magnifier held close (object inside F) and a convex mirror all give virtual images, which rays only seem to come from.

questions.stem: A small bulb is placed exactly at the focal point of a concave mirror, as in a searchlight. The reflected light —
options: comes to a focus at twice the focal length
leaves as a parallel beam
spreads out as if from a point behind the mirror
forms a small, inverted image at the focal point
questions.topic: Concave mirror (source at the focal point)
questions.explain: Rays arriving parallel to the axis reflect through the focal point; run that backward and rays starting at the focal point reflect out parallel. That is how searchlights and headlights make a tight beam. Spreading as if from behind the mirror is what a convex mirror does.

questions.stem: A camera's converging lens forms an image of a person standing far beyond twice its focal length. The image on the sensor is —
options: virtual, upright and smaller than the person
real, inverted and smaller than the person
real, upright and smaller
real, inverted and larger
questions.explain: An object beyond 2F gives a real, inverted, reduced image between F and 2F on the other side. It has to be real to land on the sensor, and every real image is inverted (the camera flips it back electronically). Larger images need the object between F and 2F.

questions.stem: A ray of light passes at an angle from glass out into air. Compared with its path in the glass, the ray in the air —
options: bends toward the normal and speeds up
bends away from the normal and slows down
carries straight on, as air does not refract light
bends away from the normal and speeds up
questions.explain: Light travels faster in air than in glass. Speeding up as it crosses into the faster medium, it bends AWAY from the normal (the reverse of entering glass). The bending happens at the boundary, so the change of medium is what matters, not whether air 'refracts'.

questions.stem: An object is 12 cm from a converging lens with a focal length of 4 cm. Where does the image form, and what is it like?
options: 8 cm behind the lens; real, inverted, two-thirds size
6 cm behind the lens; real, inverted, half size
3 cm behind the lens; real, inverted, quarter size
6 cm in front of the lens; virtual, upright, half size
questions.explain: 1/d_i = 1/f − 1/d_o = 1/4 − 1/12 = 3/12 − 1/12 = 2/12, so d_i = 6 cm on the far side. Magnification = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5. The object is beyond 2F (8 cm), so the image is real, inverted and smaller. 8 cm subtracts the distances; 3 cm adds the reciprocals.

questions.stem: Why are the passenger-side mirrors on many cars convex?
options: They magnify cars behind, making them easier to see
They form a real image that stays sharp at night
They reverse left and right, unlike a flat mirror
They show a wider view, but make cars look smaller
questions.explain: A convex mirror bulges outward and diverges light, so it squeezes a wide area into the mirror: a smaller, upright, virtual image. Smaller images make cars seem farther away, hence 'objects in mirror are closer than they appear'. Convex mirrors never magnify or form real images.

questions.stem: An object is viewed through a concave (diverging) lens and moved from far away to very close to the lens. Throughout, the image —
options: flips from inverted to upright as the object passes the focal point
becomes larger than the object once it is inside the focal point
becomes real and projectable when the object is close
stays upright and virtual, and smaller than the object
questions.explain: A diverging lens can only spread light out, so it always forms an upright, virtual, reduced image on the same side as the object, whatever the distance. Flipping and enlarging at the focal point are what a CONVERGING lens does.

questions.stem: A gauge at the bottom of an open water tank 6 ft deep shows a certain pressure. A second open tank holds oil with a specific gravity of 0.75. How deep must the oil be for the gauge at its bottom to show the same pressure?
options: 8 ft
4.5 ft
6 ft
7.5 ft
questions.explain: Liquid pressure depends on density × depth (P = ρgh), so a lighter liquid needs a deeper column to give the same pressure. Oil is 0.75 as dense as water, so the depth is 6 ÷ 0.75 = 8 ft. Check: 0.75 × 8 = 6 ft of water-equivalent ✓. 4.5 ft multiplies by 0.75 instead of dividing; 6 ft forgets that density matters (only container shape does not); 7.5 ft adds 25% instead of dividing by 0.75.

questions.stem: A hand-operated suction pump stands at the top of a well and draws water up a pipe. At sea level it cannot lift water more than about 34 ft. Taken to a high mountain village, the greatest height it can lift water is —
options: more than 34 ft, because thinner air resists the rising water less
still about 34 ft, because the limit is set by the pump's own suction
less than 34 ft, because there is less air pressure to push the water up
unlimited, provided the pump can make a strong enough vacuum
questions.explain: A suction pump does not pull water up; it lowers the pressure in the pipe, and the atmosphere pressing on the well surface pushes the water up. Even a perfect vacuum only lets the air hold up a column whose weight matches atmospheric pressure, about 34 ft of water at sea level, and less where the air pressure is lower. 'Thinner air resists less' misses that air is what does the pushing; a stronger pump cannot beat the perfect-vacuum limit, which is why deep wells use submerged pumps that push water up.

questions.stem: Air has become trapped in a car's hydraulic brake line. When the driver presses the pedal, it feels soft, travels a long way and the brakes grip weakly. Why?
options: The air shrinks under pressure, so pedal travel is used up before pressure builds
Air is less dense than brake fluid, so it passes on less pressure to the pistons
The air lets fluid slip back past the master-cylinder seal, so the pressure leaks off
The bubble adds friction in the line, so part of the pedal force is lost as drag
questions.explain: Pascal's principle passes pressure through a liquid because a liquid barely compresses. A gas bubble compresses easily, so much of the pedal's travel just squeezes the bubble smaller before real pressure reaches the wheel pistons: a spongy pedal. Pressure in a fluid at rest is passed on equally whatever the density, so 'less dense' is wrong; fluid slipping past a worn seal is a different fault, a pedal that slowly sinks under steady pressure; and with the fluid at rest once pressure is held there is no flow, so line friction takes no force. Bleeding the brakes removes the air.

questions.stem: In a hydraulic jack, the small piston is 1 inch in diameter and the large piston is 4 inches in diameter. Ignoring friction, a 50 lb push on the small piston supports what load on the large piston?
options: 200 lb
800 lb
50 lb
questions.explain: The pressure is the same in both cylinders, so force scales with piston AREA, and area goes with diameter squared. The diameter ratio is 4, so the area ratio is 4² = 16 and the load is 50 × 16 = 800 lb. 200 lb uses the diameter ratio instead of the area ratio; 12.5 lb divides instead of multiplying; 50 lb confuses equal pressure with equal force.

questions.stem: Water flows steadily through a horizontal pipe that narrows to a short throat and then widens back to its original size. Open vertical tubes rise from the wide section before the throat, from the throat, and from the wide section after it. Ignoring friction, how do the water levels in the tubes compare?
options: Highest at the throat, where the water is squeezed up the tube
Equal in all three, because the same flow passes each section
Highest after the throat, where the water slows down again
Lowest at the throat; the two wide sections are level
questions.explain: Continuity: the same volume passes every section each second, so the water speeds up in the narrow throat. Bernoulli: where the speed is higher, the pressure is lower, so the throat tube stands lowest. Once the pipe widens to its original size the speed returns to its original value, so with no friction the pressure and level match the first tube. Equal flow RATE does not mean equal speed or pressure, the narrowing does not squeeze water up the tube, and the downstream speed is the same as upstream, not lower.

questions.stem: A water main 6 inches in diameter carries water at 4 ft/s. It splits into two branch pipes, each 3 inches in diameter, which share the flow equally. How fast does the water move in each branch?
options: 16 ft/s
2 ft/s
8 ft/s
4 ft/s
questions.explain: Each 3-inch branch has half the main's diameter, so a quarter of its area; the two branches together have half the main's area. The same total flow through half the area must move twice as fast: 8 ft/s. Check: main 1 area unit × 4 = 4; branches 2 × ¼ × 8 = 4 ✓. 16 ft/s sends all the flow through one branch; 2 ft/s assumes splitting the flow halves the speed; 4 ft/s ignores the change in area.

questions.stem: A tire is filled to a gauge pressure of 30 psi at 27 °C, where the atmosphere adds another 15 psi. After a long drive the air in the tire is at 87 °C. Assuming the tire's volume does not change, what does the gauge read now?
options: 36 psi
39 psi
54 psi
about 97 psi
questions.topic: Pressure and temperature of a gas
questions.explain: Gas laws need absolute pressure and kelvins. Absolute pressure = 30 + 15 = 45 psi; the temperatures are 300 K and 360 K, a ratio of 1.2. New absolute pressure = 45 × 1.2 = 54 psi, so the gauge shows 54 − 15 = 39 psi. 36 psi scales the gauge reading instead of the absolute pressure; 54 psi forgets to subtract the atmosphere again; about 97 psi uses the Celsius ratio 87 ÷ 27.

questions.stem: A gas is compressed to one third of its original volume, and in the process its absolute temperature rises by 50%. Its pressure is now how many times the original?
options: 2 times
3 times
0.5 times
4.5 times
questions.explain: PV ÷ T stays constant, so pressure rises in proportion to the squeeze AND to the absolute temperature: P₂ = P₁ × 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 P₁. 3 times ignores the heating; 2 times divides the two effects (3 ÷ 1.5) instead of multiplying them; 0.5 times treats pressure as falling when volume falls, which is Boyle's law upside down.

questions.stem: A submarine hovers fully submerged at a depth of 100 ft. Without changing its ballast, it descends to 300 ft. Ignoring any squeezing of the hull and any change in seawater density, the buoyant force on it at 300 ft is —
options: about three times as great, because the water pressure is greater
greater, because the deeper water presses harder on the bottom of the hull
the same as at 100 ft
smaller, because more water above pushes down on the hull
questions.explain: Buoyant force = weight of the water displaced, and a fully submerged hull of fixed size displaces the same volume at any depth. The pressure on every surface does rise with depth, but the pressures on the top and the bottom rise by the same amount, so their DIFFERENCE, which is the buoyant force, does not change. The tripling and 'presses harder on the bottom' options forget the top gets the same increase; 'more water above' forgets the bottom does.

questions.stem: A metal casting weighs 50 lb in air and 30 lb when hung completely under water from a spring scale. What is the casting's specific gravity?
options: about 1.67
questions.explain: The 20 lb it seems to lose under water is the buoyant force, which equals the weight of water with the same volume as the casting. Specific gravity = its weight ÷ weight of an equal volume of water = 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5. About 1.67 divides by the underwater weight (50 ÷ 30); 0.6 divides 30 by 50; 0.4 is the right ratio upside down. Any value below 1 would float, yet the casting still pulls 30 lb on the scale under water.

questions.stem: Three identical lamps are connected to a battery: lamp A is in series with a parallel pair, lamps B and C. Lamp C is then unscrewed. What happens to the brightness of lamps A and B?
options: A and B both get dimmer
A and B both get brighter
A gets dimmer and B gets brighter
A gets brighter and B gets dimmer
questions.explain: Call each lamp R. Before, the circuit was R + R/2 = 1.5R, so A took 2/3 of the battery voltage and B only 1/3. With C removed, A and B are simply in series (2R) and each gets 1/2. The total resistance rises, so the current falls and A dims, while B, no longer sharing with C, rises from 1/3 to 1/2 of the voltage and brightens. 'Both dimmer' forgets B's share; 'both brighter' assumes removing a lamp frees power for the rest; the last option gets the total-resistance change backward.

questions.stem: A 40 W bulb and a 100 W bulb, both rated for 120 V, are connected in series across a 120 V supply. Which bulb glows brighter?
options: The 100 W bulb
The 40 W bulb
Both equally, because the same current flows through each
Neither lights, because each gets less than its rated voltage
questions.explain: From P = V² ÷ R at rated voltage, the 40 W bulb has the higher resistance (14,400 ÷ 40 = 360 Ω against 14,400 ÷ 100 = 144 Ω). In series both carry the same current, and power = I²R, so the higher-resistance 40 W bulb takes the larger share and glows brighter. The 100 W rating applies only when that bulb gets the full 120 V. Same current does not mean same power when the resistances differ, and both bulbs do light, just below full brightness.

questions.stem: A 1,500 W space heater runs 4 hours a day for 30 days. Electricity costs 12 cents per kilowatt-hour. What does it cost to run for the month?
questions.explain: Energy = power × time: 1.5 kW × 4 h × 30 days = 180 kWh. Cost = 180 × $0.12 = $21.60. $0.72 is one day's cost; $5.40 leaves out the 4 hours per day; $216.00 is a decimal slip (180 × 12 = 2,160 cents, which is $21.60).

questions.stem: A 120 V kitchen circuit is protected by a 15 A fuse. Which set of appliances, all switched on together, will blow it?
options: A 1,500 W space heater running on its own
A 1,200 W kettle, an 800 W toaster and a 100 W radio
A 900 W microwave together with a 700 W blender
Twelve 100 W lamps, all lit at once on the same circuit
questions.explain: The fuse allows at most 15 A × 120 V = 1,800 W. The kettle, toaster and radio total 2,100 W and draw 2,100 ÷ 120 = 17.5 A, so the fuse blows. The heater alone draws 12.5 A, the microwave and blender 1,600 W (about 13.3 A), and the twelve lamps 1,200 W (10 A): many small loads only add up to their total wattage.

questions.stem: An ideal doorbell transformer steps 120 V AC down to 12 V. Its primary has 1,000 turns. When the secondary supplies 2 A, how many turns does the secondary have, and what current does the primary draw?
options: 100 turns; 0.2 A
100 turns; 20 A
100 turns; 2 A
questions.explain: Turns follow voltage: 12 ÷ 120 = 1/10, so the secondary has 100 turns. Power in equals power out: 12 V × 2 A = 24 W, so the primary draws 24 ÷ 120 = 0.2 A. Stepping voltage down steps current up on the secondary side, so the primary current is the smaller one. 20 A applies the ratio the wrong way; 10,000 turns would step the voltage up; 2 A on both sides would mean 240 W in for 24 W out.

questions.stem: A power station sends the same power over the same transmission line, but steps the line voltage up from 100,000 V to 200,000 V. The power wasted as heat in the line becomes —
options: a quarter as much
half as much
twice as much
four times as much
questions.explain: For the same power, doubling the voltage halves the current (P = V × I). Heat in the wires = I²R, and with R unchanged, half the current gives (½)² = ¼ of the loss. 'Half' forgets to square the current. 'Twice' and 'four times' wrongly plug the line voltage into V² ÷ R, but that voltage is not dropped across the wire; only the small drop along the wire heats it. This is why grids transmit at high voltage.

questions.stem: An uncharged capacitor is connected in series with a resistor across a 9 V battery. Long after the switch is closed, what are the current in the circuit and the voltage across the capacitor?
options: A steady current of 9 V ÷ R; 0 V across the capacitor
Zero current; 4.5 V across the capacitor
Zero current; 9 V across the capacitor
A steady current of 9 V ÷ R; 9 V across the capacitor
questions.explain: Current flows at first while charge builds up on the plates, but the charging capacitor pushes back with a growing voltage. When its voltage reaches the battery's 9 V nothing is left to drive current, so it stops: a capacitor blocks steady DC. With no current, no voltage is lost across the resistor, so the full 9 V sits across the capacitor, not a half share. A current of 9 V ÷ R is what flows at the very first instant, not later.

questions.stem: Two 10 µF capacitors are connected in series. What is their combined capacitance?
options: 20 µF
10 µF
100 µF
5 µF
questions.explain: Capacitors combine the opposite way to resistors. In series, 1/C = 1/10 + 1/10 = 2/10, so C = 5 µF: the pair behaves like one capacitor with its plates twice as far apart. 20 µF is the parallel total (the series rule for resistors); 10 µF assumes the second capacitor changes nothing; 100 µF multiplies the values.

questions.stem: A hand-cranked generator is lighting one lamp. A second identical lamp is then switched on in parallel with the first. To keep the crank turning at the same speed, the operator must —
options: push less hard, because the current is now shared between two lamps
push just as hard, because crank speed alone sets the output
push harder only if the lamps are connected in series instead
push harder, because more current means a stronger opposing force
questions.explain: Adding a lamp in parallel lowers the total resistance, so the generator delivers more current and more power. That current in the coil produces a magnetic force opposing the rotation (Lenz's law), and the extra electrical energy has to come from the operator's arm. Sharing current between lamps does not reduce the total; a lamp added in series would RAISE the resistance, cut the current and make cranking easier.

questions.stem: A simple single-coil generator is changed so that its spinning coil connects to the outside circuit through a split-ring commutator instead of two solid slip rings. Its output changes from —
options: alternating current to a pulsing current that never reverses
direct current to alternating current
alternating current to perfectly smooth, steady direct current
a high voltage to a lower voltage at the same frequency
questions.explain: The coil itself always produces a voltage that reverses every half turn. Slip rings pass this on unchanged, giving AC. A split-ring commutator swaps the coil's connections at the instant the voltage reverses, so the outside circuit always gets the same direction: pulsating DC that rises and falls but never reverses. 'DC to AC' has it backward, the output is not smooth (that needs many coils or filtering), and the commutator does not change the voltage.

questions.stem: A bar magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a galvanometer, and the needle swings to the right. The magnet is then held still inside the coil for a few seconds, and finally pulled out twice as fast as it went in. The needle —
options: stays to the right while the magnet is still, then swings left
returns to zero while the magnet is still, then swings right, farther than before
returns to zero while the magnet is still, then swings left the same amount as before
returns to zero while the magnet is still, then swings left, farther than before
questions.explain: A voltage is induced only while the magnetic field through the coil is CHANGING. A stationary magnet gives no change, so no current. Pulling out reverses the change, so the current, and the needle, reverse. Faster motion means a faster change and a larger induced voltage, so the swing is bigger. Staying right confuses the magnet's presence with its motion; swinging right ignores the reversal; 'the same amount' ignores the doubled speed.

questions.stem: The north-seeking (N) end of a compass needle points toward Earth's geographic North Pole. Magnetically, what lies near the geographic North Pole?
options: A magnetic north pole, since like poles attract
No pole at all, since the field there runs flat along the ground
A magnetic south pole
No pole; the needle simply lines up with Earth's spin axis
questions.explain: Opposite poles attract. The needle's N end is pulled toward the Arctic, so the pole there must be magnetically a SOUTH pole, even though its location gets it called the 'north magnetic pole'. 'Like poles attract' reverses the rule. Near a magnetic pole the field actually points steeply down into the ground, not flat, and the needle follows Earth's magnetic field rather than its spin axis, which is why compasses need correcting for variation.

questions.stem: 200 g of water at 80 °C is poured into 600 g of water at 20 °C in an insulated container. Once they have mixed, what is the final temperature?
questions.explain: Heat lost by the hot water equals heat gained by the cold, and with the same liquid that is a mass-weighted average: (200 × 80 + 600 × 20) ÷ 800 = (16,000 + 12,000) ÷ 800 = 35 °C. Check: the hot water drops 45° × 200 g = 9,000; the cold rises 15° × 600 g = 9,000 ✓. 50 °C is the plain average; 65 °C weights the masses the wrong way round; 40 °C splits the 60° gap by 3 instead of by 4 (1 part hot to 3 parts cold).

questions.stem: A pot of water is boiling at 100 °C at sea level. The burner is turned up to full. What happens to the water's temperature?
options: It stays at 100 °C, and the water boils away faster
It climbs steadily above 100 °C while the extra heat is added
It rises a few degrees to a new, higher steady temperature
It stays at 100 °C, and boils at the same rate as before
questions.explain: While water boils, added heat goes into latent heat of vaporization, turning liquid into steam, not into raising the temperature. At sea-level pressure it stays at 100 °C however hard it is heated; more heat just makes steam faster. Only raising the pressure, as in a pressure cooker, raises the boiling temperature. Boiling at the same rate would mean the extra heat simply vanished.

questions.stem: It takes 80 calories to melt 1 g of ice at 0 °C, and 1 calorie to warm 1 g of water by 1 °C. How much heat turns 10 g of ice at 0 °C into water at 20 °C?
options: 200 cal
800 cal
questions.explain: Two steps. Melting: 10 g × 80 = 800 cal, with no change in temperature. Warming: 10 g × 1 × 20 °C = 200 cal. Total 1,000 cal. 200 cal skips the melting, 800 cal stops at 0 °C, and 16,000 cal multiplies the latent heat by the temperature rise, mixing the two steps together.

questions.stem: A deep pond cools on a winter night until all of its water is at 4 °C. The freezing air keeps chilling the surface. What happens next?
options: The colder surface water sinks, so the pond freezes from the bottom up
The colder water sinks and mixes, so the whole pond reaches 0 °C before ice forms
The surface water stays on top as it cools to 0 °C, so ice forms there first
Ice forms first on the bottom, where the water pressure is greatest
questions.explain: Water is densest at about 4 °C. Above 4 °C, chilled surface water is denser and sinks, mixing the pond. Below 4 °C, colder water is LESS dense, so it floats on top, cools to 0 °C and freezes there, while the bottom stays near 4 °C. Expecting it to sink applies the rule for most liquids, which water breaks below 4 °C, and higher pressure slightly LOWERS the freezing point, so the bottom does not freeze first.

questions.stem: Compared with a single-cylinder four-stroke engine running at the same rpm, a single-cylinder two-stroke engine has a power stroke —
options: twice as often, once every crank revolution
half as often, once every four revolutions
just as often, since both fire once per cycle
four times as often, on every piston stroke
questions.explain: A four-stroke needs four strokes, two crank revolutions, per cycle, so it fires every second revolution. A two-stroke folds intake and exhaust into the ends of its compression and power strokes, so it completes a cycle, and fires, every revolution: twice as often. 'Once per cycle' is true of both, but the two-stroke cycle takes half the crank turns. Only one of every two strokes in a two-stroke is a power stroke.

questions.stem: In a turbojet engine, the turbine that sits in the hot gas just behind the combustion chambers is there mainly to —
options: drive the compressor at the front of the engine through a shaft
produce the engine's thrust by pushing back against the outside air
squeeze the incoming air before the fuel is added and burned
drive a propeller that supplies most of the aircraft's thrust
questions.explain: A turbojet's turbine extracts some energy from the hot gas and uses it to spin the compressor on the same shaft, keeping the cycle going. The thrust comes from the fast jet of exhaust leaving the nozzle (Newton's third law), not from the turbine pushing on air. Compressing the air is the compressor's job, and driving a propeller describes a turboprop, not a turbojet.

questions.stem: A refrigerator is left running with its door wide open in a closed, insulated room. Over several hours, the room's air temperature —
options: rises, because the motor's energy also becomes heat in the room
falls, because the fridge blows cold air out into the room
falls at first, then settles back to its starting value
stays the same, because the fridge only moves heat from place to place
questions.explain: A refrigerator is a heat pump: it pulls heat from inside the cabinet and releases it, through the coils at the back, into the room. With the door open, the 'inside' is the room itself, so the heat it removes goes straight back out, plus the electrical energy that runs the compressor. The net effect is a heater. 'Only moves heat around' forgets the motor's energy; the cold air from the cabinet is cancelled by warm air from the coils.

questions.stem: In a reactor where ordinary water serves as both the coolant and the moderator, some of the water in the core boils into steam bubbles. What happens to the chain reaction?
options: It speeds up, because the steam is hotter than the water
It is unaffected, because only the control rods set its rate
It slows, because fewer neutrons are slowed to the speed best for fission
It speeds up, because neutrons can travel farther through the thin steam
questions.explain: The moderator slows the fast neutrons released by fission to the slow speeds at which they are most likely to split uranium-235. Steam is far less dense than water, so it slows fewer neutrons and the reaction rate drops, a built-in brake in water-moderated reactors. Heat does not drive fission, control rods are not the only thing that affects the neutrons, and neutrons that travel farther while still fast mostly fail to cause fission.

questions.stem: A sailor stands on the centerline of a long, straight, closed runway. A crash truck with its siren on drives straight toward her along the centerline at a steady speed, swerves around her at the last moment, and then drives straight away along the centerline at the same speed. Ignoring the brief swerve, compared with the siren's true pitch she hears —
options: a steady higher pitch as it approaches, then a steady lower pitch as it moves away
a pitch that rises steadily as it approaches, then falls steadily as it moves away
the true pitch throughout, only growing louder and then quieter
a steady lower pitch as it approaches, then a steady higher pitch as it moves away
questions.explain: Because she is directly in the truck's path, its whole speed is toward her while it approaches, so each wave is emitted a little closer to her and the waves arrive bunched up: a higher frequency. Moving away, the waves are stretched out: a lower frequency. At a steady speed the shift stays the same, so the pitch does not keep rising as it gets nearer; what rises is the LOUDNESS. A steadily rising pitch confuses loudness with pitch; hearing the true pitch ignores the Doppler effect; and the last option has the shifts backward.

questions.stem: A worker strikes one end of a long steel rail with a hammer. A listener at the far end, with one ear pressed against the rail, hears the blow twice. Why?
options: Sound travels much faster in steel than in air, so the rail's sound comes first
Sound travels faster in air than in steel, so the air's sound arrives first
The sound reflects off the far end of the rail and returns as an echo
The hammer bounces and strikes the rail a second, softer time
questions.topic: Speed of sound in different media
questions.explain: Sound travels faster in stiff, tightly bonded materials: about 15 times faster in steel than in air. The listener hears the sound through the rail first, then the slower sound through the air. Air is the SLOWEST of the common media (air, water, steel), so the first option has the order reversed. An echo or a second blow is not needed to explain the two sounds; two paths at two speeds already do.

questions.stem: A sound wave passes from air into water, where sound travels about 4 times faster. What happens to the wave's frequency and wavelength?
options: The frequency rises 4 times; the wavelength stays the same
The frequency stays the same; the wavelength becomes about 4 times shorter
Both stay the same; only the loudness of the sound changes
The frequency stays the same; the wavelength becomes about 4 times longer
questions.explain: Frequency is set by the source: each wave that reaches the surface sends exactly one wave onward, so it cannot change at a boundary. Speed = frequency × wavelength, so if the speed rises 4 times with the frequency fixed, the wavelength must grow 4 times. A rising frequency would change the pitch a diver hears; 'shorter' has the proportion upside down; both staying the same breaks speed = frequency × wavelength.

questions.stem: Soldiers are ordered to break step when marching across a light footbridge. The main reason is that marching in step —
options: could drive the bridge at its natural frequency and build up big swaying
puts more total weight on the bridge than walking out of step does
raises the bridge's natural frequency until the structure finally cracks
sends one large shock wave along the deck with every step
questions.explain: Every structure has natural frequencies at which it vibrates easily. A steady rhythm that matches one of them adds energy on every cycle, like well-timed pushes on a swing, and the swaying can grow dangerously large: resonance. The soldiers weigh the same in or out of step, and marching does not change the bridge's natural frequency, which is set by its mass and stiffness. Breaking step scatters the pushes so they cannot build up.

questions.stem: A guitar string is tightened without changing its vibrating length, and its pitch rises. Which statement explains why?
options: The wavelength gets shorter, while the wave speed stays the same
Waves travel more slowly on the tighter string, so they bunch up into a higher frequency
Waves travel faster on the tighter string; the wavelength is still fixed by the length
The string stretches slightly longer, and a longer string vibrates faster
questions.explain: The basic note's wavelength is set by the vibrating length (twice that length), which has not changed. Wave speed on a string rises with tension, and frequency = speed ÷ wavelength, so the frequency and the pitch go up. A shorter wavelength needs a shorter vibrating length, as when pressing a fret. Slower waves would LOWER the frequency, and a longer string would also give a lower note.

questions.stem: The critical angle for light going from water into air is about 49°. A diver's flashlight beam strikes the underside of the calm water surface at 60° from the normal. The beam —
options: passes into the air, bending away from the normal
passes into the air, bending toward the normal
passes straight into the air without bending
reflects entirely back down into the water
questions.explain: Light leaving a slower medium (water) for a faster one (air) bends away from the normal, and at the critical angle the escaping ray just skims along the surface. At any angle LARGER than the critical angle, no light can escape: it is all reflected back into the water (total internal reflection), which is how optical fibers trap light. Bending away from the normal happens only below 49°; bending toward it is what light does going from air into water; only a ray along the normal passes straight through.

questions.stem: A sailor 6 ft tall wants to see his whole body, from head to feet, in a flat mirror hung on a vertical wall. What is the shortest mirror that will do it?
options: 6 ft, the same as his height
3 ft, wherever he stands
3 ft, but only if he stands close to it
2 ft, if he stands far enough back
questions.explain: Light from his feet reaches his eyes off a point on the mirror halfway in height between his eyes and his feet; light from the top of his head reflects off a point halfway between his eyes and the top of his head. Those two points are half his height apart: 3 ft. Moving back does not help or hurt, because the reflection points stay at those same halfway heights. A full 6 ft mirror is twice what is needed.

questions.stem: A fisherman on a dock sees a fish in clear, calm water some distance out in front of him. To hit it with a spear thrown along his line of sight, he should aim —
options: exactly where the fish appears to be
below where the fish appears to be
above where the fish appears to be
slightly to one side of where the fish appears
questions.explain: Light from the fish bends away from the normal as it leaves the water, and his eye traces it back in a straight line, so the fish appears higher, shallower, than it really is. The spear does not bend, so he must aim below the image. Aiming at the image misses high, and aiming above makes the miss worse. The bending happens in the vertical plane between him and the fish, so it shifts the image up, not sideways.

questions.stem: Gear A (12 teeth) turns clockwise at 1,200 rpm and meshes with gear B (36 teeth). Gear C (10 teeth) is fixed to the same shaft as B and turns with it. Gear C meshes with gear D (40 teeth). How does gear D turn?
options: 100 rpm, counterclockwise
400 rpm, counterclockwise
300 rpm, clockwise
100 rpm, clockwise
questions.explain: A drives B at 1,200 × 12/36 = 400 rpm, and C turns at the same 400 rpm because it shares B's shaft. C then drives D at 400 × 10/40 = 100 rpm. Direction: A clockwise makes B (and C with it) counterclockwise, and D, meshed with C, turns clockwise, the same way as A. Counterclockwise treats B and C as a separate mesh that reverses direction; 400 rpm counterclockwise is the middle shaft, not the output; 300 rpm skips the first reduction (1,200 × 10/40).

questions.stem: Pulley A, 10 in in diameter, turns clockwise at 240 rpm. It drives pulley B, 4 in in diameter, through a crossed belt (the belt forms a figure eight between the two pulleys). How does pulley B turn?
options: 600 rpm, clockwise
96 rpm, counterclockwise
600 rpm, counterclockwise
96 rpm, clockwise
questions.explain: The belt moves at the same surface speed on both pulleys, so speed is inversely proportional to diameter: 240 × 10/4 = 600 rpm. Crossing the belt reverses the direction, so B turns counterclockwise. Clockwise is the rule for an open belt; 96 rpm multiplies by 4/10 instead of 10/4, which would make the smaller pulley turn slower. Check: 240 × 10 = 600 × 4 ✓.

questions.stem: On a bicycle, the pedal chainring has 48 teeth and the rear-wheel sprocket has 16 teeth. A rider pedals at 60 rpm, applying 60 lb-ft of torque to the cranks. Ignoring losses, how does the rear sprocket turn?
options: 180 rpm with 60 lb-ft of torque
180 rpm with 20 lb-ft of torque
180 rpm with 180 lb-ft of torque
20 rpm with 180 lb-ft of torque
questions.explain: Every link that leaves the chainring passes over the sprocket, so the sprocket turns 48/16 = 3 times as fast: 60 × 3 = 180 rpm. The chain has the same tension at both ends, but the sprocket's radius is one third as large, so its torque is one third: 60 ÷ 3 = 20 lb-ft. Check: torque × speed is unchanged, 60 × 60 = 20 × 180 ✓. 60 lb-ft assumes a chain passes torque along unchanged (it passes force); 180 lb-ft raises both speed and torque, which would create energy; 20 rpm divides the speed when it should multiply.

questions.stem: A 48 in pry bar is used as a first-class lever. The fulcrum block is first placed under the bar 6 in from the load end, with the effort applied at the other end. The block is then moved to 3 in from the load end. How does the bar's ideal mechanical advantage change?
options: It rises from 7 to 14
It rises from 8 to 16
It rises from 7 to 15
It falls from 7 to 3.5
questions.explain: Ideal MA = effort arm ÷ load arm. At first the effort arm is 48 − 6 = 42 in, so MA = 42 ÷ 6 = 7. With the block at 3 in, the effort arm becomes 45 in, so MA = 45 ÷ 3 = 15. 14 doubles the old value but forgets the effort arm also got longer; 8 and 16 use the whole 48 in bar as the effort arm; 3.5 has the ratio upside down (moving the fulcrum toward the load always helps).

questions.stem: A forearm is held horizontal with a 10 lb weight in the hand, 14 in from the elbow joint. The biceps pulls straight up on the forearm 2 in from the elbow. Ignoring the forearm's own weight, what force must the biceps exert, and what force does the upper-arm bone exert on the forearm at the elbow?
options: 70 lb; 80 lb pushing down
70 lb; 60 lb pushing down
60 lb; 50 lb pushing down
1.4 lb; 8.6 lb pushing up
questions.explain: This is a third-class lever with the elbow as the fulcrum. Moments about the elbow: biceps × 2 = 10 × 14, so the biceps pulls up with 70 lb. Vertical forces must also balance: 70 up = 10 down + elbow force, so the bone pushes down on the forearm with 60 lb. 80 lb adds the two forces instead of balancing them; 60 lb measures the weight's arm from the muscle (12 in) instead of from the elbow; 1.4 lb inverts the ratio, forgetting that a third-class lever has an MA below 1.

questions.stem: A block and tackle has a fixed upper block with two sheaves and a movable lower block with two sheaves; a 600 lb load hangs from the lower block. The rope's dead end is tied to the lower block. From there the rope runs up and down around all four sheaves in turn, and its free end leaves the last lower sheave going straight up to an operator standing on the beam above. Ignoring friction and block weight, what pull holds the load, and how much rope must the operator take in to raise the load 2 ft?
options: 150 lb; 8 ft
300 lb; 4 ft
120 lb; 2 ft
120 lb; 10 ft
questions.explain: Count the rope segments pulling up on the lower block: the dead end, two at the first lower sheave and two at the second (the last one being the free end, which pulls upward), 5 in all. Each carries the same tension, so the pull is 600 ÷ 5 = 120 lb, and since every segment shortens by 2 ft, the operator takes in 5 × 2 = 10 ft. 150 lb and 8 ft count sheaves (4) instead of supporting segments; 300 lb and 4 ft count only the two movable sheaves; 2 ft forgets that force saved is paid for in distance. Check: 120 × 10 = 600 × 2 ✓.

questions.stem: A sailor sits in a bosun's chair. A rope tied to the chair runs up over a single fixed pulley and back down to the sailor's own hands. Sailor and chair together weigh 180 lb. Ignoring friction, how hard must the sailor pull down on the rope to hoist himself up at a steady speed?
options: 90 lb
180 lb
360 lb
60 lb
questions.explain: Treat sailor and chair as one object. Two rope segments pull it upward: the one tied to the chair and the one in his hands, because when he pulls down on the rope, the rope pulls up on him with the same tension. At steady speed 2T = 180 lb, so T = 90 lb. 180 lb is the fixed-pulley answer for hoisting someone else from the deck; 360 lb doubles instead of halving; 60 lb counts three supporting segments. Check: 90 + 90 = 180 ✓.

questions.stem: An operator pulls 20 ft of rope through a pulley system with a steady 50 lb pull, and the 160 lb load rises 5 ft. What are the system's actual mechanical advantage and its efficiency?
questions.explain: Actual MA is the ratio of the forces really involved: 160 ÷ 50 = 3.2. The ideal MA is the ratio of distances, 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Efficiency = work out ÷ work in = (160 × 5) ÷ (50 × 20) = 800 ÷ 1,000 = 80%. Check: AMA ÷ IMA = 3.2 ÷ 4 = 0.8 ✓. 4 is the ideal MA, not the actual one; 125% turns the work ratio upside down (no machine exceeds 100%); 4 and 100% ignore the friction loss.

questions.stem: A 60 lb weight hangs from spring P (20 lb/in). Spring P hangs from spring Q (60 lb/in), which is attached to the ceiling. Ignoring the springs' own weight, how far does the weight move down as the springs stretch?
options: 4 in
2 in
1.5 in
questions.explain: Springs hooked end to end each carry the FULL load. P stretches 60 ÷ 20 = 3 in and Q stretches 60 ÷ 60 = 1 in, so the weight drops 3 + 1 = 4 in. 2 in splits the load, 30 lb to each spring; 0.75 in treats the springs as side by side, adding their stiffnesses to 80 lb/in; 1.5 in uses the average stiffness of 40 lb/in.

questions.stem: A coil spring stretches 2 in when a 12 lb weight hangs from it. The spring is cut exactly in half, and the same 12 lb weight is hung from one of the halves. How far does that half stretch?
options: 2 in
4 in
1 in
0.5 in
questions.explain: Under a load, every coil carries the full 12 lb and opens up by the same small amount, so half the coils give half the total stretch: 1 in. Put another way, the whole spring's stiffness is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 lb/in and the half spring is twice as stiff, 12 lb/in, so 12 ÷ 12 = 1 in ✓. 2 in assumes stiffness depends only on the wire, not the length; 4 in thinks a shorter spring is weaker; 0.5 in halves the stretch twice.

questions.stem: A cam with three identical lobes, evenly spaced around its edge, turns at 240 rpm. A follower rides on the cam's edge. How many times each second does the follower reach its highest point?
questions.explain: 240 rpm is 240 ÷ 60 = 4 revolutions per second. Each revolution brings three lobes under the follower, so it peaks 4 × 3 = 12 times a second. 4 counts revolutions, not lobes; 80 divides by the number of lobes instead of multiplying; 720 is the count per minute, not per second.

questions.stem: In a crank-and-slider mechanism, the crankpin is 4 in from the center of the crankshaft and the connecting rod is 14 in long. The crankshaft turns at a steady speed. How far does the slider travel from one end of its stroke to the other, and how does it move?
options: 4 in, stopping for an instant once each turn
8 in, never stopping, since the crank turns steadily
18 in, stopping for an instant twice each turn
8 in, stopping for an instant twice each turn
questions.explain: The slider reaches its two end positions when the crankpin is in line with the rod, on the near and far sides of the shaft, so the stroke is the diameter of the crankpin's circle: 2 × 4 = 8 in, whatever the rod's length. At each end the slider reverses, so it stops for an instant twice per revolution even though the crank never slows. 4 in uses the crank radius instead of twice it; 18 in adds the rod length to the crank radius; never stopping ignores that the slider must reverse.

questions.stem: The adjusting screw on a vise has a double thread: two separate threads wound side by side. The distance between adjacent crests (the pitch) is 1/8 in. How many full turns of the screw move the jaw 1 in?
questions.explain: With two thread starts, each turn advances the screw by two pitches, so the lead is 2 × 1/8 = 1/4 in per turn. Moving 1 in takes 1 ÷ 1/4 = 4 turns. 8 treats it as a single thread, advancing only 1/8 in per turn; 16 halves the advance per turn instead of doubling it; 2 takes the lead as 1/2 in.

questions.stem: Four sailors work a capstan, each pushing with 60 lb at right angles on a bar, 5 ft from the capstan's center. The anchor cable winds onto the capstan drum, which is 2 ft in diameter. Ignoring friction, what pull do they put on the cable?
options: 600 lb
300 lb
240 lb
questions.explain: Total torque = 4 × 60 lb × 5 ft = 1,200 lb-ft. The cable pulls at the drum's radius, 1 ft, so the cable pull is 1,200 ÷ 1 = 1,200 lb. 600 lb uses the 2 ft diameter as the lever arm instead of the radius; 300 lb is only one sailor's share (60 × 5); 240 lb simply adds the four pushes and ignores the leverage.

questions.stem: A salesman claims his chain hoist lets an operator raise a 1,000 lb engine 2 ft by pulling 15 ft of chain with a steady 100 lb force. What, if anything, is wrong with the claim?
options: It is impossible: it puts out more work than it takes in
Nothing: its mechanical advantage of 10 makes it work
Nothing: it simply runs at 75% efficiency
Nothing, provided its sprockets have no friction
questions.explain: Work in = 100 lb × 15 ft = 1,500 ft-lb; work out = 1,000 lb × 2 ft = 2,000 ft-lb. That is an efficiency of 2,000 ÷ 1,500, about 133%, and no machine can deliver more work than it receives. A force ratio of 10 would need at least 10 × 2 = 20 ft of chain, not 15; 75% turns the work ratio upside down; even with zero friction the best possible is 100%.

questions.stem: An electric motor turning at 1,800 rpm delivers 10 lb-ft of torque into a gearbox. The gearbox's output shaft turns at 300 rpm, and the gearbox is 90% efficient. What torque does the output shaft deliver, and what is the gearbox's actual mechanical advantage?
options: 60 lb-ft; 6
54 lb-ft; 6
About 67 lb-ft; 6.7
questions.explain: The speed ratio 1,800 ÷ 300 = 6 is the ideal MA, so a perfect gearbox would give 10 × 6 = 60 lb-ft. At 90% efficiency the output is 60 × 0.9 = 54 lb-ft. Actual MA is the ratio of output torque to input torque, 54 ÷ 10 = 5.4. 60 lb-ft ignores the loss; 54 lb-ft with 6 quotes the ideal MA as the actual one; about 67 lb-ft divides by 0.9 instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A 200 lb crate sits on a level deck. The coefficient of static friction is 0.5 and the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. A sailor pushes the crate horizontally with 80 lb, and it does not move. How large is the friction force on the crate?
options: 80 lb
100 lb
60 lb
0 lb
questions.explain: Static friction is not a fixed value: it grows to match the push, up to a maximum of 0.5 × 200 = 100 lb. The crate is at rest, so the forces balance and friction equals the 80 lb push. 100 lb is only the maximum, reached just as the crate is about to slide; 60 lb is kinetic friction (0.3 × 200), which acts only once it is sliding; 0 lb forgets that something must cancel the push.

questions.stem: A car with anti-lock brakes, which keep the wheels rolling while braking hard, usually stops in a shorter distance than a car whose wheels lock and skid. Why?
options: Kinetic friction is larger than static friction, so a locked wheel overheats and loses its grip
A rolling tire's contact patch is momentarily at rest on the road, so the larger static friction acts
Locking the wheels lifts weight off the road, so the normal force and the friction both drop
A rolling tire's contact patch moves forward at the car's speed, so it pushes back on the road harder
questions.explain: A wheel rolling without slipping has its contact point momentarily at rest relative to the road, so its grip is static friction. A locked wheel slides, so only kinetic friction acts, and for rubber on pavement the maximum static friction is larger than kinetic friction. The first wrong option reverses that rule; locking the wheels does not change the car's weight on the road; the contact patch is at rest, not moving at the car's speed (it is the top of the tire that moves at twice the car's speed).

questions.stem: A sailor carries a 50 lb box 100 ft along a level deck at a steady walking speed, holding it at the same height the whole way. How much work does his upward holding force do on the box?
options: 5,000 ft-lb
0 ft-lb
50 ft-lb
It depends on how fast he walks
questions.explain: Work = force × distance moved in the direction of the force. His holding force points straight up, but the box moves only horizontally, so that force does no work on it (his muscles still burn energy, but no mechanical work is done on the box). 5,000 ft-lb multiplies the force by a distance at right angles to it; 50 ft-lb is just the size of the force; walking speed would affect power, not work.

questions.stem: A winch lifts a 550 lb load 30 ft straight up at a steady speed in 15 seconds. Ignoring losses, what power does the winch deliver? (1 hp = 550 ft-lb per second.)
options: 30 hp
2 hp
0.5 hp
questions.explain: Work = 550 lb × 30 ft = 16,500 ft-lb. Power = work ÷ time = 16,500 ÷ 15 = 1,100 ft-lb/s, and 1,100 ÷ 550 = 2 hp. Check: the load rises at 2 ft/s, and 550 lb × 2 ft/s = 1,100 ft-lb/s ✓. 30 hp forgets to divide by the time; 1,100 hp forgets to convert ft-lb/s into horsepower; 0.5 hp divides the time by the height.

questions.stem: A car's speed increases from 20 mph to 60 mph. With the same braking force and no skidding, how does its braking distance at 60 mph compare with its braking distance at 20 mph?
options: 3 times as long
4 times as long
9 times as long
27 times as long
questions.explain: The brakes must remove all the kinetic energy, and the work they do equals braking force × distance. Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so tripling the speed gives 3² = 9 times the energy and, with the same force, 9 times the distance. 3 times treats energy as proportional to speed; 4 times recalls the rule for DOUBLING speed; 27 cubes the ratio.

questions.stem: A solid sphere, a solid cylinder and a thin-walled hoop, all with different masses and radii, are released together from rest at the top of the same ramp. Each rolls without slipping. In what order do they reach the bottom?
options: All three together, since they start from the same height
Heaviest first, whatever its shape
Hoop, then cylinder, then sphere
Sphere, then cylinder, then hoop
questions.explain: A rolling object splits its energy between moving along and spinning, and the more of its mass that sits far from the axis, the bigger the share that goes into spin and the slower it travels. The hoop has all its mass at the rim (half its energy goes into spin), the cylinder less (one third) and the sphere least (two sevenths), so the sphere wins and the hoop comes last. Mass and radius cancel out, so weight gives no advantage; arriving together is true only for objects sliding without friction; hoop first reverses the rule.

questions.stem: A 3,000 lb car moving east at 20 mph collides head-on with a 2,000 lb car moving west at 30 mph. The cars lock together. Ignoring friction from the road, how do they move just after the crash?
options: East at 24 mph
West at 10 mph
West at 12 mph
They stop at the point of impact
questions.explain: Momentum is conserved, and direction matters. East: 3,000 × 20 = 60,000; west: 2,000 × 30 = 60,000. The total is 60,000 − 60,000 = 0, so the wreck has no momentum and stops dead. 24 mph adds the two momenta as if both moved east (120,000 ÷ 5,000); 10 mph subtracts the speeds and ignores the masses; 12 mph counts only the westbound car's momentum (60,000 ÷ 5,000).

questions.stem: When catching a heavy heaving-line bag, a deckhand lets his hands move back with the bag instead of holding them rigid. Why does this reduce the force on his hands?
options: The bag loses less momentum, so the impulse on it is smaller
The longer stopping time increases the impulse, which absorbs the force
The force is spread over a larger area of his hands
The bag loses the same momentum over a longer time, so the force is smaller
questions.explain: Impulse = force × time = change in momentum. The bag must go from its speed to zero either way, so its momentum change, and the impulse, is fixed; stretching the stopping time makes the average force smaller (double the time, half the force). The bag still loses all its momentum, so less momentum is wrong; the impulse stays the same rather than growing; the contact area of his hands does not change.

questions.stem: A highway curve is banked so that a car traveling at 40 mph can take it with no help from friction. One day the road is glare ice, with no friction at all, and a car enters the curve at 25 mph. What happens?
options: It holds the curve, since the banking works at any speed up to 40 mph
It slides up the bank toward the outside of the curve
It slides down the bank toward the inside of the curve
It holds the curve if the car is heavy enough
questions.explain: On a banked curve the road's push on the car is tilted toward the center of the curve, and at the design speed its sideways part supplies exactly the centripetal force needed. At a lower speed less centripetal force is needed, so with no friction to hold it, the car slides down the slope toward the inside. Sliding toward the outside happens when going FASTER than the design speed; weight does not help, because the force needed and the force available both scale with the car's mass.

questions.stem: On a firing range, a target hangs from an electromagnet. A rifle is aimed straight at the target, and a switch releases the target at the instant the bullet leaves the muzzle. Ignoring air resistance, and assuming the bullet reaches the target's line of fall before the target hits the ground, what happens?
options: The bullet passes above the target
The bullet hits the target
The bullet passes below the target
The bullet hits only at one particular muzzle speed
questions.explain: Without gravity the bullet would fly along the line of aim straight to the target. With gravity, the bullet and the target both start falling at the same instant and drop at the same rate, so at every moment each is the same distance below where it would have been. The bullet stays on line with the target and hits it. Passing above assumes only the target falls; passing below assumes the bullet falls faster; the muzzle speed changes only how far the pair have dropped when they meet, not whether they meet.

questions.stem: A stone is dropped from rest off a tall cliff. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², how far does it fall during the third second of its fall (from t = 2 s to t = 3 s)?
questions.explain: Distance fallen from rest is d = ½gt² = 5t². By 2 s it has fallen 5 × 4 = 20 m, and by 3 s, 5 × 9 = 45 m, so during the third second it falls 45 − 20 = 25 m. Check: successive seconds give 5, 15, 25 m, the odd-number pattern ✓. 45 m is the total after three seconds; 30 m is the speed at 3 s (30 m/s) mistaken for a distance; 20 m is the total after two seconds.

questions.stem: A 1.5 kg pendulum bob on a 2 m string is pulled aside until it is 0.8 m above its lowest point, then released from rest. Ignoring friction and air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², how fast is it moving at the lowest point?
options: 16 m/s
About 6.3 m/s
About 2.8 m/s
4 m/s
questions.explain: Potential energy lost becomes kinetic energy: mgh = ½mv², so v² = 2gh = 2 × 10 × 0.8 = 16 and v = 4 m/s. The mass cancels, and the string length plays no part; only the height dropped counts. 16 m/s forgets the square root; about 6.3 m/s uses the 2 m string length as the drop; about 2.8 m/s leaves out the 2 in 2gh.

questions.stem: A 40,000 lb fuel truck and a 4,000 lb car collide. During the collision, how do the forces they exert on each other, and their accelerations, compare?
options: Equal forces; the car's acceleration is 10 times the truck's
The truck's force is 10 times larger; equal accelerations
Equal forces; equal accelerations
The truck's force is 10 times larger; the car's acceleration is 100 times the truck's
questions.explain: By Newton's third law the two forces are an action-reaction pair, so they are always equal in size and opposite in direction, whatever the masses or speeds. With the same force, acceleration = force ÷ mass, so the car, with one tenth the mass, gets 10 times the acceleration. Unequal forces breaks the third law; equal accelerations ignores the second law; 100 times counts the mass ratio twice.

questions.stem: A sailor stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator that is moving DOWN and slowing to a stop at a lower deck. While the elevator is slowing, the scale reads —
options: more than her weight
less than her weight
exactly her weight
her weight, rising above it only once the car has stopped
questions.explain: Slowing a downward motion means the acceleration points UP. To give her an upward acceleration, the scale must push up on her with more than her weight: reading = m(g + a). The reading depends on the direction of the acceleration, not the direction of travel. Less than her weight comes from looking at the downward motion; exactly her weight is true only at constant speed; once the car has stopped the scale reads her plain weight again.

questions.stem: A uniform board 12 ft long and weighing 60 lb rests on a pivot 4 ft from its left end. What weight hung from the left end makes the board balance level?
options: 30 lb
120 lb
60 lb
15 lb
questions.explain: A uniform board's weight acts at its center, 6 ft from the left end, which is 2 ft to the right of the pivot, giving a turning effect of 60 × 2 = 120 lb-ft. The hung weight acts 4 ft to the left of the pivot: W × 4 = 120, so W = 30 lb. 120 lb puts the board's whole weight at the far right end (60 × 8 ÷ 4); 60 lb just matches the weights and ignores the lever arms; 15 lb divides by the 8 ft right-hand length instead of the 4 ft arm.

questions.stem: A uniform 120 lb cabinet is 6 ft tall and 2 ft deep, front to back. Friction keeps it from sliding. What horizontal push, applied toward the front at the top of the back edge, will just start to tip it forward over its front bottom edge?
options: 40 lb
120 lb
360 lb
20 lb
questions.explain: The cabinet pivots on its front bottom edge. Its weight acts at its center, 1 ft back from that edge, giving a moment of 120 × 1 = 120 lb-ft that holds it down. The push acts 6 ft above the floor, so F × 6 = 120 and F = 20 lb. 40 lb uses the full 2 ft depth as the weight's lever arm; 120 lb assumes the push must equal the weight; 360 lb inverts the ratio (120 × 6 ÷ 2). A push high up has a long lever arm, which is why tall, narrow loads tip so easily.

questions.stem: A light 10 ft beam is bolted to support A at its left end and rests on support B 6 ft from the left end, so 4 ft of beam overhangs beyond B. A 300 lb load hangs from the right end. What forces do the supports exert on the beam?
