options: B pushes up 300 lb; A carries nothing
B pushes up 500 lb; A pushes up 200 lb
B pushes up 500 lb; A must hold the beam down with 200 lb
B pushes up 180 lb; A pushes up 120 lb
questions.explain: Take moments about A: B × 6 = 300 × 10, so B = 500 lb upward. Vertical forces must balance: 500 up = 300 down + A, so A = 200 lb DOWNWARD; the bolts at A hold the left end down, and without them the beam would tip about B. 300 lb at B ignores the leverage of the overhang; 200 lb up at A gets the sign wrong (that would put 700 lb up against 300 lb down); 180 and 120 lb split the load as if it hung between the supports.

questions.stem: A 1,000 lb load is lifted from a crane hook by a two-leg sling. Each leg makes an angle of 60° with the vertical, so the legs are 120° apart. What is the tension in each leg?
options: 500 lb
About 577 lb
questions.explain: The vertical part of each leg's pull must carry half the load: T × cos 60° = 500 lb. Since cos 60° = 0.5, T = 500 ÷ 0.5 = 1,000 lb, so each leg carries as much as the whole load. 500 lb assumes the legs hang straight down; about 577 lb treats the 60° as measured from the horizontal (500 ÷ cos 30°); 2,000 lb gives each leg the whole load before dividing by cos 60°. Wider sling angles always raise leg tension, which is why riggers limit them.

questions.stem: A simple roof truss is a triangle: two rafters, each sloping at 45°, meet at the peak, and a horizontal tie beam joins their lower ends. The truss rests on supports under its two lower corners, which push straight up only. A 1,000 lb load acts down at the peak. Ignoring the members' own weights, what is the force in the tie beam?
options: 500 lb, in tension
500 lb, in compression
About 707 lb, in tension
1,000 lb, in tension
questions.explain: By symmetry each support pushes up 500 lb. At a lower corner the rafter pushes down and outward along its 45° slope; its vertical part must equal the 500 lb support force, and at 45° its horizontal part is the same, 500 lb, pushing the corner outward. The tie beam must pull the corner back in with 500 lb, so it is in tension, while the rafters (about 707 lb each) are in compression. Compression swaps the roles of the members; 707 lb is the rafter force, not the tie force; 1,000 lb puts the whole load on one corner.

questions.stem: A light horizontal boom is hinged to a wall at one end. A 200 lb load hangs from its outer end, which is held up by a cable running back to the wall at a point above the hinge. The cable makes a 30° angle with the boom. What is the tension in the cable?
options: 200 lb
About 231 lb
400 lb
100 lb
questions.explain: Taking moments about the hinge, only the cable's vertical component holds up the end of the boom, so T × sin 30° = 200 lb. With sin 30° = 0.5, T = 400 lb (the cable's horizontal part, about 346 lb, presses the boom into the wall). 200 lb assumes the cable pulls straight up; about 231 lb uses cos 30° instead of sin 30°; 100 lb multiplies by 0.5 instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A mechanic pulls with 50 lb on the end of an 18 in wrench, but the pull is at 30° to the line of the handle instead of square to it. What torque does the pull apply to the bolt?
options: 37.5 lb-ft
75 lb-ft
About 65 lb-ft
450 lb-ft
questions.explain: Only the part of the pull at right angles to the handle turns the bolt: 50 × sin 30° = 25 lb. Torque = 25 lb × 1.5 ft = 37.5 lb-ft. 75 lb-ft assumes the pull is square to the handle; about 65 lb-ft uses cos 30°, the part of the pull that merely tugs along the handle; 450 is the correct figure in lb-in (25 × 18) mislabeled as lb-ft.

questions.stem: Movement of an airplane about its lateral axis is called ___ and is controlled mainly by the ___.
options: roll; ailerons
yaw; rudder
pitch; rudder
pitch; elevator
questions.explain: The lateral axis runs wingtip to wingtip; rotation about it is pitch, controlled by the elevator (or stabilator). Roll is about the longitudinal axis (ailerons) and yaw is about the vertical axis (rudder).

questions.stem: Wing dihedral mainly improves an airplane's stability about which axis?
options: Lateral axis
Longitudinal axis
Vertical axis
All three axes equally
questions.explain: Dihedral gives lateral (roll) stability, and rolling happens about the LONGITUDINAL axis (nose to tail). The trap is the word 'lateral': stability about the lateral axis is pitch (longitudinal) stability, which comes mainly from the horizontal tail.

questions.stem: A control surface that combines the jobs of the elevator and the ailerons, common on delta-wing and flying-wing aircraft, is a(n):
options: Ruddervator
Flaperon
Elevon
Stabilator
questions.explain: Elevon = ELEVator + ailerON. A ruddervator combines rudder and elevator on a V-tail, a flaperon combines flap and aileron, and a stabilator is a one-piece moving horizontal tail.

questions.stem: On a stabilator, the antiservo tab moves:
options: Opposite to the stabilator's trailing edge
Only when the trim wheel is turned
In the same direction as the stabilator's trailing edge
Independently, under autopilot control only
questions.explain: An antiservo tab moves the SAME way as the stabilator's trailing edge, making the very sensitive stabilator heavier and less likely to be over-controlled; it also works as the trim tab (FAA PHAK). A tab that moves opposite to its surface is a servo or trim tab.

questions.stem: To hold the nose up without back pressure on the yoke, a pilot trims the elevator. The elevator trim tab moves:
options: Up, which holds the elevator up
Down, which holds the elevator down
Down, which holds the elevator up
Up, which holds the elevator down
questions.explain: A trim tab deflects opposite to the surface it trims: air striking the lowered tab pushes the elevator's trailing edge UP, holding nose-up attitude. 'Up holds the elevator up' is the common reversal.

questions.stem: A pilot rolls into a right turn using ailerons alone. Adverse yaw makes the nose initially yaw:
options: Right, into the turn
Right, toward the lowered wing
Neither way, because the ailerons balance
Left, toward the rising wing
questions.explain: The left wing's lowered aileron raises that wing's lift and its induced drag, dragging the left wing back, so the nose swings left, opposite the turn. Coordinated right rudder corrects it.

questions.stem: Differential ailerons reduce adverse yaw by:
options: Lowering both ailerons together like flaps
Raising one aileron farther than the other is lowered
Linking the ailerons to a yaw damper
Pushing the raised aileron's nose into the airflow on an offset hinge
questions.explain: With differential ailerons the up-going aileron deflects more than the down-going one, adding drag on the descending wing to balance the induced drag of the rising wing. The offset-hinge method is the Frise aileron, a different design.

questions.stem: With Frise-type ailerons, the extra drag that offsets adverse yaw comes from the:
options: Lowered aileron deflecting farther than the raised one
Spoiler rising on the wing with the lowered aileron
Trim tab on the lowered aileron moving up
Leading edge of the raised aileron projecting below the wing
questions.explain: A Frise aileron pivots on an offset hinge, so as it is raised its leading edge pokes into the airflow below the wing, creating parasite drag on the descending wing (FAA PHAK). Unequal travel is the differential-aileron method.

questions.stem: Which type of flap slides aft on tracks as it lowers, increasing both wing area and camber?
options: Fowler flap
Split flap
Plain flap
Krueger flap
questions.explain: The Fowler flap moves rearward and down, adding wing area as well as camber, and gives the largest lift increase. A plain flap just hinges down, a split flap hinges from the lower surface only, and a Krueger flap is a leading-edge device.

questions.stem: Leading-edge slots and slats mainly allow a wing to:
options: Fly faster by cutting parasite drag
Dump lift quickly after touchdown
Trim out control forces in cruise
Reach a higher angle of attack before stalling
questions.explain: Slots and slats direct high-energy air over the upper surface, delaying flow separation so the wing can fly at a higher angle of attack (and slower) before it stalls. Dumping lift is the spoilers' job.

questions.stem: If a spoiler is raised on the left wing only, the airplane will tend to:
options: Roll right, because that wing gains drag
Roll left, because that wing loses lift
Pitch nose-up with no roll
Yaw right with no roll
questions.explain: A spoiler 'spoils' lift and adds drag on its own wing, so that wing drops: the airplane rolls (and yaws) toward the raised spoiler. Many jets use spoilers this way for roll control.

questions.stem: In straight-and-level, unaccelerated flight:
options: Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag
Lift exceeds weight and thrust exceeds drag
Thrust equals lift and weight equals drag
Lift equals drag and thrust equals weight
questions.explain: Steady flight means the opposing forces balance: lift opposes weight and thrust opposes drag. If lift exceeded weight the airplane would climb; if thrust exceeded drag it would accelerate.

questions.stem: The fixed angle between the wing's chord line and the airplane's longitudinal axis is the:
options: Angle of incidence
Angle of attack
Dihedral angle
Sweep angle
questions.explain: Incidence is built in and never changes. Angle of attack is measured between the chord line and the RELATIVE WIND and changes constantly in flight. Dihedral is the upward tilt of the wings; sweep is their backward angle.

questions.stem: Which statement about a wing stall is true?
options: It occurs whenever the critical angle of attack is exceeded
It occurs only below the published stall speed
It cannot occur in a nose-low attitude
It occurs only when engine power is lost
questions.explain: A wing stalls when it exceeds its critical angle of attack, at any airspeed, attitude, weight or power setting. Published stall speeds apply only to stated conditions (1 G, a given weight and configuration).

questions.stem: In a coordinated level turn at 60° of bank, the load factor is:
options: 3 G
2 G
questions.explain: Load factor in a level turn = 1 / cos(bank). cos 60° = 0.5, so 1 / 0.5 = 2 G. About 1.41 G is the figure for a 45° bank.

questions.stem: An airplane stalls at 50 knots in wings-level flight. In a level 60°-bank turn, it will stall at about:
options: 50 knots
100 knots
71 knots
60 knots
questions.explain: Stall speed rises with the SQUARE ROOT of load factor. At 60° the load factor is 2, so 50 × √2 ≈ 50 × 1.41 ≈ 71 knots. 100 knots wrongly multiplies by the load factor itself.

questions.stem: As an airplane climbs out of ground effect after takeoff, it will experience:
options: A decrease in induced drag
An increase in induced drag
A decrease in the angle of attack needed for lift
A sudden drop in parasite drag
questions.explain: Within about one wingspan of the ground, the surface restricts downwash and wingtip vortices, so induced drag is lower. Climbing out, induced drag rises and a higher angle of attack is needed (FAA PHAK). An airplane that lifts off too slowly in ground effect can settle back.

questions.stem: Wingtip vortices are strongest when the generating aircraft is:
options: Light, dirty and fast
Heavy, clean and slow
Heavy, dirty and fast
Light, clean and slow
questions.explain: Vortex strength depends on weight, speed and wing shape: the greatest vortices come from a heavy aircraft at high angle of attack, which means slow and clean (gear and flaps up). AIM 7-4-3.

questions.stem: Which wind is most hazardous for wake turbulence because it can carry a landing airliner's vortices forward into the touchdown zone?
options: A strong direct crosswind
A strong steady headwind
A strong quartering headwind
A light quartering tailwind
questions.explain: The AIM singles out a light quartering tailwind: it can move the vortices of a preceding aircraft forward into the touchdown zone. Strong winds break vortices up quickly.

questions.stem: When landing behind a large aircraft on the same runway, a pilot should:
options: Stay below its flight path and land before its touchdown point
Stay at or above its flight path and land beyond its touchdown point
Stay at or above its flight path and land before its touchdown point
Fly below its flight path and land beyond its touchdown point
questions.explain: Vortices sink below the generating aircraft's path and stop forming when its wheels touch down. So stay at or above its glide path and touch down beyond the point where it landed (AIM 7-4-6).

questions.stem: In a high-angle-of-attack climb, P-factor yaws a single-engine airplane with a clockwise propeller (seen from the cockpit) to the left because:
options: The descending blade on the right takes a bigger bite of air
The ascending blade on the left takes a bigger bite of air
The spiraling slipstream strikes the right side of the tail
Engine torque rolls the airplane to the right
questions.explain: At high angle of attack the descending (right) blade meets the air at a greater angle than the ascending (left) blade, so the right side makes more thrust and the nose yaws left. The slipstream strikes the LEFT side of the fin, and torque rolls the airplane LEFT.

questions.stem: As airspeed increases in level flight, induced drag ___ and parasite drag ___.
options: decreases; increases
increases; increases
increases; decreases
decreases; decreases
questions.explain: Induced drag is a by-product of lift and is greatest at high angle of attack, so it falls as speed rises. Parasite drag rises with the square of airspeed. Total drag is lowest where they cross, at L/D max.

questions.stem: In a four-stroke piston engine, how many crankshaft revolutions make up one complete cycle?
options: Two
One
Three
Four
questions.explain: Each stroke (intake, compression, power, exhaust) is half a turn of the crankshaft, so the cycle takes two revolutions and each cylinder fires once every two turns.

questions.stem: In an airplane with a fixed-pitch propeller, the first indication of carburetor ice is usually:
options: A loss of RPM
A drop in manifold pressure
A rise in oil temperature
A rise in RPM with roughness
questions.explain: With a fixed-pitch prop, ice choking the venturi first shows as falling RPM, then roughness. A drop in manifold pressure is the first sign with a CONSTANT-SPEED propeller, where the governor holds RPM.

questions.stem: When carburetor heat is applied, the fuel-air mixture becomes:
options: Leaner, because warm air is less dense
Richer, because warm air is denser
Richer, because warm air is less dense
Unchanged, because the mixture control sets it
questions.explain: Heated air is less dense, so the same fuel flow meets less air: the mixture richens and power drops slightly. If ice is present, RPM typically drops, then rises as the ice melts.

questions.stem: If a piston airplane's alternator and battery both fail in flight, the engine will:
options: Stop, because the spark plugs lose power
Keep running, because the magnetos are engine-driven
Run on one cylinder bank only
Stop once the battery's reserve is used up
questions.explain: Magnetos are self-contained generators driven by the engine. They make their own high-voltage current for the plugs, independent of the aircraft's electrical system.

questions.stem: In a turbojet engine, the compressor is driven by the:
options: Combustion chamber
Exhaust nozzle
Starter-generator
Turbine
questions.explain: Intake, compressor, combustor, turbine, exhaust ('suck, squeeze, bang, blow'). Hot gas spinning the turbine turns a shaft that drives the compressor. The starter only spins the engine up for starting.

questions.stem: A gas-turbine engine that delivers its power through a shaft to drive a helicopter's rotor is a:
options: Turbojet
Turboshaft
Turbofan
Ramjet
questions.explain: A turboshaft (e.g. the T700 in the MH-60) extracts nearly all its energy through a power turbine and shaft. A turboprop is similar but drives a propeller; turbojets and turbofans make thrust from their exhaust and fan.

questions.stem: In an airplane with a constant-speed propeller, the propeller control directly sets:
options: Engine RPM
Manifold pressure
Fuel-air mixture
Exhaust gas temperature
questions.explain: The prop control sets the RPM that the governor holds by changing blade angle; the throttle sets manifold pressure. Confusing the two is a classic trap.

questions.stem: Ice blocks the pitot tube's ram-air inlet AND its drain hole, but the static port stays open. As the airplane climbs, the airspeed indicator will:
options: Show an increasing airspeed
Show a decreasing airspeed
Drop to zero
Stay frozen at its last reading
questions.explain: Pressure is trapped in the pitot line while static pressure falls in the climb, so the difference grows and the ASI reads higher, acting like an altimeter (FAA PHAK). If only the inlet blocks and the drain stays open, it drops toward zero.

questions.stem: The turn coordinator's gyro operates on the principle of:
options: Rigidity in space
Precession
Magnetic dip
Centrifugal force
questions.explain: Rate instruments (turn coordinator, turn-and-slip) sense the gyro's precession as the airplane turns. The attitude and heading indicators rely on rigidity in space. Magnetic dip affects the compass.

questions.stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, accelerating on an easterly heading causes the magnetic compass to indicate:
options: A turn toward south
A turn toward north
No change, since the heading is constant
A turn toward west
questions.explain: Acceleration error, remembered as ANDS: Accelerate North, Decelerate South. It is greatest on east and west headings and caused by magnetic dip.

questions.stem: On an airspeed indicator, the upper limit of the white arc marks:
options: The never-exceed speed (VNE)
The maximum structural cruising speed (VNO)
The stall speed with flaps down (VSO)
The maximum flaps-extended speed (VFE)
questions.explain: The white arc is the flap operating range: VSO at the bottom, VFE at the top. VNO is the top of the green arc, and VNE is the red line.

questions.stem: A pilot flies from an area of high pressure into an area of low pressure without resetting the altimeter. The airplane is actually:
options: Higher than the altimeter indicates
At exactly the indicated altitude
Lower only if the air is also warmer
Lower than the altimeter indicates
questions.explain: 'High to low, look out below.' Flying into lower pressure with the old setting, the altimeter over-reads, so true altitude is below the indicated one. The same is true flying from warm air into colder air.

questions.stem: A pilot has 29.92 set in the altimeter, but the correct local setting is 30.42. With the altimeter reading 5,500 feet, the airplane's true altitude is about (standard temperature):
options: 6,000 feet
5,000 feet
5,500 feet
6,500 feet
questions.explain: One inch of mercury ≈ 1,000 feet. The setting is 0.50 in too LOW, so the altimeter reads about 500 feet low; setting 30.42 would raise the reading to 6,000 feet, which is the true altitude.

questions.stem: Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature is:
options: True altitude
Absolute altitude
Density altitude
Indicated altitude
questions.explain: Pressure altitude is read with 29.92 set; correct it for nonstandard temperature and you have density altitude, the figure that governs aircraft performance. True altitude is height above MSL; absolute altitude is height above the ground.

questions.stem: In the standard atmosphere at sea level, temperature and pressure are:
options: 0°C and 29.92 in Hg
15°C and 30.00 in Hg
15°C and 29.92 in Hg
20°C and 29.92 in Hg
questions.explain: ISA sea level is 15°C (59°F) and 29.92 inches of mercury (1013.2 hPa), with a temperature lapse of about 2°C per 1,000 feet.

questions.stem: High density altitude (hot, high and humid conditions) causes:
options: Shorter takeoff rolls and better climb
Higher indicated stall speeds only
Longer takeoff rolls and reduced climb rates
Increased engine power output
questions.explain: Thin air reduces engine power, propeller efficiency and lift, so takeoff runs lengthen and climb performance falls. Indicated stall speed stays about the same, but true airspeed and groundspeed are higher.

questions.stem: Class A airspace extends from 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL600. Within it:
options: VFR is allowed with 5 miles' visibility
Only military aircraft may operate
All operations must be under IFR
Two-way radio is optional above FL450
questions.explain: Class A is IFR-only airspace; every aircraft needs an IFR clearance, an instrument-rated pilot and an ADS-B Out/Mode C transponder.

questions.stem: Before a VFR pilot enters Class C airspace, the pilot must:
options: Establish two-way radio communication with ATC
Receive an explicit ATC clearance to enter
File a VFR flight plan with flight service
Hold at least a private pilot certificate
questions.explain: Class C (and D) only require two-way radio contact: ATC answering with your call sign is enough. An explicit clearance and a private pilot certificate (or student endorsement) are Class B requirements.

questions.stem: Basic VFR weather minimums in Class B airspace are:
options: 3 SM; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
1 statute mile, clear of clouds
5 SM; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 SM horizontal
3 statute miles, clear of clouds
questions.explain: Class B is the only airspace with '3 miles and clear of clouds' (14 CFR 91.155); ATC separates all traffic there. '3 SM, 500/1,000/2,000' applies in Classes C, D and E below 10,000 feet MSL.

questions.stem: In Class G airspace during the day, at or below 1,200 feet AGL, VFR minimums are:
options: 3 statute miles, clear of clouds
1 statute mile, clear of clouds
1 SM; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
3 SM; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
questions.explain: Low-level uncontrolled airspace by day needs only 1 SM and clear of clouds (14 CFR 91.155). '1 SM, 500/1,000/2,000' is Class G above 1,200 ft AGL by day (below 10,000 MSL).

questions.stem: The maximum indicated airspeed in the airspace underlying a Class B shelf, or in a VFR corridor through Class B, is:
options: 250 knots
200 knots
230 knots
156 knots
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.117: 250 knots below 10,000 feet MSL in general, but 200 knots beneath a Class B shelf, in a VFR corridor through Class B, and within 4 NM of the primary airport of Class C or D at or below 2,500 feet AGL.

questions.stem: A VFR pilot flying a magnetic course of 135°, more than 3,000 feet AGL, should choose which cruising altitude?
options: 6,500 feet MSL
5,000 feet MSL
5,500 feet MSL
6,000 feet MSL
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.159: magnetic courses 0°–179° fly ODD thousands plus 500 (3,500, 5,500…); 180°–359° fly EVEN thousands plus 500. Round thousands are for IFR.

questions.stem: An airplane overtaking another airplane should:
options: Alter course to the right to pass well clear
Alter course to the left to pass well clear
Climb above it and pass directly overhead
Descend below it and pass on the left
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.113(f): the aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way, and the overtaking pilot alters course to the RIGHT to pass well clear. Passing over or under is not permitted.

questions.stem: At a runway holding position marking (two solid and two dashed yellow lines), an aircraft taxiing toward the runway must stop:
options: On the side with the dashed lines
Directly on top of the marking
Only if the tower has not yet called
On the side with the solid lines
questions.explain: The solid lines face the holding aircraft; stop short of them unless cleared onto or across the runway. The dashed lines face the runway, so an aircraft exiting may cross from that side.

questions.stem: Taxiway edge lights are:
options: Green
White
Blue
Yellow
questions.explain: Taxiway edges are blue and taxiway centerlines green. Runway edge lights are white (yellow in the caution zone of instrument runways), thresholds green and runway ends red (AIM 2-1).

questions.stem: An airport rotating beacon showing two quick white flashes between green flashes identifies a:
options: Military airport
Lighted civilian land airport
Water airport
Heliport
questions.explain: AIM 2-1-9: civil land airports alternate white and green; military airports show a dual-peaked (two quick) white flash between greens. Water airports are white-yellow; heliports green-yellow-white.

questions.stem: On approach, a PAPI shows two white lights and two red lights. The airplane is:
options: Slightly high
Slightly low
On the glide path
Well below the glide path
questions.explain: Two white and two red is on glide path; three white is slightly high and four white high; three red is slightly low and four red is low.

questions.stem: A steady green light-gun signal to an aircraft in flight means:
options: Cleared to land
Return for landing
Cleared to taxi
Give way and continue circling
questions.explain: In flight: steady green = cleared to land, flashing green = return for landing, steady red = give way and keep circling, flashing red = airport unsafe, do not land. 'Cleared to taxi' is flashing green on the ground.

questions.stem: A flashing red light-gun signal to an aircraft on the ground means:
options: Stop
Taxi clear of the runway in use
Return to the starting point on the airport
Airport unsafe, do not land
questions.explain: On the ground, flashing red = taxi clear of the runway in use; steady red = stop; flashing white = return to the starting point. 'Airport unsafe, do not land' is flashing red to an aircraft in flight.

questions.stem: Transponder code 7500 indicates:
options: A general emergency
Unlawful interference (hijacking)
Two-way radio failure
Military interceptor operations
questions.explain: 7500 = hijack, 7600 = radio failure, 7700 = emergency (memory hook: 75 taken alive, 76 radio fix, 77 going to heaven). 7777 is reserved for military interceptor operations. 1200 is the VFR code.

questions.stem: In a helicopter, the collective pitch control:
options: Changes the pitch of all main-rotor blades at once
Tilts the main-rotor disc in the desired direction
Changes the pitch of the tail-rotor blades
Sets the governor's target rotor RPM
questions.explain: Collective = all blades together, so total lift goes up or down. The cyclic tilts the disc; the pedals change tail-rotor pitch; the throttle/governor holds rotor RPM.

questions.stem: A helicopter's main rotor turns counterclockwise as seen from above. When the pilot increases power, the pilot must add:
options: Right pedal to stop the nose yawing left
Left pedal to stop the nose yawing left
Forward cyclic to stop the nose pitching up
Left pedal to stop the nose yawing right
questions.explain: More power means more torque turning the fuselage the opposite way to the rotor, clockwise from above, so the nose swings right. Left pedal adds tail-rotor thrust to hold heading.

questions.stem: Effective translational lift is typically gained as a helicopter accelerates through about:
options: 5 to 10 knots
40 to 50 knots
16 to 24 knots
60 to 70 knots
questions.explain: At about 16–24 knots the rotor outruns its own recirculating downwash into clean air and efficiency jumps, often felt as a brief vibration (FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook).

questions.stem: Immediately after an engine failure in cruise, a helicopter pilot should first:
options: Raise the collective to stop the descent
Pull the cyclic fully aft to slow down
Lower the collective to maintain rotor RPM
Apply left pedal to counter the yaw
questions.explain: Without power the blades' drag bleeds rotor RPM fast; lowering the collective flattens them so upward airflow keeps the rotor turning. With torque gone the nose yaws LEFT on a US design, so RIGHT pedal is needed.

questions.stem: The phenomenon that most limits a helicopter's maximum forward speed is:
options: Translating tendency
Retreating blade stall
Ground resonance
Effective translational lift
questions.explain: The faster a helicopter flies, the slower the air over the retreating blade, so it needs ever more angle of attack until it stalls. Ground resonance is a ground-contact vibration; ETL helps at low speed.

questions.stem: Translating tendency causes a hovering single-rotor helicopter to drift:
options: Opposite to the tail-rotor thrust
Toward the advancing blade
Straight back into its own downwash
In the direction of the tail-rotor thrust
questions.explain: Tail-rotor thrust pushes the whole aircraft sideways (to the right with a counterclockwise main rotor). Rigging or a slightly tilted mast lets a little opposite cyclic cancel it.

questions.stem: The Navy's carrier-based airborne early warning and command-and-control aircraft is the:
options: E-6B Mercury
E-2D Advanced Hawkeye
P-8A Poseidon
EA-18G Growler
questions.explain: The twin-turboprop E-2 with its rotating radar dome flies from carriers. The E-6B is a land-based 707-derived airborne command post (TACAMO), the P-8A is land-based maritime patrol, and the EA-18G is electronic attack.

questions.stem: The P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft is derived from which airliner?
options: Boeing 707
Lockheed L-188 Electra
McDonnell Douglas DC-9
Boeing 737
questions.explain: The P-8A is built on the Boeing 737-800 airframe. The P-3 Orion it replaced came from the Lockheed Electra, the E-6B Mercury from the 707, and the Navy's C-9B Skytrain II from the DC-9.

questions.stem: Which F-35 Lightning II variant is built for catapult launches and arrested landings on Navy carriers?
options: F-35C
F-35A
F-35B
F-35I
questions.explain: The F-35C has a larger, folding wing, stronger landing gear and a heavier tailhook for carrier operations. The F-35A is the Air Force version, the F-35B is the Marine STOVL version, and the F-35I is Israel's variant of the F-35A.

questions.stem: Which Navy fighter combined variable-sweep wings with the long-range AIM-54 Phoenix missile?
options: F-14 Tomcat
F-4 Phantom II
F-8 Crusader
F/A-18 Hornet
questions.explain: The F-14 (1974–2006) swept its wings automatically and was the only fighter to carry the Phoenix. The F-8 Crusader had a variable-INCIDENCE wing, a different trick; the F-4 and F/A-18 have fixed wings.

questions.stem: Which fighter destroyed more enemy aircraft than any other US Navy aircraft in World War II?
options: F4U Corsair
F6F Hellcat
F4F Wildcat
F2A Buffalo
questions.explain: NHHC credits the F6F Hellcat with over 5,000 enemy aircraft, about three-quarters of the Navy's air-to-air victories. The gull-winged F4U Corsair had a superb kill ratio but fewer total kills.

questions.stem: The Blue Angels flew their first public demonstration in June 1946 in which aircraft?
options: F8F Bearcat
F9F Panther
F4U Corsair
F6F-5 Hellcat
questions.explain: Led by Lt. Cmdr. Roy 'Butch' Voris, the team debuted on June 15, 1946, at NAS Jacksonville in F6F-5 Hellcats. They switched to the F8F Bearcat later in 1946 and to their first jet, the F9F Panther, in 1949. Today they fly F/A-18E/F Super Hornets.

questions.stem: Navy HSM (Helicopter Maritime Strike) squadrons fly the:
options: MH-60S Seahawk
CH-53E Super Stallion
MH-53E Sea Dragon
MH-60R Seahawk
questions.explain: HSM squadrons fly the antisubmarine/antisurface MH-60R. HSC (Helicopter Sea Combat) squadrons fly the MH-60S for logistics, search and rescue and combat support. The CH-53E is a Marine heavy-lift helicopter and the MH-53E is used for mine countermeasures.

questions.stem: The vertical distance from the waterline up to the main (weather) deck is the ship's:
options: Draft
Beam
Freeboard
Sheer
questions.explain: Freeboard is hull above water; draft is hull below water down to the keel; beam is the greatest width; sheer is the upward curve of the deck toward bow and stern.

questions.stem: The depth of a ship's hull below the waterline, measured to the bottom of the keel, is its:
options: Freeboard
Beam
Displacement
Draft
questions.explain: Draft tells you how much water the ship needs to float. Displacement is the ship's weight (the weight of water it displaces), not a depth.

questions.stem: Aboard a Navy ship, which term is correctly matched with its shoreside meaning?
options: Bulkhead: floor
Overhead: ceiling
Deck: wall
Hatch: window
questions.explain: Overhead = ceiling, bulkhead = wall, deck = floor, hatch = an opening in a deck (a door in a bulkhead is a door; a window is a port or porthole).

questions.stem: Navy compartment number 3-120-2-L is located:
options: On the starboard side
On the centerline
Above the main deck
On the port side
questions.explain: Deck 3 (two decks below the main deck), forward boundary at frame 120, '2' = first compartment outboard to PORT (even = port, odd = starboard, 0 = centerline), 'L' = living space. Levels above the main deck are written 01, 02…

questions.stem: A fathom, used to measure water depth, equals:
options: 3 feet
6 feet
10 feet
100 feet
questions.explain: One fathom is 6 feet (about 1.83 m), roughly the span of a sailor's outstretched arms when hauling in a sounding line.

questions.stem: One nautical mile is equal to about:
options: 5,280 feet, or one minute of latitude
6,076 feet, or one degree of latitude
6,076 feet, or one minute of latitude
1,852 feet, or one minute of longitude
questions.explain: A nautical mile is 1,852 meters (about 6,076 feet), one minute of latitude, which makes chart work easy. 5,280 feet is a statute mile; a degree is 60 nautical miles. A knot is one nautical mile per hour.

questions.stem: Two power-driven vessels meet head-on. Under the Rules of the Road, each should:
options: Alter course to port and pass starboard to starboard
Stop engines until one sounds five blasts
Alter course to starboard and pass port to port
Hold course while the larger vessel gives way
questions.explain: COLREGs Rule 14: in a head-on situation each vessel alters course to STARBOARD so they pass port side to port side. Size does not decide it.

questions.stem: Two power-driven vessels are crossing with risk of collision. Which must keep out of the way?
options: The one that has the other on its own port side
The faster of the two vessels
The smaller of the two vessels
The one that has the other on its own starboard side
questions.explain: COLREGs Rule 15: the vessel that sees the other on its STARBOARD side is the give-way vessel and should avoid crossing ahead. The other is the stand-on vessel and holds course and speed.

questions.stem: At night you see the red sidelight and the masthead light of a power-driven vessel crossing ahead of you. You are most likely:
options: The stand-on vessel
Overtaking it
The give-way vessel
Meeting it head-on
questions.explain: Seeing its red (port) light means you are on its port side, so it is on YOUR starboard side, which makes you the give-way vessel ('red means stop'). Head-on you would see both sidelights; overtaking you would see its white sternlight.

questions.stem: A vessel is 'overtaking' when it approaches another from a direction more than ___ abaft her beam.
questions.explain: COLREGs Rule 13: more than 22.5° abaft the beam, the arc where at night you would see only the sternlight and neither sidelight. The overtaking vessel must keep out of the way.

questions.stem: Under the COLREGs, a vessel's sternlight shows over an arc of:
questions.explain: Rule 21: masthead light 225° (ahead to 22.5° abaft each beam), each sidelight 112.5°, sternlight 135° (the remaining arc astern). Together the sidelights and sternlight make a full 360°.

questions.stem: In sight of another vessel, one short blast on a power-driven vessel's whistle means:
options: I am altering my course to starboard
I am altering my course to port
I am operating astern propulsion
I am in doubt of your intentions
questions.explain: Rule 34: one short blast = altering to starboard, two short = altering to port, three short = operating astern propulsion, five or more short and rapid = doubt or danger.

questions.stem: In restricted visibility, a power-driven vessel making way through the water sounds:
options: Two prolonged blasts at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
One short blast every minute
Five short blasts every 2 minutes
One prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
questions.explain: COLREGs Rule 35: making way = one prolonged blast (4–6 seconds) at least every 2 minutes; underway but stopped (not making way) = two prolonged blasts.

questions.stem: Under the US buoyage system, a vessel returning from sea keeps red buoys:
options: On its port (left) side
Dead ahead
Astern
On its starboard (right) side
questions.explain: 'Red, right, returning': heading in from sea, keep red marks (even-numbered nuns) to starboard and green marks (odd-numbered cans) to port.

questions.stem: A buoy with red and white vertical stripes marks:
options: An isolated danger with navigable water around it
A preferred-channel junction
Safe water, such as a fairway or mid-channel
A special area such as an anchorage
questions.explain: Red-and-white vertical stripes = safe water (pass on either side). An isolated danger is black with red bands; preferred-channel marks have red and green horizontal bands; special marks are yellow.

questions.stem: A vessel displaying two black balls in a vertical line is:
options: Not under command
At anchor
Aground
Restricted in its ability to maneuver
questions.explain: Rule 27: not under command = two balls (at night, two all-round red lights). At anchor = one ball; aground = three balls; restricted in ability to maneuver = ball–diamond–ball.

questions.stem: On a carrier flight deck, sailors in purple jerseys ('grapes') handle:
options: Ordnance
Aviation fuel
Catapults and arresting gear
Aircraft chocks and chains
questions.explain: Purple = fuel. Red = ordnance and crash and salvage; green = catapult and arresting gear crews; blue = plane handlers, chocks and chains, tractor drivers and elevator operators.

questions.stem: Red flight-deck jerseys are worn by:
options: Ordnance handlers and crash-and-salvage crews
Plane captains
Fuel handlers
Landing signal officers
questions.explain: Red = ordnance, crash and salvage, and explosive ordnance disposal. Plane captains wear brown, fuel handlers purple, and LSOs white.

questions.stem: The catapult officer (the 'shooter') wears which jersey color?
options: Green
Red
Yellow
White
questions.explain: Yellow is for officers and directors who control movement: aircraft handling officers, catapult and arresting gear officers, and plane directors. The catapult and arresting gear CREWS wear green, which is the trap.

questions.stem: Ford-class carriers, starting with USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN-78), launch aircraft with:
options: Steam catapults
Electromagnetic catapults (EMALS)
Hydraulic catapults
Ski-jump ramps
questions.explain: The Ford class uses EMALS (Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System) and Advanced Arresting Gear. Nimitz-class carriers use steam catapults; ski jumps are used by STOVL carriers in other navies.

questions.stem: At touchdown during an arrested carrier landing, a Navy pilot moves the throttles to:
options: Idle
Half power
Full (military) power
Reverse thrust
questions.explain: Pilots go to full power at touchdown in case the hook misses the wires (a bolter) or a wire breaks, so they can fly off again; power comes back only after the aircraft is stopped.

questions.stem: When an aircraft's tailhook misses every arresting wire and the aircraft must fly off again, it is called a:
options: Bolter
Wave-off
Trap
Ramp strike
questions.explain: A bolter is a touchdown without catching a wire. A wave-off is an aborted approach ordered (usually by the LSO) before touchdown; a trap is a successful arrested landing; a ramp strike is hitting the stern ramp.

questions.stem: On a carrier's Fresnel lens optical landing system, if the 'meatball' appears above the green datum lights, the pilot is:
options: Low on the glide slope
Lined up left of centerline
High on the glide slope
On the glide slope
questions.explain: The ball moves with the aircraft's position: centered on the datum lights = on glide slope; above = high; below = low; red = dangerously low. Lineup is judged from the deck centerline, not the ball.

questions.stem: A main advantage of the angled flight deck is that:
options: It shortens the catapult stroke needed for launch
It lets the ship steam faster into the wind
It removes the need for arresting wires
An aircraft that bolters can fly off without hitting aircraft parked forward
questions.explain: Angling the landing area off the centerline lets a pilot who misses the wires go to full power and fly off the angled end, clear of aircraft on the bow, and allows launch and recovery at the same time.

questions.stem: The panel raised from the deck behind an aircraft on the catapult, protecting crew and aircraft from its exhaust, is the:
options: Jet blast deflector (JBD)
Arresting gear barricade
Island
Catapult shuttle
questions.explain: The JBD rises behind the aircraft before full power is applied. The barricade is an emergency net for recovering a damaged aircraft; the shuttle is the part of the catapult that tows the aircraft.

questions.stem: The officer who guides and grades each pilot's carrier approach, and can order a wave-off, is the:
options: Air boss
Aircraft handling officer
Landing signal officer (LSO)
Catapult officer
questions.explain: The LSO ('Paddles') stands on a platform on the port side aft, talks pilots down, and grades every pass. The air boss runs flight operations from Pri-Fly; the handler arranges aircraft on deck.

questions.stem: A Navy carrier air wing (CVW) is led by a commander called the 'CAG,' who typically holds the rank of:
options: Commander (O-5)
Captain (O-6)
Rear admiral (O-7)
Lieutenant commander (O-4)
questions.explain: The air wing commander, still called CAG from the old 'Commander, Air Group' title, is a Navy captain. Each squadron in the wing is commanded by a commander (O-5); the strike group is led by a rear admiral.

questions.stem: The Navy rating ABF works with:
options: Catapults and arresting gear
Aviation fuels
Aircraft handling and crash firefighting
Aircraft engines
questions.explain: Aviation Boatswain's Mates come in three types: ABF (fuels), ABE (launching and recovery equipment, i.e. catapults and arresting gear) and ABH (aircraft handling and crash and salvage). Engines belong to the AD, Aviation Machinist's Mate.

questions.stem: The Navy rating that packs parachutes and maintains aircrew survival equipment is the:
options: Aviation Structural Mechanic (AM)
Aviation Boatswain's Mate – Handling (ABH)
Aircrew Survival Equipmentman (PR)
Naval Aircrewman (AW)
questions.explain: PRs ('riggers') maintain parachutes, flight gear, life rafts and oxygen equipment. AMs maintain airframes and hydraulics; ABHs move aircraft; AWs fly as enlisted aircrew.

questions.stem: In November 1910, Eugene Ely made the first airplane takeoff from a ship, flying from the deck of the cruiser:
options: USS Pennsylvania
USS Birmingham
USS Langley
USS Jupiter
questions.explain: Ely, a civilian Curtiss pilot, flew off a platform on USS Birmingham at Hampton Roads on November 14, 1910. On January 18, 1911, he made the first shipboard landing on USS Pennsylvania in San Francisco Bay.

questions.stem: The Navy's first aircraft carrier, USS Langley (CV-1), commissioned in 1922, was converted from a:
options: Collier (coal ship)
Battlecruiser
Passenger liner
Light cruiser
questions.explain: Langley was the former collier USS Jupiter. The next carriers, Lexington and Saratoga, were converted from unfinished battlecruisers, which is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.stem: The Battle of the Coral Sea (May 1942) is notable as the first naval battle in which:
options: Jet aircraft attacked a carrier
A carrier was sunk by a submarine
Radar was used at sea
The opposing ships never sighted each other
questions.explain: Coral Sea was fought entirely by carrier aircraft, with the fleets never in sight of each other. The US lost USS Lexington; Japan lost the light carrier Shoho. Jets did not fly in combat until 1944, and shipboard radar was already in use.

questions.stem: Which US carrier was lost as a result of the Battle of Midway (June 1942)?
options: USS Lexington (CV-2)
USS Enterprise (CV-6)
USS Hornet (CV-8)
USS Yorktown (CV-5)
questions.explain: Yorktown, damaged by Japanese aircraft, was sunk by the submarine I-168. Lexington was lost a month earlier at Coral Sea, and Hornet at Santa Cruz in October 1942. Enterprise survived the war. Japan lost four carriers, sunk mainly by SBD Dauntless dive bombers.

questions.stem: In the April 1942 Doolittle Raid, 16 Army bombers launched from USS Hornet to strike Japan. They were:
options: B-17 Flying Fortresses
B-25 Mitchells
B-26 Marauders
TBF Avengers
questions.explain: Lt. Col. Jimmy Doolittle's 16 B-25B Mitchells took off from Hornet on April 18, 1942. The B-25 was chosen because a medium bomber could get airborne in the deck run available; the four-engine B-17 could not.

questions.stem: The first US jet to take off from and land on an American aircraft carrier, in July 1946, was the McDonnell:
options: F2H Banshee
F9F Panther
XFD-1 (later FH-1) Phantom
F-4 Phantom II
questions.explain: On July 21, 1946, Lt. Cmdr. James Davidson flew the XFD-1 Phantom off and back onto USS Franklin D. Roosevelt (NHHC). The F-4 Phantom II reused the name more than a decade later; the F9F Panther is a Grumman jet.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the airspeed corrections, from the instrument reading to the aircraft's actual speed through the air mass?
options: Indicated, true, calibrated, equivalent
Indicated, equivalent, calibrated, true
Indicated, calibrated, equivalent, true
Calibrated, indicated, equivalent, true
questions.explain: 'ICE-T': indicated (read off the dial) → calibrated (corrected for instrument and position error) → equivalent (corrected for compressibility) → true (corrected for altitude and nonstandard temperature). Correcting true airspeed for wind then gives ground speed.

questions.stem: Indicated airspeed and calibrated airspeed differ the most when an airplane is:
options: Slow, at a high angle of attack with flaps extended
In high-speed cruise at low altitude
Climbing through cold air at high altitude
Flying in a strong direct crosswind
questions.explain: Calibrated airspeed is indicated airspeed corrected for instrument and position (installation) error. Those errors are greatest at low airspeed and high angle of attack, when the pitot-static ports sit in disturbed air; in cruise IAS and CAS are nearly equal (FAA PHAK). Altitude and temperature separate CAS from TRUE airspeed, and wind affects only ground speed.

questions.stem: A pilot climbs from 2,000 to 10,000 feet while holding exactly 150 knots indicated airspeed. The airplane's true airspeed:
options: Decreases, because the air is thinner
Stays the same, because the indicated airspeed is unchanged
Increases, because the thinner air presses less on the pitot tube
Increases only if the air is warmer than standard
questions.explain: In less dense air the airplane must move faster through it to make the same pitot pressure, and so the same indicated airspeed. At a constant IAS, TAS rises with altitude (roughly 2% per 1,000 feet in standard conditions); warmer-than-standard air raises it further, but it rises either way.

questions.stem: Using the rule of thumb that true airspeed is about 2% greater than indicated airspeed for each 1,000 feet of altitude, an airplane indicating 150 knots at 8,000 feet has a true airspeed of about:
options: 174 knots
162 knots
166 knots
150 knots
questions.explain: 8 × 2% = 16%, and 150 × 1.16 = 174 knots. 166 adds 16 KNOTS instead of 16 percent, 162 uses 1% per 1,000 feet, and 150 forgets that TAS exceeds IAS at altitude.

questions.stem: A pilot flying at a true airspeed of 220 knots covers 300 nautical miles over the ground in 1 hour 30 minutes. The average wind component along the route was a:
options: 20-knot tailwind
80-knot headwind
20-knot headwind
Zero wind, since the true airspeed was constant
questions.explain: Ground speed = 300 NM ÷ 1.5 h = 200 knots, which is 20 knots LESS than the true airspeed, so the wind was a 20-knot headwind component. A tailwind would make ground speed higher than TAS; 80 wrongly subtracts the TAS from the distance.

questions.stem: Two jets fly at the same true airspeed: one at sea level on a standard day, the other at 35,000 feet where the air is far colder. Which has the higher Mach number, and why?
options: The sea-level jet, because denser air raises the Mach number
Neither, because the same true airspeed gives the same Mach number
The high-altitude jet, because the speed of sound falls as air pressure falls
The high-altitude jet, because the speed of sound is lower in colder air
questions.explain: Mach = true airspeed ÷ local speed of sound, and the speed of sound depends only on temperature: about 661 knots at 15°C but about 577 knots at the −54°C of standard 35,000 feet. The same TAS over a smaller speed of sound is a higher Mach. Pressure does not set the speed of sound, which is the trap.

questions.stem: On a single-engine airplane's airspeed indicator, the green arc runs from:
options: VSO to VFE
VS1 to VNO
VNO to VNE
VS1 to VNE
questions.explain: Green is the normal operating range, from VS1 (stall speed in a specified configuration, usually clean) to VNO (maximum structural cruising speed). VSO to VFE is the white flap arc, VNO to VNE the yellow caution arc, and VNE alone the red line.

questions.stem: Which statement about design maneuvering speed (VA) is correct?
options: It is marked at the top of the green arc and never changes
It is not marked on the airspeed indicator, and it decreases as weight decreases
It is marked by a red radial line on the airspeed indicator
It is not marked on the airspeed indicator, and it increases as weight decreases
questions.explain: VA is not shown on the airspeed indicator; it comes from the flight manual or a placard. A lighter airplane is accelerated more by the same gust or control input, so it reaches its load limit at a lower speed: VA goes DOWN as weight goes down (FAA PHAK). The top of the green arc is VNO.

questions.stem: On a light twin-engine airplane's airspeed indicator, the blue radial line marks:
options: VMC, minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative
VYSE, best rate-of-climb speed with one engine inoperative
VXSE, best angle-of-climb speed with one engine inoperative
VLE, maximum landing-gear-extended speed
questions.explain: Light twins carry two extra marks: a red radial line at VMC (minimum control speed, critical engine inoperative) and a blue radial line at VYSE (best single-engine rate of climb, the 'blue line'). VXSE and VLE are not marked with radial lines.

questions.stem: For weight-and-balance planning, the standard weight of aviation gasoline (100LL) is:
options: 6.7 pounds per gallon
6 pounds per gallon
7.5 pounds per gallon
8.35 pounds per gallon
questions.explain: FAA planning figures: avgas 6 lb/gal, jet (turbine) fuel 6.7 lb/gal, oil 7.5 lb/gal and water 8.35 lb/gal (FAA-H-8083-1). Each wrong option is the weight of one of the other fluids.

questions.stem: A Navy jet takes on 1,200 gallons of JP-5. Using about 6.8 pounds per gallon, the fuel weighs about:
options: 7,200 pounds
9,000 pounds
8,160 pounds
10,020 pounds
questions.explain: 1,200 × 6.8 = 8,160 lb. The distractors multiply by the avgas figure (6 → 7,200), the oil figure (7.5 → 9,000) and the water figure (8.35 → 10,020). JP-5, the Navy's high-flash-point shipboard fuel, is slightly denser than the 6.7 lb/gal planning figure for jet fuel.

questions.stem: An engine holds 8 quarts of oil. Using 7.5 pounds per gallon, the oil weighs:
options: 60 pounds
12 pounds
16 pounds
15 pounds
questions.explain: Convert first: 8 quarts ÷ 4 = 2 gallons, and 2 × 7.5 = 15 lb. 60 treats the quarts as gallons, 12 uses the avgas figure (6 lb/gal), and 16 rounds oil up to 2 lb per quart instead of 1.875.

questions.stem: An airplane's useful load is its:
options: Maximum allowable weight minus basic empty weight
Basic empty weight plus usable fuel
Maximum weight minus the weight of fuel and oil
Passengers and baggage only
questions.explain: Useful load = maximum allowable weight − basic empty weight: everything that can be added, meaning crew, passengers, baggage, usable fuel and drainable oil (FAA PHAK). 'Passengers and baggage only' is closer to payload, which leaves out the fuel.

questions.stem: An airplane is loaded to its maximum takeoff weight with full tanks of avgas. To carry an extra 180-pound passenger without exceeding that weight, the pilot must remove about how much fuel?
options: 30 gallons
27 gallons
24 gallons
22 gallons
questions.explain: 180 lb ÷ 6 lb per gallon of avgas = 30 gallons. 27 gallons divides by the jet-fuel figure (6.7), 24 by the oil figure (7.5) and 22 by the water figure (8.35).

questions.stem: An airplane weighs 1,500 pounds with its center of gravity 40 inches aft of the datum. A 300-pound load is added at 80 inches aft of the datum. The new CG is about:
options: 60.0 inches aft of the datum
46.7 inches aft of the datum
56.0 inches aft of the datum
50.0 inches aft of the datum
questions.explain: Moment = weight × arm: 1,500 × 40 = 60,000 and 300 × 80 = 24,000, for 84,000 in-lb in all. Total weight is 1,800 lb, so CG = 84,000 ÷ 1,800 ≈ 46.7 inches. 60 averages the two arms and ignores weight; 56 divides by the old weight only.

questions.stem: An airplane's position (navigation) lights are:
options: Green on the left wingtip, red on the right wingtip, white on the tail
Red on the left wingtip, green on the right wingtip, red on the tail
Red on the left wingtip, green on the right wingtip, flashing white on top
Red on the left wingtip, green on the right wingtip, white on the tail
questions.explain: As on a ship: red on the left (port) side, green on the right (starboard) and a steady white light facing aft. Flashing red or white lights are the separate anti-collision beacon and strobes.

questions.stem: At night you see another aircraft's steady red position light on YOUR right and its steady green position light on YOUR left, level with each other. The aircraft is most likely:
options: Flying away from you
Heading toward you
Crossing from your left to your right
Crossing from your right to your left
questions.explain: Facing you, its left wing (red) is on your right and its right wing (green) on your left: it is head-on, so both aircraft alter course to the right (14 CFR 91.113). An aircraft flying away shows its white tail light, and a crossing aircraft shows only one wingtip color.

questions.stem: At night, at your altitude, you see only the steady red position light of another airplane off your right side, and its bearing is not changing. Which airplane has the right-of-way?
options: Yours, because you see its red light
The other airplane, because it is on your right
Yours, because it is crossing from your left
Neither; both must turn left
questions.explain: Seeing its red (left) wingtip means it is pointed across your path from the right. When aircraft of the same category converge, the one on the RIGHT has the right-of-way (14 CFR 91.113(d)), so you give way: as on the water, 'see red, give way'. A steady bearing means a collision course.

questions.stem: An aircraft's rear (white) position light must show over a horizontal arc of:
questions.explain: Each wingtip light covers 110° (from dead ahead out to its side) and the tail light 140° (70° either side of dead astern), for a full 360° (14 CFR 25.1387). 135° and 225° are a ship's sternlight and masthead arcs under the COLREGs, a tempting mix-up.

questions.stem: Under 14 CFR 91.209, an aircraft being operated must display lighted position lights:
options: From the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight
From one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise
Only when flying in instrument conditions
From sunset to sunrise
questions.explain: Position lights are required from sunset to sunrise (91.209(a)). The civil-twilight period is the definition of 'night' in 14 CFR 1.1, used for logging night time, and one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise is the window for night passenger-carrying currency (61.57). Each is a real rule, just not the lighting one.

questions.stem: While flying in cloud, a pilot finds the reflected flashes of the white strobe lights disorienting. Under 14 CFR 91.209, the pilot:
options: May turn them off if the pilot in command decides it is in the interest of safety
Must leave them on, since anti-collision lights are always required
Must also turn off the position lights
May turn them off only after declaring an emergency
questions.explain: An aircraft equipped with anti-collision lights must have them on, day and night, BUT the pilot in command may switch them off when operating conditions make that safer, such as strobe reflections in cloud or haze (91.209(b)). Position lights are a separate requirement.

questions.stem: The hull classification symbol CVN identifies a:
options: Conventionally powered aircraft carrier
Nuclear-powered guided-missile cruiser
Nuclear-powered aircraft carrier
Nuclear-powered attack submarine
questions.explain: CV = aircraft carrier and N = nuclear propulsion; every US carrier in commission, Nimitz and Ford classes, is a CVN. A conventional carrier is a CV, a nuclear guided-missile cruiser was a CGN, and a nuclear attack submarine is an SSN.

questions.stem: A submarine whose primary mission is strategic nuclear deterrence, carrying submarine-launched ballistic missiles, has the hull symbol:
options: SSBN
SSN
SSGN
SSK
questions.explain: SS = submarine, B = ballistic missile, N = nuclear powered: the Ohio-class SSBNs, to be replaced by the Columbia class. SSN is a nuclear attack submarine, SSGN a nuclear guided-missile (Tomahawk) submarine, and SSK a diesel-electric hunter-killer type the US no longer operates.

questions.stem: Which hull symbol identifies an amphibious transport dock, such as the San Antonio class?
options: LHD
LSD
LCS
LPD
questions.explain: LPD = amphibious transport dock, carrying Marines, vehicles and landing craft in a well deck. LHD is a Wasp-class amphibious assault ship, LSD a dock landing ship, and LCS a littoral combat ship, which is not an amphibious ship at all.

questions.stem: In a hull symbol such as T-AO or T-AKE, the 'T-' prefix means the ship:
options: Is operated by Military Sealift Command with a mostly civilian crew
Is a training ship assigned to the Naval Academy
Is a tender that repairs other ships
Is an older ship held out of commission in reserve
questions.explain: T- marks a Military Sealift Command ship, crewed mainly by civil-service mariners. A = auxiliary, so T-AO is a fleet replenishment oiler and T-AKE a dry cargo/ammunition ship. Tenders have their own symbols, such as AS for a submarine tender.

questions.stem: In US Navy hull symbols such as CG, DDG, FFG and SSGN, the letter G stands for:
options: Gas-turbine propulsion
General purpose
Guided missiles
Gun armament
questions.explain: G = guided missile. The trap is gas turbine: Arleigh Burke destroyers ARE gas-turbine powered, but that isn't what the G means. N = nuclear power and B = ballistic missile.

questions.stem: Which is the oldest commissioned warship still afloat in the world?
options: HMS Victory
USS Constitution
USS Constellation
USS Missouri
questions.explain: USS Constitution, one of the six frigates ordered by the Naval Act of 1794, was launched in Boston in 1797 and is still a commissioned Navy ship. HMS Victory is older and still commissioned but sits in dry dock, not afloat. The Constellation in Baltimore (an 1854 sloop) and USS Missouri are museum ships.

questions.stem: The US Navy marks its birthday on October 13 because on that date in 1775:
options: The Department of the Navy was established
Congress ordered the six original frigates
The Naval Academy opened at Annapolis
The Continental Congress authorized the first armed vessels
questions.explain: On October 13, 1775, the Continental Congress voted to fit out two armed vessels, founding the Continental Navy. The six frigates came with the Naval Act of 1794, the Department of the Navy in 1798 and the Naval Academy in 1845. (The Marine Corps' birthday is November 10, 1775.)

questions.stem: John Paul Jones is credited with 'I have not yet begun to fight!' during the 1779 battle between:
options: USS Constitution and HMS Guerriere
Ranger and HMS Drake
USS Chesapeake and HMS Shannon
Bonhomme Richard and HMS Serapis
questions.explain: Off Flamborough Head, England, on September 23, 1779, Jones refused to surrender and went on to take Serapis even though his own Bonhomme Richard sank. He did capture HMS Drake with Ranger, but in 1778. Constitution beat Guerriere in 1812, earning 'Old Ironsides', and Chesapeake lost to Shannon in 1813.

questions.stem: 'Don't give up the ship!', later sewn on Oliver Hazard Perry's battle flag, were the dying words of:
options: Oliver Hazard Perry
Stephen Decatur
David Farragut
James Lawrence
questions.explain: Capt. James Lawrence was mortally wounded commanding USS Chesapeake against HMS Shannon in June 1813. Perry flew his friend's words at the Battle of Lake Erie that September and reported 'We have met the enemy and they are ours.'

questions.stem: 'Damn the torpedoes! Full speed ahead!' was David Farragut's order at the Battle of:
options: New Orleans, 1862
Hampton Roads, 1862
Lake Erie, 1813
Mobile Bay, 1864
questions.explain: At Mobile Bay on August 5, 1864, after the monitor Tecumseh struck a mine (then called a torpedo), Farragut led his fleet on through the minefield. He had captured New Orleans in 1862, the tempting wrong answer. In 1866 he became the Navy's first full admiral.

questions.stem: In 1958, USS Nautilus (SSN-571), the first nuclear-powered submarine, became the first ship to:
options: Circumnavigate the globe submerged
Travel submerged under the North Pole
Fire a Polaris missile while submerged
Surface at the North Pole
questions.explain: On August 3, 1958 (Operation Sunshine), Nautilus crossed under the North Pole. USS Skate first surfaced at the Pole (1959), USS Triton made the first submerged circumnavigation (1960), and USS George Washington made the first submerged Polaris launch (1960). Nautilus's 1955 signal 'Underway on nuclear power' began the nuclear Navy built by Adm. Hyman Rickover.

questions.stem: Japan lost four fleet carriers at the Battle of Midway (June 1942). Which carrier was NOT one of them?
options: Shokaku
Akagi
Kaga
Hiryu
questions.explain: The four lost were Akagi, Kaga, Soryu and Hiryu. Shokaku had been damaged at the Coral Sea a month earlier and Zuikaku had lost many of its aircraft there, so neither sailed for Midway, one reason the US could win.

questions.stem: The October 1944 battle in the Philippines, often called the largest naval battle in history and the first to see organized kamikaze attacks, was the Battle of:
options: the Philippine Sea
Leyte Gulf
Midway
Savo Island
questions.explain: Leyte Gulf (October 23–26, 1944) broke the Japanese fleet and saw the first organized kamikaze attacks. The Philippine Sea (June 1944) was the 'Great Marianas Turkey Shoot', Midway was June 1942, and Savo Island (August 1942) was a US defeat off Guadalcanal.

questions.stem: Who holds the designation Naval Aviator No. 1?
options: Eugene Ely
Theodore G. Ellyson
John Towers
Glenn Curtiss
questions.explain: Lt. Theodore 'Spuds' Ellyson, trained by Glenn Curtiss in 1911, was the Navy's first aviator; John Rodgers was No. 2 and John Towers No. 3. Eugene Ely made the first shipboard takeoff and landing but was a civilian Curtiss pilot, and Curtiss himself was the civilian builder who trained Ellyson.

questions.stem: On an airfoil, the chord line is:
options: The line halfway between the upper and lower surfaces, from leading edge to trailing edge
A line from the wing root to the wingtip
A straight line from the leading edge to the trailing edge
The line along which the relative wind meets the wing
questions.explain: The chord line is the straight line joining the leading and trailing edges. The trap is the mean camber line: the curved line halfway between the upper and lower surfaces. How far it bulges from the chord line is the camber. Root to tip is the span, and the angle between the chord line and the relative wind is the angle of attack.

questions.stem: On a symmetrical airfoil, used on many aerobatic airplanes and helicopter rotor blades, the mean camber line:
options: Lies above the chord line along its whole length
Lies below the chord line along its whole length
Coincides with the chord line
Crosses the chord line at the point of maximum thickness
questions.explain: A symmetrical airfoil has identical upper and lower surfaces, so it has zero camber: its mean camber line IS the chord line, and it makes no lift at zero angle of attack. On a cambered (asymmetrical) airfoil the mean camber line lies above the chord line, which is why it makes some lift even at zero angle of attack.

questions.stem: An airplane is in a steady glide with its longitudinal axis exactly level with the horizon. Its angle of attack is:
options: Zero, because the nose is level with the horizon
Greater than its angle of incidence, because the relative wind meets the wing from below
Equal to its angle of incidence, because the pitch attitude is zero
Less than its angle of incidence, because the airplane is descending
questions.explain: Relative wind is parallel to and opposite the flight path. In a descent the flight path points below the horizon, so the relative wind comes up from below and the glide angle adds to the built-in angle of incidence. Angle of attack is measured from the chord line to the relative wind, not to the horizon, so pitch attitude and angle of attack are not the same thing.

questions.stem: Lowering a PLAIN flap increases a wing's lift at a given airspeed mainly by:
options: Raising the wing's critical angle of attack
Increasing the wing's camber
Adding wing area as the flap slides aft
Reducing induced drag
questions.explain: A plain flap hinges down at the trailing edge, increasing the wing's camber, so the wing makes more lift (and more drag) at the same airspeed and can fly slower. It adds no wing area; the Fowler flap does that by sliding aft. Raising the critical angle of attack is the job of leading-edge slots and slats, and flaps increase drag rather than reduce it.

questions.stem: Besides letting a pilot who bolters fly off safely, the angled flight deck lets a carrier:
options: Recover aircraft without turning into the wind
Land aircraft without using arresting wires
Launch aircraft from the bow catapults while recovering others on the angled deck
Land aircraft from either end of the ship
questions.explain: On the old straight (axial) deck, landing aircraft used the same strip as the launch area and aircraft parked forward sat behind a crash barrier. Angling the landing area off to port separates it from the bow, so the bow catapults and forward deck stay clear while aircraft trap. The ship still steams into the wind for launch and recovery, and the arresting wires are still needed.

questions.stem: The angled flight deck, now standard on US aircraft carriers, was invented by:
options: The US Navy, for the Forrestal-class supercarriers
The French Navy
The British Royal Navy
The US Navy, for the Midway-class carriers
questions.explain: Royal Navy officers devised the angled deck in 1951. The US Navy fitted the first true angled deck to USS Antietam (CV-36) in 1952, later rebuilt Essex- and Midway-class carriers with one, and USS Forrestal (1955) was the first US carrier completed with an angled deck, which is why it is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.stem: A Nimitz-class carrier has four catapults: two on the bow and two in the waist. While aircraft are landing, which catapults can still launch?
options: The two waist catapults only
All four catapults
None, because launch and recovery can never overlap
The two bow catapults only
questions.explain: The waist catapults (3 and 4) run across the angled landing area on the port side, so they are fouled whenever aircraft are being recovered. The bow catapults (1 and 2) sit clear of the landing area and can keep launching, which is the point of the angled deck.

questions.stem: In May 1972 a modified Navy F-8 Crusader flown by NASA became the first aircraft to fly with:
options: A variable-incidence wing
Thrust-vectoring nozzles
Digital fly-by-wire flight controls
A forward-swept wing
questions.explain: NASA's F-8 Digital Fly-By-Wire aircraft first flew on May 25, 1972, using a digital computer (initially an Apollo guidance computer) in place of mechanical control linkages; it was the first digital fly-by-wire aircraft to fly without a mechanical backup, paving the way for systems in the F/A-18 and the Space Shuttle. The variable-incidence wing is the trap: the F-8 had one from the 1950s, tilting up for slow carrier approaches, but it was not new in 1972.

questions.stem: When Eugene Ely made the first landing aboard a ship, on USS Pennsylvania in January 1911, his airplane was stopped by:
options: Ropes weighted with sandbags, snagged by hooks on the airplane
A net barricade strung across the end of the platform
Steam-powered arresting wires
Sailors who grabbed the wings as it rolled past
questions.explain: On January 18, 1911, in San Francisco Bay, Ely landed his Curtiss pusher on a platform built over the armored cruiser's stern. Ropes stretched across the deck were tied to sandbags at each end; hooks under the airplane caught them and the dragging sandbags stopped it, the forerunner of today's arresting gear. Two months earlier he had made the first takeoff from a ship, USS Birmingham.

questions.stem: Which statement about USS Langley (CV-1) is TRUE?
options: It was the first US carrier designed as a carrier from the keel up
Nicknamed the 'Covered Wagon', it was the US Navy's first aircraft carrier
It was converted from an unfinished battlecruiser
It was sunk by Japanese carrier aircraft at the Battle of Midway
questions.explain: Langley, converted from the collier USS Jupiter and commissioned in 1922, was the Navy's first carrier, nicknamed the 'Covered Wagon' for the flat deck built over the old hull. USS Ranger (CV-4, 1934) was the first designed as a carrier from the keel up, and Lexington and Saratoga were the converted battlecruisers. Langley, by then a seaplane tender, was lost to Japanese air attack south of Java in February 1942, months before Midway.

questions.stem: An airplane in level flight slows from 140 knots to 70 knots at the same weight and altitude. To keep producing the same lift, its lift coefficient (set by angle of attack) must become about:
options: 2 times as great
1.4 times as great
4 times as great
Half as great
questions.explain: Lift = CL × ½ × density × V² × wing area, so lift varies with the SQUARE of airspeed. Halving the speed cuts V² to one quarter, so with weight, density and wing area unchanged, CL must rise 4 times to hold lift equal to weight (FAA-H-8083-25). Check: (1/2)² × 4 = 1 ✓. 2 times forgets to square the speed, 1.4 times takes a square root instead of squaring, and half as great gets the relationship backwards.

questions.stem: An airplane's maximum lift-to-drag ratio (L/DMAX) occurs at the airspeed where:
options: Induced drag equals parasite drag
Induced drag reaches its minimum
Parasite drag reaches its minimum
The wing reaches its critical angle of attack
questions.explain: Induced drag falls and parasite drag rises as airspeed increases; where the two curves cross, total drag is lowest, and that point is L/DMAX (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 5). For a given weight it also gives the best glide. Induced drag keeps shrinking toward high speed and parasite drag keeps shrinking toward low speed, so neither of their minimums marks L/DMAX, and the critical angle of attack is the stall, far from the best ratio.

questions.stem: Compared with loading at the forward CG limit, loading the same airplane near its aft CG limit generally gives:
options: A higher stall speed and less longitudinal stability
A lower stall speed and more longitudinal stability
A higher stall speed and more longitudinal stability
A lower stall speed and less longitudinal stability
questions.explain: With a forward CG the tail must push down harder, adding to the load the wing carries, which raises stall speed but makes the airplane more stable. Moving the CG aft reduces that tail download, so stall speed and cruise drag drop, but the airplane becomes less stable and stall/spin recovery gets harder (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 10). The other three options each mix up one or both halves of that trade.

questions.stem: A pilot holds a constant 30° bank in a level turn and increases airspeed from 90 to 120 knots. The turn's radius and rate will:
options: Radius decreases; rate increases
Radius increases; rate increases
Both stay the same, because bank angle sets the turn
Radius increases; rate decreases
questions.explain: At a fixed bank angle the horizontal lift component that turns the airplane is fixed, so a faster airplane curves less sharply: the radius grows (with the square of speed) and the rate of turn in degrees per second falls (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 5). The reversed option describes slowing down, 'both increase' forgets that rate falls as speed rises, and bank alone does not fix the turn unless airspeed is also constant.

questions.stem: An airplane is in a fully developed spin to the LEFT. Using the standard recovery from the Airplane Flying Handbook, the pilot should:
options: Close the throttle, neutralize the ailerons, apply full right rudder, then move the elevator briskly forward
Close the throttle, neutralize the ailerons, apply full left rudder, then move the elevator briskly forward
Close the throttle, apply full right aileron, then hold the elevator full aft
Add full power, neutralize the ailerons, apply full right rudder, then move the elevator briskly forward
questions.explain: The FAA recovery is power to idle, ailerons neutral, full rudder OPPOSITE the rotation, then brisk forward elevator to break the stall (FAA-H-8083-3). A left spin needs right rudder, so left rudder is a sign slip that feeds the rotation. Aileron against the spin can deepen it and holding full back elevator keeps the wing stalled. Power can flatten the spin and is removed first.

questions.stem: The main aerodynamic reason high-speed jets use swept-back wings is to:
options: Raise the maximum lift coefficient for slower landings
Make the wing roots stall before the wingtips
Delay shock waves and raise the critical Mach number
Cut induced drag during takeoff and climb
questions.explain: Sweep means the airflow 'sees' a slower effective speed across the wing's chord, so local supersonic flow and shock waves come later and the critical Mach number goes up (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 5). The trade-off is the opposite of two distractors: sweep LOWERS maximum lift (higher approach speeds) and tends to make the TIPS stall first. Sweep is not a tool for cutting low-speed induced drag; high aspect ratio does that.

questions.stem: A pilot lands at a high-elevation airport on a hot day, flying the normal indicated approach speed from the flight manual. Compared with a sea-level landing on a standard day:
options: Indicated approach speed should be reduced because the air is thinner
Groundspeed and landing roll are the same because indicated airspeed is unchanged
True airspeed and groundspeed are higher, so the landing roll is longer
The airplane stalls at a higher indicated airspeed, so the approach must be faster
questions.explain: The wing responds to indicated airspeed, so the same IAS is correct, but in thin air that IAS means a higher true airspeed and groundspeed at touchdown, while the braking force available does not grow, so the roll is longer (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 11). Flying a lower IAS invites a stall, the same IAS does NOT mean the same groundspeed, and the indicated stall speed stays essentially the same.

questions.stem: A pilot leans the mixture for cruise at 9,500 feet, then descends to pattern altitude without touching the mixture control. During the descent the fuel-air mixture becomes:
options: Richer, because denser air carries more fuel into the cylinders
Unchanged, because the carburetor corrects for air density
Leaner, which cools the cylinders and protects against detonation
Leaner, raising the risk of overheating and detonation
questions.explain: A carburetor meters fuel by airflow volume, not air density, so as the air gets denser on descent the same fuel meets more air and the mixture leans out (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 7). The mixture must be enriched on descent; an excessively lean mixture runs hot and can cause detonation. 'Richer' reverses the effect (that is what happens on a climb), a standard carburetor has no automatic density correction, and excessive leaning heats the engine rather than cooling it.

questions.stem: In an aircraft piston engine, preignition is best described as:
options: Explosive, uncontrolled burning of the charge after the spark plug fires, often from using too low a fuel grade
Burning of unburned fuel in the exhaust system after the charge leaves the cylinder
Firing of the spark plugs before the piston reaches top dead center, as set by magneto timing
Ignition of the charge before the spark plug fires, usually from a hot spot such as a carbon deposit
questions.explain: The PHAK defines preignition as the mixture igniting before the engine's normal ignition event, usually from a residual hot spot such as a carbon deposit or cracked plug insulator (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 7). The first distractor is detonation, the classic mix-up. Exhaust burning is afterfiring, and firing before top dead center is NORMAL spark advance, not preignition.

questions.stem: In an airplane with a constant-speed propeller, the FAA-recommended order for INCREASING power, to avoid high manifold pressure at low RPM, is:
options: Increase manifold pressure with the throttle first, then increase RPM with the propeller control
Increase manifold pressure with the throttle only, since the governor will raise RPM automatically
Increase RPM with the propeller control first, then increase manifold pressure with the throttle
Enrich the mixture, then increase manifold pressure first and RPM last
questions.explain: High manifold pressure combined with low RPM overstresses the cylinders, so when adding power the pilot raises RPM first and then manifold pressure; when reducing power the order reverses, manifold pressure first, then RPM (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 7). Throttle first is the reversed sequence. The governor HOLDS the selected RPM rather than raising it, so throttle alone just raises manifold pressure at the old RPM.

questions.stem: Air enters the fan of a turbofan engine at 120 pounds per second, and the engine has a bypass ratio of 5:1. How much air per second passes through the core?
options: 24 pounds
100 pounds
20 pounds
96 pounds
questions.explain: Bypass ratio compares the mass of air the fan pushes AROUND the core with the mass that goes THROUGH it (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 7), so 5:1 splits the 120 pounds into 6 parts: 100 pounds bypass and 20 pounds through the core.
