Check: 100 ÷ 20 = 5 ✓. 24 pounds divides the total by 5, treating the ratio as bypass to total airflow; 100 pounds is the bypass flow, not the core flow; 96 pounds is what is left after wrongly taking 24 pounds as the core flow.

questions.stem: An hour after takeoff, in steady cruise, the airplane's center-zero ammeter shows a full-scale POSITIVE (charge) deflection. This most likely indicates:
options: A failed alternator, with the battery carrying the load
Normal recharging of the battery after engine start
A fully charged battery and an idle alternator
A malfunctioning voltage regulator
questions.explain: The PHAK says a plus indication shows the battery charging rate, a full-scale MINUS deflection indicates an alternator or generator malfunction, and a full-scale POSITIVE deflection indicates a regulator malfunction (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 7). Alternator failure shows a discharge, the after-start recharge tapers toward zero within minutes, not an hour later, and a fully charged battery reads near zero.

questions.stem: A pilot of a piston airplane that requires 100LL avgas drains a fuel sample and finds it clear to straw-colored, with no dye. The pilot should suspect:
options: Jet fuel, which is colorless or straw-colored
Grade 100 avgas, which is dyed this color
Grade 80 avgas, an approved lower-octane substitute
Fresh 100LL, before its dye has had time to develop
questions.explain: Avgas grades are dyed: 80 is red, 100 is green and 100LL is blue, while jet fuel is clear or straw-colored (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 7). An undyed sample in an avgas airplane points to jet fuel contamination, which can destroy a piston engine, so the airplane must not fly until the fuel is sorted out. Grade 100 is green, grade 80 is red and too low an octane for an engine that requires 100LL, and 100LL is blue as delivered.

questions.stem: Ice completely blocks the static ports while an airplane is cruising at 8,000 feet; the pitot tube stays open. The pilot then descends to 5,000 feet. During the descent:
options: The altimeter stays at 8,000 feet, the VSI shows zero, and the airspeed indicator reads higher than actual
The altimeter stays at 8,000 feet, the VSI shows zero, and the airspeed indicator reads lower than actual
The altimeter and VSI work normally, and only the airspeed indicator is affected
The altimeter stays at 8,000 feet, the VSI shows a climb, and the airspeed indicator reads correctly
questions.explain: With the static ports blocked, the altimeter and VSI are trapped at the 8,000-foot pressure, so the altimeter freezes there and the VSI reads zero. The airspeed indicator compares ram pressure against that trapped, LOWER static pressure, so on a descent it reads too high (on a climb it would read too low) (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 8). The first distractor uses the climb case, the altimeter and VSI depend entirely on static pressure, and the VSI cannot show a climb with no change in static pressure.

questions.stem: In an unpressurized airplane, the pilot selects the alternate static source, which vents inside the cabin. Compared with normal readings, the instruments will typically show:
options: A lower altitude, a lower airspeed, and a momentary descent on the VSI
A higher altitude, a lower airspeed, and a momentary climb on the VSI
No change, because cabin and outside pressure are the same
A higher altitude, a higher airspeed, and a momentary climb on the VSI
questions.explain: Air flowing past the fuselage lowers cabin pressure slightly below outside static pressure. Lower static pressure makes the altimeter read higher, the airspeed indicator read faster (ram pressure minus a smaller static pressure) and the VSI show a brief climb as the pressure drops (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 8). The reversed option assumes cabin pressure is higher, the mixed option gets the airspeed effect backwards, and the pressures are not equal, which is why the error exists.

questions.stem: During a rapid acceleration on the takeoff roll, a vacuum-driven attitude indicator tends to show:
options: A false slight nose-down (descent) indication
A false slight nose-up (climb) indication
A false bank toward the left wing
No error, because attitude indicators are free of acceleration errors
questions.explain: Rapid acceleration makes the erecting mechanism of a vacuum attitude indicator precess the gyro so the horizon bar moves down, falsely showing a climb; a pilot who 'corrects' it ends up flatter than intended. Deceleration gives the opposite error, a false descent (FAA Instrument Flying Handbook, FAA-H-8083-15). The nose-down option is the deceleration case, a left bank is not the classic acceleration error, and attitude indicators are only MOSTLY free of errors.

questions.stem: In a level turn to the right, the ball of the turn coordinator sits to the LEFT of center, toward the outside of the turn. The turn is a:
options: Slip; add right rudder pressure
Skid; add more right rudder pressure
Skid; reduce right rudder pressure
Slip; reduce the angle of bank
questions.explain: A ball on the OUTSIDE of the turn means a skid: too much rudder in the direction of the turn, so the rate of turn is too great for the bank (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 8). The fix is to 'step on the ball', here by reducing right rudder (left rudder pressure). A slip shows the ball on the INSIDE of the turn, and adding more right rudder makes the skid worse.

questions.stem: From level flight, a pilot abruptly lowers the nose into a steady descent. The vertical speed indicator will:
options: Show the trend at once, but take 6 to 9 seconds to show an accurate rate
Show the exact rate at once, because it compares pitot and static pressure
Stay at zero for about 6 to 9 seconds, then jump to the full rate
Show an accurate rate at once, but show the trend only after 6 to 9 seconds
questions.explain: The VSI senses static pressure only, comparing pressure in its diaphragm with case pressure that changes slowly through a calibrated leak. It shows the TREND immediately, but the RATE takes about 6 to 9 seconds to stabilize (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 8). It has no pitot connection, it does not wait at zero, and the last option swaps trend and rate.

questions.stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, a pilot turning onto a heading of NORTH using only the magnetic compass should stop the turn:
options: Before the compass reads north, because the compass lags on northerly headings
After the compass passes north, because the compass leads on northerly headings
Exactly as the compass reads north, because turning error affects only east and west
Before the compass reads north, because the compass leads on northerly headings
questions.explain: Magnetic dip makes the compass lag in turns through north and lead in turns through south, hence 'undershoot north, overshoot south' (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 8). Because the card shows less turn than has really happened near north, the pilot rolls out before it reaches north. Overshooting is the rule for SOUTH, the east/west error is the ACCELERATION error, and a compass that led would need the rollout after north, not before.

questions.stem: As a cold front passes a weather station in the Northern Hemisphere, observers would typically record:
options: Falling temperature, falling pressure, and a counterclockwise wind shift (for example, southwest to southeast)
Rising temperature, rising pressure, and a clockwise wind shift (for example, southwest to northwest)
Falling temperature, rising pressure, and a counterclockwise wind shift (for example, northwest to southwest)
Falling temperature, rising pressure, and a clockwise wind shift (for example, southwest to northwest)
questions.explain: Pressure falls as the front approaches, then rises after it passes; colder, drier air follows; and in the Northern Hemisphere the wind veers, shifting clockwise, typically from south or southwest to west or northwest (FAA Aviation Weather Handbook, FAA-H-8083-28). Falling pressure describes the approach, not the passage. Rising temperature belongs to a warm front, and a counterclockwise (backing) shift is the wrong direction.

questions.stem: Which change in conditions would usually help ADVECTION fog form and thicken, but would prevent or break up RADIATION fog?
options: The surface wind picking up from calm to about 25 knots
A clear sky through a long night
The surface wind picking up from calm to about 10 knots
The sun rising and heating the ground
questions.explain: Radiation fog forms only in calm or nearly calm air, and a breeze mixes it out, while advection fog needs moist air to be moved over a colder surface, and winds up to about 15 knots let it form and thicken (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 12). At about 25 knots the wind is too strong even for advection fog, which lifts into low stratus. A clear sky through a long night favors radiation fog, not advection fog. Daytime heating burns off radiation fog but does nothing to thicken advection fog.

questions.stem: A pilot flying in below-freezing air encounters ice pellets. This most likely means:
options: Freezing rain exists higher up, in a layer of above-freezing air
The air is below freezing at all levels, so no liquid water exists aloft
Hail is falling from a nearby thunderstorm's strong updrafts
Snow is melting just above the aircraft, so a short descent will escape the icing
questions.explain: Ice pellets form when rain falls out of an above-freezing layer aloft and refreezes in colder air below, so their presence signals freezing rain at a higher altitude (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 12). That warm layer aloft is exactly what the 'below freezing at all levels' option denies. Hail comes from convective updrafts, not a temperature inversion, and descending deeper into the subfreezing layer does not escape freezing precipitation.

questions.stem: On final approach, an airplane's airspeed suddenly jumps and it balloons above the glidepath, so the pilot reduces power. If this is the edge of a microburst, the greatest danger now comes from:
options: A growing headwind that makes the airplane float far down the runway
An updraft in the core that carries the airplane well above the glidepath
Hail falling from the core, which is the main microburst hazard
The downdraft and tailwind that follow, sharply cutting airspeed and lift
questions.explain: An airplane flying through a microburst first meets a performance-increasing headwind, then a strong downdraft, then a performance-decreasing tailwind (AIM Chapter 7, microbursts). A pilot who pulls power for the initial gain is badly placed when the downdraft and tailwind arrive, which is why microbursts cause approach accidents. The headwind is only the first phase, the core is a DOWNdraft, and hail is not the defining microburst hazard.

questions.stem: METAR KNPA 191755Z 18012G20KT 4SM -RA BR SCT006 BKN012 OVC025 21/19 A2998. The ceiling at the field is:
options: 1,200 feet AGL
600 feet AGL
2,500 feet AGL
12,000 feet AGL
questions.explain: A ceiling is the lowest layer reported as broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC), or a vertical visibility; cloud heights in a METAR are in hundreds of feet above ground level (AIM Chapter 7; 14 CFR 1.1). BKN012 = 1,200 feet AGL. SCT006 is scattered, so it does not count as a ceiling; 2,500 feet assumes only overcast layers count; 12,000 feet reads the code in thousands instead of hundreds.

questions.stem: A pilot crosses a ridge whose highest point is 7,600 feet MSL. The altimeter is set to the correct local setting and reads 8,000 feet, but the air is much colder than standard. The actual clearance above the ridge is:
options: More than 400 feet
Less than 400 feet
Exactly 400 feet, since the altimeter setting is correct
Impossible to judge without knowing the airplane's heading
questions.explain: In air colder than standard, the pressure levels sit lower, so the altimeter reads HIGHER than true altitude: 'from high to low (temperature), look out below' (FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 8). The airplane is below 8,000 feet MSL, so it has less than 400 feet over the ridge. 'More than 400' is the warm-air case. A correct altimeter setting removes pressure error but not temperature error, and heading plays no part.

questions.stem: A VFR pilot calls approach control before entering Class C airspace. The controller replies, 'Navy 4AB, stand by.' The pilot:
options: May not enter until hearing 'cleared into the Class C airspace'
May enter, because the controller used the aircraft's call sign
May not enter until a transponder code has been assigned
May enter even if the reply had been just 'Aircraft calling, stand by'
questions.explain: Class C entry requires two-way radio communication, which is established when the controller responds using the aircraft's call sign, even if the reply is 'stand by' (AIM 3-2-4). A reply without the call sign, such as 'aircraft calling, stand by', does NOT establish communication. An explicit clearance is the Class B rule, and a squawk code is not what establishes communication.

questions.stem: A VFR pilot is cruising at 11,500 feet MSL, more than 1,200 feet above the surface, in Class E airspace. Under 14 CFR 91.155, the minimum flight visibility and cloud clearances are:
options: 3 statute miles; 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontally
5 statute miles; 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontally
5 statute miles; 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 1 statute mile horizontally
3 statute miles; 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 1 statute mile horizontally
questions.explain: In Class E airspace more than 1,200 feet above the surface and at or above 10,000 feet MSL, 91.155 requires 5 statute miles visibility and 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 1 statute mile horizontally from clouds. The '3 miles, 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal' set applies BELOW 10,000 feet MSL. The other two options each mix one half of the high-altitude rule with the low-altitude one.

questions.stem: Which type of special use airspace exists to separate certain military training activities from IFR traffic, which ATC may clear through it only if IFR separation can be provided?
options: Military operations area
Alert area
Restricted area
Controlled firing area
questions.explain: The AIM defines a military operations area (MOA) as airspace established to separate certain military training activities from IFR traffic; VFR pilots may fly through without a clearance but should use extreme caution (AIM 3-4-5). An alert area warns of a high volume of pilot training or unusual activity, a restricted area holds hazards such as artillery fire and needs authorization when active, and a controlled firing area is suspended when aircraft approach, so it is not charted for avoidance.

questions.stem: On an IFR flight plan, a pilot loses two-way radio communication while flying in VFR conditions. Under 14 CFR 91.185 and the AIM, the pilot should:
options: Squawk 7700, and continue to the destination at the assigned route and altitude
Squawk 7600, and continue to the destination at the highest of the assigned, minimum or expected altitude
Squawk 7500, and land at the nearest airport with an operating control tower
Squawk 7600, continue the flight under VFR, and land as soon as practicable
questions.explain: Code 7600 signals radio failure (AIM 6-4-1), and 91.185(b) says that if the failure happens in VFR conditions, the pilot continues under VFR and lands as soon as practicable. The 'highest of assigned, MEA or expected altitude' route rule applies only when the pilot is in IMC. Code 7700 is a general emergency and 7500 means unlawful interference.

questions.stem: A runway's centerline lies along a magnetic heading of 047° in one direction. The numbers painted on its two ends are:
options: 4 and 22
6 and 24
5 and 23
5 and 25
questions.explain: A runway number is its magnetic direction rounded to the nearest 10° with the last zero dropped: 047° rounds to 050°, so Runway 5. The opposite end is 047 + 180 = 227°, which rounds to 230°, so Runway 23 (AIM 2-3-3). Check: 23 − 5 = 18 ✓. '4 and 22' truncates instead of rounding, '6 and 24' rounds the wrong way, and '5 and 25' adds 200 instead of 180.

questions.stem: A taxiing pilot sees a sign with a black background, a yellow letter 'B' and a yellow border. The sign tells the pilot:
options: Hold short of Runway B here
The aircraft is on Taxiway B
Taxiway B turns off ahead in the direction shown
Taxiway B is closed ahead
questions.explain: Black with a yellow inscription and border is a LOCATION sign, which names the taxiway or runway the aircraft is on (AIM 2-3-9). Mandatory hold signs are red with white letters, direction signs are yellow with black letters and an arrow, and a closed taxiway is marked with yellow X's, not a black sign.

questions.stem: The airport wind sock is fully extended with its small (tail) end pointing toward the east. Which runway is best aligned for landing?
options: Runway 9
Runway 36
Runway 27
Runway 18
questions.explain: Wind blows into the large end of a wind sock and out the small end, so a tail pointing east means the wind is FROM the west. Pilots land into the wind, heading west, about 270°, which is Runway 27 (FAA-H-8083-25, Airport Operations chapter). Runway 9 lands with a direct tailwind (reading the sock backwards), and Runways 36 and 18 face a direct crosswind.

questions.stem: An airport uses RIGHT traffic for Runway 27. On the downwind leg, an airplane flies a heading of about:
options: 090°, with the runway on its right
090°, with the runway on its left
270°, with the runway on its right
270°, with the runway on its left
questions.explain: Downwind runs parallel to the landing direction but opposite, so for Runway 27 (landing toward 270°) downwind is flown at about 090°. In a right-hand pattern every turn is to the right, so the runway stays on the pilot's right side (AIM 4-3-3). Check: right turn from 090° to base at 180°, then right again to final at 270° ✓. 'Runway on the left' is a standard left pattern, and 270° is the landing direction, not downwind.

questions.stem: In forward flight, a helicopter's advancing blade meets a faster relative wind than the retreating blade. To help equalize lift across the rotor disk, the advancing blade:
options: Flaps down, which reduces its angle of attack
Flaps up, which increases its angle of attack
Flaps down, which increases its angle of attack
Flaps up, which reduces its angle of attack
questions.explain: Blade flapping compensates for dissymmetry of lift: the advancing blade's extra lift makes it rise, and the upward motion changes the relative wind so its angle of attack decreases; the retreating blade flaps down, increasing its angle of attack (FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook, FAA-H-8083-21). Cyclic feathering helps too. 'Flaps down' describes the retreating blade, and an increase in angle of attack on the advancing side would make the imbalance worse.

questions.stem: A US helicopter with a counterclockwise-turning main rotor (seen from above) approaches retreating blade stall at high forward speed. The typical warning signs and correct first response are:
options: Low-frequency vibration, nose pitch-up and a roll to the right; lower the collective
Low-frequency vibration, nose pitch-up and a roll to the left; lower the collective
Low-frequency vibration, nose pitch-up and a roll to the left; push the cyclic forward
High-frequency vibration, nose pitch-down and a roll to the left; raise the collective
questions.explain: Retreating blade stall brings abnormal low-frequency vibration, pitch-up and a roll toward the retreating side, which is the LEFT for a counterclockwise US rotor. Lowering the collective reduces blade angle of attack and is the first correction, followed by reducing airspeed and maneuvering (FAA-H-8083-21). Rolling right puts the retreating side on the wrong side, and forward cyclic adds airspeed and worsens the stall. Raising the collective adds blade pitch and deepens the stall.

questions.stem: Which combination of conditions sets up vortex ring state (settling with power) in a helicopter?
options: High forward airspeed, high gross weight, and low rotor RPM
A near-vertical descent of 300+ fpm, below ETL, with 20 to 100 percent power in use
A fast autorotative descent with the collective fully down and no engine power
A hover in ground effect with a strong crosswind from the right
questions.explain: Vortex ring state needs a near-vertical descent of roughly 300 fpm or more, horizontal speed below ETL, and the rotor using some power (about 20 to 100 percent) without enough left to stop the descent; the rotor then settles into its own downwash (FAA-H-8083-21). High speed with high weight and low RPM sets up RETREATING BLADE STALL. In autorotation the airflow comes up through the rotor, not down, and a crosswind hover in ground effect is not a vortex ring setup.

questions.stem: During a slope takeoff, one of a helicopter's skids stays on the ground and the helicopter begins rolling about that skid. The most effective way to stop the roll is to:
options: Raise the collective quickly to lift the skid clear
Apply full cyclic opposite the roll and hold it
Smoothly and moderately lower the collective
Apply full pedal in the direction of the roll
questions.explain: In dynamic rollover the rotor thrust is rolling the helicopter about the skid that is touching the ground, so smoothly reducing collective cuts that thrust and is the most effective recovery (FAA-H-8083-21). Raising collective adds thrust and speeds the roll, cyclic loses authority once the critical rollover angle is approached, and pedal does not counter a roll about a skid.

questions.stem: A helicopter with a fully articulated rotor touches down hard on one side, and a rapidly growing rocking oscillation starts. Rotor RPM is in the normal operating range. The pilot should:
options: Lift off to a hover
Close the throttle and lower the collective fully
Stay on the ground and wait for the dampers to stop the oscillation
Apply cyclic opposite each rock to damp the motion
questions.explain: Ground resonance is a self-feeding oscillation set up when the rotor blades are thrown out of phase while the helicopter sits on its landing gear. With rotor RPM in the normal range, the fix is to fly off the ground so the blades rephase themselves; closing the throttle and lowering the collective is the action only when RPM is LOW (FAA-H-8083-21). Waiting lets the oscillation destroy the helicopter in seconds, and cyclic inputs on the ground cannot keep up with it.

questions.stem: A carrier is planning a daytime recovery. In the carrier control zone the ceiling is 2,000 feet and visibility is 8 nautical miles. Under CV NATOPS fixed-wing weather criteria, which recovery will be flown?
options: Case I, because visibility is better than 5 nautical miles
Case II, letting aircraft descend through cloud to a visual pattern
Case III, because the ceiling is below 3,000 feet
Case III, because any cloud layer requires an instrument approach
questions.explain: CV NATOPS (NAVAIR 00-80T-105): Case I needs a ceiling of at least 3,000 feet and 5 nm visibility; Case II needs at least 1,000 feet and 5 nm, for when aircraft may meet cloud on the way down to the visual pattern; Case III applies below 1,000 feet or 5 nm, and at night. A 2,000-foot ceiling with 8 nm visibility misses Case I only on ceiling, so it is Case II. 'Case I' ignores the ceiling minimum, and both Case III options put the cutoff at 3,000 feet or any cloud, when Case III starts below 1,000 feet.

questions.stem: On final approach to a carrier, the pilot has a centered ball, is on centerline and is on speed when the flashing red lights on both sides of the optical landing system's lens come on. The pilot should:
options: Climb back up to the glide slope, since the red lights mean the aircraft is low
Touch down and go to full power at once, as for a bolter
Hold the glide path and wait for the LSO to explain by radio
Add power and climb away without touching down
questions.explain: Flashing red lights on both sides of the lens are the wave-off lights, an order from the LSO (often because the deck is foul) that the pilot must obey at once, however good the approach looks. A dangerously low aircraft is shown by the ball itself turning red, not by the side lights, so correcting to the glide slope misreads the signal. Going to full power on touchdown is the normal arrested-landing technique, but a wave-off means not touching down at all. Waiting for a radio call treats a mandatory signal as advice.

questions.stem: About three-quarters of a mile behind the carrier, a pilot calls '204, Rhino ball, 5.2.' The '5.2' tells the LSO the aircraft's:
options: Gross weight, 52,000 pounds
Glide-slope angle, 5.2 degrees
Height above the water, 520 feet
Fuel state, 5,200 pounds
questions.explain: The ball call gives the side number, the aircraft type ('Rhino' = F/A-18E/F Super Hornet), 'ball' to confirm the pilot sees the meatball, and the fuel state in thousands of pounds, so 5.2 = 5,200 pounds. The LSO answers 'Roger ball.' Fuel tells the LSO and the Air Boss how many more passes the pilot can afford. Gross weight and height are not part of the call, and a carrier glide slope is only about 3 to 4 degrees.

questions.stem: During a night Case III recovery, which carrier agency controls each aircraft from marshal down the approach until the pilot calls the ball at about three-quarters of a mile?
options: Carrier Air Traffic Control Center (CATCC)
Primary Flight Control (Pri-Fly)
Flight Deck Control (the handler)
Combat Information Center (CIC)
questions.explain: In Case III, aircraft fly instrument approaches under CATCC's marshal, approach and final controllers until the ball call, when the LSO takes over for the last part. Pri-Fly, run by the Air Boss, controls aircraft visually in the carrier control zone during Case I and II. Flight Deck Control, run by the aircraft handling officer, moves and parks aircraft on deck, and CIC manages the tactical picture, not the recovery.

questions.stem: During daytime Case I flight operations, which officer controls the launch and recovery of aircraft and all aircraft flying visually in the carrier control zone?
options: The aircraft handling officer, known as the handler
The air officer, known as the Air Boss
The air operations officer in CATCC
The landing signal officer (LSO)
questions.explain: The Air Boss, helped by the assistant air officer (the Mini Boss), runs Primary Flight Control, the carrier's control tower, and controls flight-deck launches and recoveries and every aircraft flying visually in the carrier control zone (about 5 nm around the ship, up to 2,500 feet) in Case I and II. The handler moves and spots aircraft from Flight Deck Control; CATCC's air operations officer runs radar control outside the zone and in Case III; the LSO controls only the final approach and landing.

questions.stem: Which flight-deck jersey color is correctly matched with the job?
options: Blue: arresting-gear crew
White: aircraft handling officer
Green: chock-and-chain runner
Brown: squadron plane captain
questions.explain: Per navy.mil's flight-deck color guide, brown shirts are the air wing's plane captains, who prepare and look after their squadron's aircraft. Arresting-gear and catapult crews wear green; aircraft handling officers and plane directors wear yellow; chock-and-chain crews, tractor drivers and elevator operators wear blue.

questions.stem: A Nimitz-class carrier moves aircraft between the hangar deck and the flight deck using:
options: Four deck-edge elevators, two to starboard and two to port
Three deck-edge elevators, two to starboard and one to port
Four deck-edge elevators, three to starboard and one to port
Two centerline elevators and two deck-edge elevators to starboard
questions.explain: A Nimitz-class carrier has four deck-edge elevators: two forward of the island and one aft of it on the starboard side, and one on the port side aft. Putting elevators on the deck edge, rather than on the centerline as on WWII-era carriers, keeps the flight deck usable while they move. Three elevators (two starboard, one port) describes the newer Ford class, and two-and-two is not a Nimitz layout.

questions.stem: On the catapult at night, how does a pilot tell the catapult officer that the aircraft is at launch power and ready to go?
options: By switching the exterior lights on
By saluting the catapult officer
By flashing the landing light twice
By calling 'ready' on the radio
questions.explain: By day the pilot salutes the shooter, but a salute cannot be seen at night, so the pilot switches the exterior (navigation) lights on steady instead, and the shooter takes that as the ready signal. That is why the lights stay off until the pilot is ready. A salute is the daytime signal, flashing a landing light is not a launch signal, and the readiness signal is visual, not a radio call.

questions.stem: A ship sets material condition ZEBRA. Which damage-control fittings are closed?
options: Only the fittings marked Z
The fittings marked Y and Z only
The fittings marked X and Z only
All fittings marked X, Y or Z
questions.explain: Material conditions build on each other (Naval Orientation, NAVEDTRA 12966). X-RAY, the least protective, closes X fittings; YOKE, normally set at sea and in port in wartime, closes X and Y; ZEBRA, set for general quarters and maximum watertight integrity, closes X, Y and Z. 'Only Z' and 'Y and Z' forget that each higher condition keeps the lower ones set, and 'X and Z' skips YOKE.

questions.stem: During the afternoon watch (1200 to 1600), how many bells are struck at 1430?
options: Five bells
Two bells
Six bells
Three bells
questions.explain: One bell is added for each half hour of a four-hour watch, ending at eight bells. 1230 = one, 1300 = two, 1330 = three, 1400 = four, 1430 = five bells. Two comes from the clock hour (2:30 p.m.); six counts 1200 as one bell, but 1200 is eight bells, ending the forenoon watch; three is the 1330 count.

questions.stem: Using Navy compartment numbers (deck-frame-position-use), which compartment is ABOVE the main deck and FARTHEST FORWARD?
questions.explain: Levels above the main deck are numbered 01, 02 and so on; 1 is the main deck itself, and 2, 3 and lower are below it. Frame numbers run from bow to stern, so a lower frame number is farther forward. Of the two compartments above the main deck, 01-75 sits at a lower frame than 02-140, so it is farther forward. 2-60 is farther forward but one deck below the main deck, and 1-75 is on the main deck, not above it.

questions.stem: Navy compartment 4-110-0-M is a:
options: Machinery space
Magazine (ammunition stowage)
Medical treatment space
Messing space
questions.explain: The final letter shows how the space is used, and M means ammunition, so this is a magazine on the fourth deck, at frame 110, on the centerline (0). Machinery and engineering spaces use E. Sick bay and messing spaces are both living spaces and use L, so neither has an M code.

questions.stem: A ship steams due north along a meridian from latitude 10°15'N to 12°45'N at 15 knots. How long does the passage take?
options: 9 hours 12 minutes
11 hours 30 minutes
10 hours
16 hours 40 minutes
questions.explain: Along a meridian, one minute of latitude is one nautical mile. 12°45' minus 10°15' = 2°30' = 150 minutes = 150 nm, and at 15 knots (15 nm per hour) that takes 150 ÷ 15 = 10 hours. 9 h 12 min treats 2°30' as 2.30° (138 minutes); 11 h 30 min wrongly converts to about 172.5 statute miles; 16 h 40 min treats a degree as 100 minutes. Check: 15 × 10 = 150 ✓

questions.stem: Two ships are both at latitude 60°N and 60 minutes of longitude apart. The distance between them along that parallel is about:
options: 60 nautical miles
120 nautical miles
52 nautical miles
30 nautical miles
questions.explain: Only a minute of LATITUDE is always about 1 nm. Meridians converge toward the poles, so a minute of longitude is worth cos(latitude) nm: cos 60° = 0.5, so 60 × 0.5 = 30 nm. 60 nm treats longitude like latitude, 120 nm divides by the cosine instead of multiplying, and 52 nm uses sin 60° (about 0.87).

questions.stem: A ship's true course is 090°. Variation is 10°W, and the steering compass has 2°E deviation on this heading. What compass course should the helmsman steer?
questions.explain: Working from true toward compass (True, Variation, Magnetic, Deviation, Compass), add westerly errors and subtract easterly ones. Magnetic = 090° + 10° (W) = 100°; compass = 100° − 2° (E) = 098°. 078° applies both corrections backwards, 102° adds the easterly deviation, and 082° subtracts the westerly variation while adding the deviation.

questions.stem: A lookout reports a contact bearing 225° relative. The contact is:
options: Broad on the starboard quarter
Broad on the port quarter
Broad on the port bow
On the port beam
questions.explain: Relative bearings are measured clockwise from the ship's bow: 000° dead ahead, 090° starboard beam, 180° dead astern, 270° port beam. 225° is halfway between dead astern and the port beam, which is broad on the port quarter. The starboard quarter is 135°, the port bow is 315°, and the port beam is exactly 270°.

questions.stem: In restricted visibility, your power-driven vessel is underway but has stopped its engines and is making no way through the water. Under Rule 35, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes, you sound:
options: One prolonged blast
Two prolonged blasts, about 2 seconds apart
One prolonged blast followed by two short blasts
Rapid ringing of the bell for about 5 seconds
questions.explain: Under Rule 3 a vessel that is not anchored, made fast or aground is underway even when stopped, and Rule 35(b) gives a power-driven vessel underway but making no way two prolonged blasts about 2 seconds apart. One prolonged blast is for a vessel making way (35(a)); prolonged-short-short is for vessels such as those not under command or restricted in their ability to maneuver (35(c)); ringing the bell is the signal for a vessel at anchor (35(g)).

questions.stem: At night you see three all-round lights in a vertical line: red over white over red. Under the COLREGs, this vessel is:
options: Not under command
Restricted in her ability to maneuver
Constrained by her draft
Aground
questions.explain: Rule 27(b): red-white-red all-round lights (by day, ball-diamond-ball) mark a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, which Rule 3 says includes one replenishing underway or launching and recovering aircraft. Not under command shows two all-round red lights (Rule 27(a)); a vessel constrained by her draft may show three all-round red lights (Rule 28); a vessel aground shows anchor lights plus two all-round red lights (Rule 30).

questions.stem: A sailing vessel is overtaking a power-driven vessel in open water. Under the COLREGs, which vessel must keep out of the way?
options: The power-driven vessel, because power gives way to sail
Whichever vessel has the other on its starboard side
Both, each altering course to starboard
The sailing vessel, because it is overtaking
questions.explain: Rule 13 says an overtaking vessel must keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken 'notwithstanding' the other steering rules, so the overtaking sailboat keeps clear. 'Power gives way to sail' (Rule 18) is real but is overridden by Rule 13. The starboard-side test is the crossing rule for two power-driven vessels (Rule 15), and both turning to starboard is the head-on rule (Rule 14).

questions.stem: You are the stand-on power-driven vessel in a crossing situation, and the give-way vessel, on your port side, is clearly not taking action. If you now maneuver to avoid a collision, Rule 17 says you should, if the circumstances allow, NOT:
options: Alter course to port
Alter course to starboard
Reduce speed or stop
Sound five or more short blasts
questions.explain: Rule 17(a)(ii) lets the stand-on vessel act once it is apparent the give-way vessel is not, and Rule 17(c) adds that a power-driven vessel doing so in a crossing situation shall not, if circumstances allow, alter course to port for a vessel on her own port side, because a late turn to starboard by the give-way vessel would then bring the two together. Turning to starboard and slowing are allowed, and five or more short blasts is the doubt signal the stand-on vessel should sound (Rule 34(d)).

questions.stem: Outside US waters you sight an IALA cardinal mark painted black above yellow, with a topmark of two black cones both pointing up. The safest water lies:
options: To the south of the mark
To the east of the mark
To the north of the mark
On any side; it marks an isolated danger
questions.explain: A cardinal mark is named for the side of the danger on which you should pass. A north cardinal has both cones pointing up (north), and the black band is on the end the cones point to, so black is on top: pass north of it. A south cardinal has cones pointing down and yellow over black; an east cardinal has its cones base to base. An isolated danger mark is black with red bands and two black balls. The US lateral system does not use cardinal marks, but IALA waters do.

questions.stem: Returning from sea in US waters, you reach a channel junction marked by a buoy with red and green horizontal bands, the TOPMOST band red. To stay in the preferred channel, you keep the buoy:
options: On your port side
On either side, since both channels are equal
On your starboard side
On the same side you would keep a green buoy
questions.explain: On a preferred-channel mark, the color of the top band tells you how to treat it for the preferred (main) channel. Top band red means treat it as a red mark, and 'red, right, returning' puts it on your starboard side. Keeping it to port, as you would a green buoy, follows the secondary channel, and 'either side' describes a safe-water mark, not a junction. Preferred-channel marks are lettered, not numbered.

questions.stem: At night a buoy in US waters shows a white light flashing Morse code 'A' (a short flash followed by a long flash). It is a:
options: Isolated danger mark
Preferred-channel mark
Safe-water mark
Special mark
questions.explain: In the US Aids to Navigation System, safe-water marks (red and white vertical stripes, red spherical topmark) show a white Morse 'A' light. Isolated danger marks show a white group-flashing (2) light; preferred-channel marks show composite group-flashing (2+1) in red or green; special marks show yellow lights.

questions.stem: Which pair holds the SAME pay grade?
options: Navy captain and Marine Corps captain
Navy chief petty officer and Marine staff sergeant
Navy lieutenant and Marine Corps captain
Navy lieutenant commander and Marine lieutenant colonel
questions.explain: A Navy lieutenant and a Marine captain are both O-3 and wear two silver bars. A Navy captain is O-6, equal to a Marine colonel; a chief petty officer is E-7, equal to a gunnery sergeant (a staff sergeant is E-6); a lieutenant commander is O-4, equal to a Marine major.

questions.stem: A Navy officer's service dress blue sleeves carry three gold stripes of equal width. The equivalent Marine Corps rank is:
options: Lieutenant colonel
Major
Colonel
Captain
questions.explain: Three equal stripes mark a Navy commander (O-5), whose Marine Corps equivalent is a lieutenant colonel; both wear a silver oak leaf. A major (O-4) matches a lieutenant commander, who wears two and a half stripes; a colonel (O-6) matches a Navy captain, who wears four; and a Marine captain is only O-3, the equal of a Navy lieutenant with two stripes, a mix-up caused by the shared title.

questions.stem: Which Navy squadron designation is correctly matched with the aircraft it flies?
options: VAW: P-8A Poseidon
VAQ: EA-18G Growler
HSC: MH-60R Seahawk
VP: E-2D Hawkeye
questions.explain: VAQ (electronic attack) squadrons fly the EA-18G Growler. VAW (carrier airborne early warning) squadrons fly the E-2D Hawkeye, VP (patrol) squadrons fly the P-8A Poseidon, and HSC (helicopter sea combat) squadrons fly the MH-60S; the MH-60R belongs to HSM squadrons.

questions.stem: Under the DoD aircraft designation system, what do the letters M and R mean in 'MH-60R'?
options: M = maritime (basic mission); R = reconnaissance
M = Marine Corps (operator); R = rescue
M = multimission (modified mission); R = reconnaissance
M = multimission (modified mission); R = series
questions.explain: A designation reads modified mission, basic mission, vehicle type, design number, then series (DoD 4120.15-L). In MH-60R, M is the multimission modified mission, H is the vehicle type (helicopter), 60 is the design number, and R is the series letter marking one version of the H-60. R means reconnaissance only when it appears in a mission position, before the dash; designations never name the operating service, and there is no 'maritime' mission letter.

questions.stem: Which two aircraft BOTH carry the vehicle-type symbol V (VTOL/STOL) in their DoD designations?
options: F-35B Lightning II and AV-8B Harrier II
MV-22B Osprey and MH-60S Seahawk
AV-8B Harrier II and MV-22B Osprey
F-35B Lightning II and MV-22B Osprey
questions.explain: In AV-8B, A is the attack basic mission and V is the VTOL/STOL vehicle type; in MV-22B, M is multimission and V is VTOL/STOL. The F-35B is a short-takeoff, vertical-landing jet, but its designation is just F (fighter) with variant letter B, so it carries no V. In MH-60S, the H marks a helicopter.

questions.stem: The carrier onboard delivery (COD) squadrons that fly the CMV-22B Osprey are designated:
options: VRC
VMM
HSC
VRM
questions.explain: Fleet Logistics Multi-Mission squadrons (VRM), such as VRM-30, fly the CMV-22B and are taking over the COD role from the C-2A Greyhound. VRC is the designation of the Greyhound squadrons; VMM is a Marine medium tiltrotor squadron flying the MV-22B; HSC squadrons fly MH-60S helicopters.

questions.stem: The Navy rating ABE operates and maintains:
options: Catapults, arresting gear and barricades
Jet engines and their accessories
Aviation fuel systems and fuel lines
Aircraft handling and crash-rescue gear
questions.explain: Aviation Boatswain's Mates come in three types: ABE (Equipment) run catapults, arresting gear, barricades and visual landing aids; ABF (Fuels) handle aviation fuel; ABH (Handling) move aircraft and fight flight-deck crashes and fires. Jet engines belong to the Aviation Machinist's Mate (AD).

questions.stem: Fought while US forces were invading Saipan, which carrier battle saw Japanese carrier air groups lose hundreds of aircraft in a single day of air combat?
options: The Battle of Leyte Gulf
The Battle of the Philippine Sea
The Battle of Midway
The Battle of the Eastern Solomons
questions.explain: The Battle of the Philippine Sea (19 to 20 June 1944) was fought to cover the Marianas landings that began on Saipan on 15 June, and its first day of lopsided air combat became known as the 'Great Marianas Turkey Shoot' (NHHC). Leyte Gulf came four months later, in October 1944, covering the Philippine landings; Midway was also fought in June, but in 1942, and its decisive losses were four Japanese carriers; the Eastern Solomons (August 1942) was a carrier battle of the Guadalcanal campaign.

questions.stem: In February 1974, who became the first woman designated a US Naval Aviator?
options: Barbara Allen (later Rainey)
Rosemary Bryant (later Mariner)
Kara Hultgreen
Grace Hopper
questions.explain: LTJG Barbara Allen Rainey received her wings on 22 February 1974 (NHHC). Rosemary Mariner, from the same first group of women in flight training, earned her wings a few months later and went on to command an operational aviation squadron. Kara Hultgreen was one of the first women to fly the F-14 Tomcat in the 1990s, and Grace Hopper was a computing pioneer, not an aviator.

questions.stem: Which carrier, modified in 1952, was the first US carrier with an angled flight deck?
options: USS Antietam (CV-36)
USS Forrestal (CV-59)
USS Hancock (CV-19)
USS Midway (CVB-41)
questions.explain: Antietam was given an experimental angled deck in 1952 and proved the British idea in US service (NHHC). Forrestal (1955) was the first US carrier designed and built with an angled deck; Hancock is known for the first US steam-catapult launch (1954); Midway received its angled deck in a later 1950s modernization.

questions.stem: In 1964's Operation Sea Orbit, a three-ship task force sailed around the world without taking on fuel. Its aircraft carrier was:
options: USS Enterprise
USS Nimitz
USS Dwight D. Eisenhower
USS Carl Vinson
questions.explain: Enterprise (CVAN-65), commissioned in 1961, remained the Navy's only nuclear-powered carrier until Nimitz joined the fleet, and in 1964 she sailed with the nuclear-powered cruiser Long Beach and frigate Bainbridge as Task Force One around the globe without refueling (NHHC). Nimitz was not commissioned until 1975, Dwight D. Eisenhower until 1977 and Carl Vinson until 1982, so none existed in 1964.

questions.stem: During the Korean War, Lt. (j.g.) Thomas Hudner received the Medal of Honor for:
options: Scoring the Navy's first jet-versus-jet aerial victory
Leading the torpedo strike that breached the Hwachon Dam
Landing a burning Panther jet aboard a carrier at night
Crash-landing his Corsair to try to save a downed wingman
questions.explain: On 4 December 1950, near the Chosin Reservoir, Hudner deliberately crash-landed his F4U Corsair beside the downed Ensign Jesse L. Brown, the Navy's first African American naval aviator, and tried to free him from the wreck. The Navy's first jet kill was scored by LCDR William Amen in an F9F Panther in November 1950, and the Hwachon Dam was hit with torpedoes by AD Skyraiders in 1951.

questions.stem: Which list puts three jets flown by the Blue Angels in the order the team flew them, earliest first?
options: F11F Tiger, A-4F Skyhawk II, F-4J Phantom II
F-4J Phantom II, F11F Tiger, A-4F Skyhawk II
A-4F Skyhawk II, F11F Tiger, F-4J Phantom II
F11F Tiger, F-4J Phantom II, A-4F Skyhawk II
questions.explain: The Blue Angels flew the F11F Tiger from 1957 to 1969, the F-4J Phantom II from 1969 to 1974 and the A-4F Skyhawk II from 1974 to 1986, before the F/A-18 Hornet (1986 to 2020) and the Super Hornet (from 2021). Putting the Skyhawk before the Phantom follows the order the two designs first flew, not the order the team used them; the other two lists misplace the Tiger, the earliest of the three.

questions.stem: In May 1919 the Navy flying boat NC-4, commanded by Lt. Cmdr. Albert C. Read, became the first aircraft to:
options: Fly nonstop across the Atlantic
Fly across the Atlantic Ocean
Fly from California to Hawaii
Launch by catapult from a ship
questions.explain: NC-4 crossed in stages from Newfoundland by way of the Azores to Lisbon, arriving 27 May 1919 to complete the first transatlantic flight, then flew on to Plymouth, England (NHHC). The first NONSTOP crossing came weeks later, by Alcock and Brown in June 1919. A Navy PN-9 attempt to reach Hawaii in 1925 ran out of fuel short of the islands, and the first catapult launch from a ship came in 1915.
